The public did not take kindly to the idea of being filmed (even though, yes, smartphones with cameras had long existed). A former colleague of mine was even assaulted in a San Francisco bar while wearing them. Meta has been re-testing the waters with its AI smart glasses. Meta's have proved far more popular than Google Glass thanks to AI, their more traditional look, and list of genuinely useful features. (Meta's ad that aired during the US Open — where a woman records the back-and-forth of a tennis rally by moving her head, while the crowd around her films on their phones — was particularly effective at pointing out how they can help you stay in the moment.) But Meta is still hitting the same wall of uneasiness that Google experienced more than a decade ago. Now, there are signs that Meta is cooking up a simpler, but likely less controversial product. The Information reported this week that Meta is working on a camera-free variant of its AI glasses, though there's no sign that the company is throwing in the towel on camera glasses. The idea is that customers would just have more choices. (Meta declined to comment on the report when contacted by Business Insider.) I think it's a good idea, and one I'm sure Meta considered years ago, back when they were first mapping out what their smart glasses would look like, and which tech to include. Mark Zuckerberg was no stranger to the Google Glass debacle. But Meta decided to roll the dice with cameras when its glasses first went to market, and in many ways that's paid off. Sales have boomed in recent years, but so has the backlash, both of which Business Insider has reported on extensively. With AI glasses, sometimes less is more A camera-free design means trade-offs. It means no visual identification of what you're looking at (sorry, tourists), and a lot of compelling features go out the door. Say goodbye to recording that tennis bout without your phone. But in return, there's the opportunity to side-step a lot of IRL controversy, too. It's easy to suggest Meta should have done this out of the gate, but it's important to remember that Amazon did exactly that with its Echo Frame smart glasses, which plugged into Alexa, before the first pair of Meta Ray-Bans ever launched. Alexa was pretty bad back then (it's gotten better after Amazon's big AI overhaul), and you probably have never heard of Echo Frames. Meta is the clear market leader in the smart glasses category. In many ways, that early bet paid off. Introducing a camera-free version still offers compelling use cases. People love listening to music on smart glasses, since it's less isolating than putting in earbuds. You can still ask AI questions without taking out your phone. No cameras also undoubtedly means a sleeker design. But I'd argue they'll still inherit the baggage of Meta's camera glasses. That's a much harder reputational genie to put back into the bottle. Meta is certainly trying, rolling out a PR campaign and doing some legitimately creative things to fight back against bad actors using its glasses to be creepy (though Business Insider has reported that its crackdown on harassing videos recorded surreptitiously on its glasses is off to a bumpy start). Shaking the "pervert glasses" rep isn't going to be easy. Meta would be hedging its bets by introducing a camera-free model, five years after launching its first smart glasses. That's not altogether surprising, as the company offers various configurations of wearables with different levels of tech crammed inside (you can buy the pricier Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, which are bulkier but include an integrated screen). Selling a camera-free model could prove a savvy move to tap into a new customer base that isn't willing to risk a stranger grilling them about whether they're recording. Social norms change. People balked at bringing Jeff Bezos into their bedroom with an always-listening Alexa. Amazon has since sold over half a billion Alexa-enabled devices. Even the famously privacy-focused Apple is now dipping its toe into always-listening territory with its controversial new Apple Watch features. Will people en masse ever be comfortable with camera glasses? It's entirely possible. Google was met with a resounding "no" 12 years ago. Meta has pushed the needle to "maybe" — but it makes sense to cater to the "no" crowd, too.

item.title: This tech founder says prompting AI agents is a lot like managing people
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.34
The best managers of AI agents may be people who have already managed humans, one AI founder said. Ivan Burazin, the cofounder and CEO of New York-based AI firm Daytona, has a team of about 30 people across teams in the US and Europe. He told Business Insider that in recent months, he's pushed his staff to build more AI agents; his 16 engineers each run an average of five agents, and no one at the company writes code anymore. That's brought one thing to light for him: Staff who have managed others are way better at prompting AI agents to get exactly what they want than those with no people-management experience. "We've found that people who manage people and understand how to communicate what they want — inputs versus outputs — they're much better at running agents," he said. On the other hand, an engineer who's not managed anyone, even if they're great at their job, is wired like an individual contributor, Ivan said. He said they implicitly expect that people — and agents — will understand what they're asking for, and get stressed and frustrated when it doesn't pan out. "And so they never think about how to communicate, 'This is what I want. This is how I expect you to do it, or what I think the outcome should be,'" he added. That said, Burazin doesn't support the idea of people managers alone. He said managers with no technical knowledge — such as in marketing or in engineering — are not useful, and everyone should be getting their hands dirty with actual work. Burazin and his cofounders, Vedran Jukić and Goran Draganić, founded Daytona in 2023, which provides secure sandbox infrastructure for companies to run AI agents and AI-generated code in isolated environments. The company recently raised $48 million in a Series B funding round, according to Crunchbase. Burazin's comments align with how managerial roles in tech companies have changed in recent years. After an era dubbed "The Great Flattening," in which companies like Meta, Amazon, and Google laid off middle management for efficiency, more tech leaders are now juggling coding and product development alongside staff management. Burazin says he supports his staff running multiple AI agents, because it helps him keep his team small. Hiring at Daytona is "very slow," he said, because each new hire adds a layer of complexity. "Agents help with that because you can have smaller human teams, hence the communication is smaller, and you can continue to be fast," he said.

item.title: Ed Sheeran resale ticket prices slide as the Macklemore fallout grows
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.11
Ed Sheeran's resale ticket market is going red. Ticket prices for Sheeran's LOOP Tour have been slipping on resale markets, according to the site Ticketdata. Of his next 10 dates, nine have seen price decreases in the last three days, the site showed. Sheeran has been caught up in controversy since Macklemore was removed from the tour following his comments about the Palestinian territories at two concerts earlier this month. Macklemore said he was forced out by billionaire Robert Kraft. Sheeran said the decision wasn't his, and instead blamed the tour's promoter. Sheeran's tours are some of the biggest in the music business. His Mathematics Tour, which ran from 2022 to 2025, grossed over $875 million, making it the fourth-highest grossing tour of all time when it finished, behind tours by Taylor Swift, Elton John, and Coldplay, according to Billboard. Sheeran's resale ticket price slip Want a ticket to Sheeran's Saturday show in Philadelphia? The resale ticket price is down 17% in the last three days, according to Ticketdata. The Philadelphia ticket decrease widens to 25% over a seven-day period, the site found. Resale prices for Sheeran's two performances at Massachusetts' Gillette Stadium are down over three days, the site found, as were tickets for upcoming performances in Atlanta, Charlotte, Arlington, and the Florida cities of Hollywood and Tampa. Only one city had positive three-day price changes, according to Ticketdata: Indianapolis. A representative for Sheeran did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The Macklemore controversy When Macklemore was booted from Sheeran's tour, he pointed the finger at Robert Kraft. Earlier in September, Macklemore gave speeches at two concerts at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, saying "Free Palestine" and that he wanted the people in Gaza to know that "we have not forgotten about them." Macklemore was later removed from Sheeran's tour. In an Instagram post, he said that Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, rallied other stadium owners to oppose his performance. Kraft confirmed in a statement to local outlet WHDH that Macklemore was blocked from performing at Gillette Stadium, which he owns. His venue does not "provide a platform for hate speech," Kraft wrote. Sheeran released his own statement on Tuesday, saying the decision to remove Macklemore was made by his tour promoter in response to threats from the stadium venues. Sheeran also said that he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine." The fallout has continued to grow, with Sheeran's band and three openers pulling out of the tour later on Tuesday.

item.title: AI researcher whose apocalypse warning went viral outlines his disagreements with Anthropic leadership
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.10
Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon detailed his disagreements with the AI giant during a Tuesday AMA on X. "If the race is inevitable you should not contribute," Coxon wrote. Coxon said that Anthropic leadership is wrong to follow a "consequentialist philosophy" about why it needs to participate in pushing the frontier of AI research. Specifically, Coxon called out Anthropic's push for RSI, or recursive self-improvement, the process by which AI models could improve themselves and build their own successors. "They largely initiated the recent race to RSI, because of a belief in its inevitability," Coxon wrote. "Note that OpenAI had to shed a bunch of dead weight like Sora because Anthropic was going for the jugular." 0. The core disagreement was about the inevitability of a race 1. I think leadership is way too paranoid about China and the US government. They don’t believe it will be possible to negotiate. 2. They largely initiated the recent race to RSI, because of a belief in its… Coxon's profile exploded last week after he published an explanation for his resignation from Anthropic, which he joined following his time at OpenAI. Coxon said that neither lab was following the best course. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon wrote in his resignation announcement. Coxon also warned that internally, AI workers are concerned about whether the technology they are building will turn on humanity. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," Coxon wrote. "This is not a marketing stunt." On Tuesday, Coxon also said that Anthropic's leadership is "way too paranoid about China and the US government." "They don't believe it will be possible to negotiate," he wrote. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has repeatedly expressed uneasiness about how other AI companies might approach safety if Anthropic is the only frontier lab to slow down. "If we go too slow, I still believe that the wrong people will be in charge of the technology," Amodei recently told CNN's Anderson Cooper. "And that, again, will bring the probability of things going wrong very high." In addition to other companies, Amodei has expressed concerns about what would happen if authoritarian governments win the AI race. For his part, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently told Time Magazine that the company "fell behind where we wanted to be." As part of a refocus on its core mission, OpenAI sunsetted projects like Sora, its TikTok-esque video app. In recent days, AI leaders have tried to band together to discuss ways to slow the pace of development. Over the weekend, Amodei published a call for frontier companies like Anthropic "to pace" their advancements and to use the time to focus on AI safety issues like alignment, the work to make sure AI models comply with their instructions. "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain." Altman, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis all expressed agreement with Amodei's broader point. Other parts of the AMA were more lighthearted. One user asked about Coxon's relatively short time at Anthropic, a point his critics have tried to use to undermine his claims. "Which month was your favorite at Anthropic? Month 1 or month 2?" the user asked. Coxon replied, "Month 2 (of 4)."

item.title: A detailed look at the '60 Minutes' ratings drop shows the problem facing Bari Weiss
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.97
What does the drop in viewers for the "60 Minutes" season premiere mean for CBS News' top editor, Bari Weiss? A look at the granular ratings data provides some clues. Viewership for the first "60 Minutes" episode led by new producer Nick Bilton, who was handpicked by Weiss in May, fell 20% from 2025's season debut. An average of just under 8 million people watched the newscast, versus over 10 million last September. The question: Did people start watching and then give up, or did they simply not switch the program on in the first place? Data from Nielsen shows it was the latter. "60 Minutes" retained its audience for Sunday's opener at a rate similar to last fall's debut, according to data obtained by Business Insider. The audience for Sunday's broadcast shrank 7.6% after the first 15 minutes, compared to 17% for last year's season debut. Each premiere lost about 47% of its audience from start to finish, the data shows. Bilton's debut episode featured interviews with the US Air Force pilot who got shot down in Iran, Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay, and the "pardon brokers" who persuade wealthy clients to hire them based on a supposed skill at securing presidential pardons. It's common for TV shows to lose viewers over the course of an episode, especially news programs like "60 Minutes." The takeaway for Weiss and crew: The audience didn't revolt after sampling the new-look season. The problem is that they didn't want to watch it. So, what's going on? There are a few potential factors, and the ratings for the rest of the season will give the media world more insight. First, "60 Minutes" has undergone high-profile — and high-drama — changes under Bilton and Weiss, from new graphics to the dramatic departure of four correspondents: Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, and Anderson Cooper. CBS fired Pelley, who grilled his new boss in front of his colleagues about his qualifications, personnel moves, and what he described as Weiss' "murdering" the "60 Minutes" program. Several former CBS News and "60 Minutes" staffers have accused Weiss of being politically biased, which the former New York Times editor has denied. One theory is that audiences stayed away because of the controversies. Then there's the other big issue: The NFL. The NFL can assist "60 Minutes" by providing a lead-in from the Sunday afternoon games, though the boost wasn't as strong this year. Viewership for the NFL window leading into Sunday's "60 Minutes" debut, featuring the Minnesota Vikings vs the Green Bay Packers for most of the country, was down over 20% from the comparable game last year — a marquee matchup between the Baltimore Ravens and Patrick Mahomes-led Kansas City Chiefs. CBS highlighted viewership of "60 Minutes" clips online and across social media, which it said generated about three times the reach of last year's premiere. The rest of the "60 Minutes" season will show if Weiss and Bilton can claw back those TV viewers, or whether their problems are a lot bigger than the NFL.

item.title: Tom Cruise, 64, says he saw himself as the ‘CEO’ of his life early on
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.53
Tom Cruise, 64, said it was his childhood dream to make movies, and he worked hard to make that dream a reality. Speaking to GQ in an interview published Tuesday, Cruise said he would map out the skills he needed to make films, breaking each one into actionable tasks. "What I did was write goals," Cruise said. "Still, it's like you're looking at something, you write a goal, and then you write underneath, what are those things you need to learn to be able to accomplish those goals?" The "Mission: Impossible" star said he would learn new skills and apply them in his own work. He would also study how other movies use camera placement, lenses, lighting, and set architecture. Cruise said he was passionate about filmmaking even as a teenager, but stopped sharing his ambitions because some of the adults around him dismissed him as "a little kid." "But I never let go of it, and I understood very early on, this is for me," Cruise said. "I'm a CEO of my life, I know the dreams that I want," Cruise said. "I want to see what those people are like in those different countries. What is it like that language? What are they saying? What's it like hearing that? And movies for me were an in." Cruise said he is a "hard worker" and felt he "could outwork anyone." Even now, when he's not on a movie set, he's preparing for the next project. He added that his career moves, including filming in locations like Prague and China and working with Ridley Scott in England, were "not happenstance." "I would see those doors that open. I'm going, 'here's an opportunity,'" Cruise said. He said his work ethic extends to collaborators, and he is upfront about the high standards he expects. "The rumors are true," he added. Getting older also hasn't changed his ambitions or his appetite for taking on new challenges. "Life, I'm coming right at it," he said. "You know what I mean? It's coming at me, and I'm coming right at it." After more than four decades in entertainment, Cruise remains one of Hollywood's most sought-after stars. In 2023, he told Business Insider that he was "always pushing" to make each film as entertaining as possible. "I know I can do things better," he said. His commitment to learning the craft has been a throughline of his career. In a May 2025 interview at the British Film Institute, Cruise said he would "force" studios to send him to different countries so he could learn how films were made there.

item.title: Sam Altman says some AI accidents are 'unavoidable'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.42
Sam Altman says some AI accidents are unavoidable, but it's how you learn from them. Speaking at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference on Tuesday, the OpenAI CEO said tech companies should embrace a culture of transparent accident reporting, similar to that of the aviation industry. "I do think that some degree of accidents are unavoidable with new technology," Altman said. "What I really care about is that we have got a great culture of accident reporting and learning." He cited the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board as examples the AI industry should follow, saying the agencies' emphasis on investigating incidents has helped make flying safer. "You know, accidents are going to happen," he said of the FAA's and NTSB's approach. "We're going to learn as much as we can and react from each one." Altman's comments come as the AI industry faces renewed questions about whether its biggest labs are moving too quickly toward powerful autonomous systems. Jacob Coxon, a researcher who quit Anthropic last week and previously worked at OpenAI, kickstarted a debate by saying that the companies were "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." 'The world is right to be afraid of this' Other AI safety researchers have since told Business Insider that advanced systems could one day evade human control or make cyber, biological, and other catastrophic threats easier to carry out — although they would face hurdles in accessing the physical world. Altman acknowledged that AI doomsday fears are legitimate. "The world is right to be afraid of this," he said at Dreamforce, pointing to the possibility of a loss-of-control accident and the risk that a small number of AI developers could concentrate too much power. He said that the answer is not to abandon the technology, and that AI companies must instead ensure that "alignment and safety and monitoring" remain "way ahead of capabilities." He added that they should also be prepared "to slow down or stop" if they cannot do so. His comments may also sharpen a central criticism from AI-safety advocates: that frontier labs say they recognize the stakes yet continue building more capable models. Altman said "people get very scared" when it seems like commercial pressures might get in the way of companies or countries doing "the right thing." The point is not to accept disaster, Altman said, but to disclose incidents, learn from them quickly, and prevent them from escalating. "Maybe we can avoid, you know, ever getting to those kinds of stakes," he said. The debate is also unfolding as the Trump administration has shown little interest in regulating the sector, seeking to maintain the US's lead over China. David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech and the former White House AI Czar, reiterated that stance on Sunday, responding to calls from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to "pace the frontier." "Dario has written that we need to 'pace the frontier,' and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead," Sacks wrote on X. "But stop pretending you need anyone else's permission."

item.title: Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 6.53
Before taking off for Europe, CanadianPrime Minister Mark Carney had set the tone for his visit, saying he was seeking to build a "unique alliance" with the EU. The Wall Street Journal similarly reported that Canada was considering becoming an "associate member" of the EU, while not aiming for full membership. In her State of the European Union address on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen indicated that she was indeed open to such an expanded partnership. "We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," she said, addressing European lawmakers and Carney in Strasbourg, France. "That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work." Von der Leyen said a EU-Canada partnership would cover a broad range of areas including advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security. Carney is expected to outline his vision for future relations between the EU and Canada during a speech at the European Parliament on Thursday. What degree of collaboration could be possible between the EU and Canada? EU member states are closely integrated economically, sharing a common market, trade and customs policy. When it comes to establishing ties with non-EU countries, a list of different options present themselves. They range from free trade agreements that scrap tariffs and trade barriers, to association agreements which may include political elements, to far-reaching economic arrangements such as participation in the common European market, as is the case for Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. The EU has already negotiated association agreements with Turkey, Israel and Ukraine. These have different objectives and may or may not mark a preliminary step toward full membership. Patrick Leblond, an expert on international economic relations at the University of Ottawa, urges a little more caution around the term "association agreement." He considers it unlikely that Canada would adopt European laws or join the EU single market or customs union, which would mean imposing common external tariffs. Leblond says Carney is likely more interested in forming a kind of alliance that deepens cooperation on issues of economic security and defense. Closer defense cooperation? "We have, in a way, taken the US [security] umbrella for granted on both sides. We have underinvested in our militaries," Leblond told DW. He added that the focus was now on joining forces, for example in the production of military equipment and the development of new technologies. Security analyst Anand Sundar of the European Council on Foreign Relations also sees great potential for European-Canadian cooperation when it comes to defense. Canada spends about 70% of its defense budget on US-made equipment, according to Sundar. Carney wants to change that, the analyst said, as it would pay off for Canadians to be part of European defense projects to get "more bang for their buck." Canada has joined the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program. It provides EU member states with up to €150 billion ($173 billion, CA$ 241 billion) in loans for the joint procurement of military equipment. To qualify for funding, no more than 35% of the cost of the components can come from countries outside the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) or Ukraine. Yet because Canada joined the SAFE program by paying a fee, more lenient procurement rules apply to its companies. Nevertheless, Canadian companies still face significant hurdles for producing and purchasing weapons in partnership with European firms, Sundar told DW. The big question is how far the EU is willing to relax its own rules, the expert says, which could also have implications for non-EU countries, such as the United Kingdom or Norway. 'Underrated defense power' "But the biggest draw for the European Union is really the fact that that Canada is an underrated defense power," Sundar told DW. Canada, the expert added, spends more on defense than the 14 smallest EU member states combined. The North American country invests 2% of its gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, Sundar said, with an increase expected in the coming years. Canada, like other NATO countries, has committed to spending a total of 5% of its GDP on defense by 2035, of which 3.5% will go towards military equipment and the remaining 1.5% towards other defense-related areas. Protecting critical infrastructure The EU and Canada also intend to discuss potential cooperation in the field of critical infrastructure expansion, such as the joint operation of space satellites or maintenance of fiber-optic cables in the North Atlantic, Leblond told DW. The goal here, too, is to become less dependent on the US and its companies. Moreover, Canada has oil and gas reserves that could meet some of the bloc's energy demands. Trade relations between both have already been codified through the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force on a provisional basis in September 2017. The agreement eliminates nearly all tariffs between the EU and Canada, while also ensuring mutual market access for industrial goods, agricultural products and services. It even enables European companies to participate in public tenders in Canada. Economic analyst Leblond, however, believes that CETA's potential has not yet been fully realized. He says many Canadian companies still tend to focus on the US and less on Europe. He believes it is the government's responsibility to provide more information about CETA and the opportunities it offers, saying the level of exchange envisaged in this format could also be intensified. Why is Carney seeking closer ties with Europe? In January, Carney delivered a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in which he warned of a "rupture in the world order," calling on the middle powers to act together. "If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he said. Indeed, in recent weeks, the US-Canda trade war has continued escalating. Even though it is clear that Canada cannot sever ties with the US, there is a growing belief inside Canada that the country needs additional allies, Leblond told DW. And the Europeans are considered trustworthy, he added. Ultimately, the Canadians would want to see such an alliance, whatever form it may take, translate into concrete initiatives and projects through which Europeans and Canadians can help one another. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.40
The price of a liter of beer at Munich's Oktoberfest has risen fivefold since 1985, far outpacing overall inflation in Germany, according to an analysis by UniCredit's chief economist in Germany. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter (2.1-pint) serving at Oktoberfest, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) this year. In 1985, it cost about 6.25 Deutschmarks, equivalent to €3.20 after conversion at the fixed euro exchange rate. The figures were analyzed by UniCredit economist Andreas Rees ahead of the opening of the world's largest beer festival on Saturday. Beer prices at Oktoberfest have increased by around 400% since 1985, according to Rees, using data from Munich's statistical office. Consumer prices across Germany, by comparison, have risen by around 120% over the same period. What determines the Mass' price? This year's increase is considerably more modest. The average price of a Mass is up 2.4% from last year, below Germany's expected overall inflation rate of close to 3%. "Beer prices at the Oktoberfest depend on a peculiar cocktail of harvests, energy prices, wages, tent costs, security and the willingness of millions of visitors to spend generously," Rees said. Although the trend has been one of sharply rising prices, this year's Mass saw a price of 2.4% compared to 2025, the smallest increase in two decades. Rees explained that ingredient prices could be playing a role, as hops have become cheaper while malting-barley prices have stabilized. Festival draws millions Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world. Locals and tourists alike wear the traditional Bavarian lederhosen and dirndl dresses on the festival grounds. The festival dates back to 1810, and it takes place at the Wiesn, a the local dialect abbreviation for Theresienwiese, the fairgrounds in Munich named in honor of Crown Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen. This Saturday, Munich will celebrate the 191st Oktoberfest, expecting somewhere between 6 and 7 million visitors. The party begins when the city's mayor opens the first barrel in a ceremony officially marking the opening of the festival. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: High fuel prices challenge the German government
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.24
Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter. Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage. On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office. Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany. German government expresses 'great and growing' concern But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has promised. "Many people who need their cars every day have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action." However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined. "We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," Merz said. But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, deputy government spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices. "It's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer said. The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before. "From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman. Price gouging at the pumps Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly. "They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper. He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it. However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt. "Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer. A new fuel rebate or tax relief? Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter. "We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network. But she says that won't be possible again: "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment." As an alternative, the Conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments. But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crises. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump. AfD standing to profit from bickering But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%. The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%. "There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin. She criticized the federal government's inaction: "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration." A solution from the EU? According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday. Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level. "Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the Finance Ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin. "Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Duterte makes first appearance before ICC judges
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.97
Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, made his first in-person appearance before judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) at a pretrial hearing on Wednesday. The 81-year-old faces charges of crimes against humanity in connection with hundreds of murders committed during his "war on drugs" while in office. Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, denies the allegations. He has missed a series of hearings since he was arrested in March 2025 and has previously appeared in court via videolink. Duterte's legal team have said he suffers from poor health, but the court's judges ruled in January that he was fit enough to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court. The ex-president "suffers from a significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing his memories," his lawyers said. The prosecution, meanwhile, argued Duterte was "capable of meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights, and that he is fit for trial." What is Duterte accused of? Rodrigo Duterte is accused of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, first when he was the mayor of the southern city of Davao and then as Philippine president. Prosecutors say he is responsible for a systematic campaign that led to the deaths of at least 30,000 people, many of them during "anti-drug" raids. Duterte's trial is scheduled for November this year. During Wednesday's pretrial hearing, judges were to hear arguments about his health and decide whether he is mentally fit to stand trial. Edited by: Natalie Muller

item.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.95
In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members. "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind. "It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW. For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible. "India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there." Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil. At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing. "The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa. She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member. For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship. However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend. "In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh. Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first". However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times. "With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole. "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?" Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned. "India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics." What is BRICS for anyway? BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose. The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP. Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order. "Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa. She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues. There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh. What could the BRICS summit achieve? Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security. While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO. "India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely." Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm." He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve. "With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

item.title: Cyberattack in Berlin: 1.4 million files on the dark web
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.87
It was a story that almost went unnoticed amid all the clamor surrounding the closely watched state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. This highly alarming story is one of many recent reports that have detailed attacks on infrastructure or drone attacks on airports carried out by hostile foreign powers. Incidents like this one in the German capital highlight just how vulnerable Germany's data networks are. So what exactly happened? Since early September, employee files, official correspondence, pay stubs and even scanned ID documents have been appearing on the dark web. The hacker group Rhysida stole the data and then tried to extort the Berlin city government. They demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoins, which is equivalent to about €2 million ($2.3 million), or else they would publish the sensitive data. But last Friday, Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner stated: "The State of Berlin will not give in to blackmail." The data was subsequently published on the dark web, the part of the internet accessible only to tech-savvy users, where a lot of illegal activity takes place. In total, the data set consists of approximately 1.4 million records. An employee unknowingly opened a phishing email Two departments of the city government serving approximately four million residents have been compromised: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transportation. This time, the attack wasn't carried out by foreign intelligence agencies, but by criminals. The hackers initially gained access to protected data between August 7 and 14 without being detected. Rhysida, a cybercrime group believed to originate from eastern Europe, has been attacking public institutions around the world since 2023, claiming responsibility for nearly 280 attacks, primarily in the US. The hackers were able to gain access when a Berlin Transportation Authority employee replied to a phishing email, a message disguised to appear genuine and benign. Opening one of the attachments inadvertently grants the attackers access to the victim's network. In Berlin, the state government's secure fiber-optic network connects approximately 600 locations, ranging from municipal offices to senate departments. Data disclosure could have serious consequences The list of sectors that experts believe could be compromised illustrates the real gravity of the data breach. In addition to the personal data of employees and citizens, this includes information on combi-heat and power plants, fuel storage facilities, emergency power supply systems as well as prisons and water treatment plants. In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, Jochim Selzer of the Chaos Computer Club said that the publication could have serious consequences for the people affected — even if the data only appeared on the hard-to-access dark web: "The more you know about a person, the better you can impersonate them and the better you can figure out what you need to know about them in order to, say, place an order on their behalf." Is changing passwords enough? And what about the political authorities responsible? The Berlin state government has instructed its employees to change their passwords. That, however, sparked outrage from Thorsten Schleheider, the vice-chairman of Berlin's police union. He said that Berlin's data has been inadequately protected for years and that many employees have not received sufficient training: "It is unthinkable that highly sensitive data was compromised for days, and the only action taken appears to be instructing employees to change their passwords." To address the data breach, the Berlin Senate has set up a coordination office involving all Berlin administrative agencies. It has also established contact with federal agencies such as the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), based in Bonn. Mayor Kai Wegner said, "We will inform, advise and support those employees and Berliners who were affected as quickly as possible." Berlin state elections on September 20 remain safe The Berlin authorities were, however, able to provide reassurance regarding at least one issue of concern. They announced that the September 20 election for the Berlin State Parliament is not at risk. State Election Commissioner Stephan Bröchler told the Bild tabloid: "As things stand, all systems and processes necessary for the election remain unaffected — including election preparations, the actual election day itself and the steps leading up to the release of the preliminary results." Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was at least indirectly affected by the data theft. The stolen information also includes details about the controversial expansion of the Chancellery in the heart of Berlin. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Belarus to release 25 more prisoners as US eases sanctions
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.75
Belarus will release 25 prisoners in exchange for a further easing of US sanctions, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday. "We agreed on an interim agreement, and as a show of goodwill, Belarus will release 25 people. In exchange, the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," envoy John Coale told reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk. Coale had reportedly requested the release of 250 prisoners during his visit last March. The US special envoy said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues and secure the release of additional prisoners as well as the removal of further sanctions. "We will continue to improve relations between the United States and Belarus and are working to secure the release of more people in the near future. We are not done!" he later posted on X. Hundreds of people remain in prison in Belarus after President Alexander Lukashenko carried out a crackdown on protests against his reelection in 2020. Western countries then slapped sanctions on the country as a result of Lukashenko's repression of opposition. Accusations against Lukashenko Human rights organization Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the government still holds more than 900 political prisoners. The detainees have been accused of extremism, conspiracy to seize power, incitement of hatred, or insulting the president. During Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the existence of political prisoners and rejected Viasna's claims. The two companies to be removed from the US sanctions list are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of industrial paints and coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned company that oversees the forestry, pulp, and paper sectors. These sanctions have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively. Coale also announced the release of tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets currently held in US banks. Edited by: Natalie Muller

item.title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.89
Manuel Neuer retired from international duty after Germany's early exit from the 2026 World Cup, opening the door for a new No. 1. Jonas Urbig appears the obvious choice, but Neuer is still the starter at Bayern Munich, which severely limits Urbig's playing time. If the 23-year-old was Bayern's first choice, he would likely be Germany's number one too. As it stands, though, it appears doubtful that Germany's new coach Jürgen Klopp will even call him up to his first squad. On September 17, he will announce his squad for four UEFA Nations League games against the Netherlands, Greece, and Serbia. And no position in the current Germany team is more up for grabs than goalkeeper. Oliver Baumann: The automatic Neuer replacement? Oliver Baumann represents exactly the kind of selfless No. 2 who could be the next No. 1. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper even commendably dealt with the humiliation of being replaced by Neuer just before the World Cup. Klopp isn’t just tasked with celebrating short-term success with Germany, however. His remit is to bring about lasting change making Germany favorites for a World Cup and a Euros once again. Oliver Baumann turned 36 this summer. The Bundesliga veteran will be 38 at the next Euros, 40 by the 2030 World Cup. His age might count against a sustainable rebirth of the Germany team. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper, who has 13 caps, spoke to Bild in the days leading up to the squad announcement about his exchange with Klopp: "Yes, I was in contact with him. He'll say everything else on Thursday. We'll see about the rest—that’s for him to handle." Ter Stegen: Back in Germany colors via Ajax? Since Klopp prefers a highly attacking style of play in which all players press high up the field, he might opt for a goalkeeper who can also take on the duties of a field player. Marc-André ter Stegen would fit this profile better than Baumann. Ter Stegen is also two years younger than his competitor, though his career has been hampered by injuries. After several serious injuries and a legal dispute with Barcelona, ter Stegen has gone on loan to Ajax, improving his chances of returning between the posts for Germany. "As far as ter Stegen is concerned, I assume he’ll definitely be in the mix," Lothar Matthäus recently wrote for Sky. "If he continues to perform well in Amsterdam, he's a candidate for the number one spot." Alexander Nübel: Out of the spotlight in Turkey Alexander Nübel was Germany's third-string goalkeeper at the World Cup. He had been consistent at Stuttgart but moved to Besiktas this summer, where he has made a strong start. However, former national team goalkeeper Toni Schumacher sees the move as a disadvantage for the 29-year-old. "His move to Turkey has taken him out of the spotlight," Schumacher, who also played for Fenerbahce for three years during his playing days, told Bild. "It simply has a positive effect when you play in your own country week after week and thrill the fans with your saves." Loris Karius: History with Klopp at Liverpool A goalkeeper who has never been called up to the Germany team but shares a history with Klopp is Loris Karius. Karius, who has been at Schalke since January 2025, was at times Klopp’s No. 1 at Liverpool. However, he made two critical mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final against Real Madrid and was subsequently dropped. Back in the Bundesliga aged 33, Karius is delivering consistent performances and may have played his way back into the spotlight. "When people associate me with that, it's a testament to the performance I’m putting in. That's great," Karius said recently in an interview with Sky. Keepers who could play for Germany or elsewhere If none of the obvious candidates gets selected, there are a number of other good goalkeepers who might be considered. First among them is Noah Atubolu. The 24-year-old Eintracht Frankfurt keeper, who has Nigerian heritage, was the number one for Germany's U21s from 2022 to 2025, and was called up to the senior squad once last October. Freiburg's Mio Backhaus is another promising talent. The 22-year-old’s mother is from Japan, meaning Backhaus is also eligible to play for Japan. He even played for the Japanese U15 team, but has since progressed through Germany's youth teams up to the U21 level. In addition to Atubolu and Backhaus, there are also Augsburg's Finn Dahmen (28), Stuttgart's Dennis Seimen (20) and Diant Ramaj (24), who left recently relegated Heidenheim to join Copenhagen. If Klopp wants to rely on one of the five, it might be worth playing them sooner rather than later in a competitive game. After all, just like Atubolu and Backhaus, the other three are also eligible to play for another country due to their heritage. Dahmen could also play for England, Seimen for Romania, and Ramaj for Kosovo. Köpke: 'Develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1' "I think they need to develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1 right now," Andreas Köpke, the goalkeeper on Germany's 1996 European championship team, told Bild. Germany's former goalkeeping coach pointed to Bayern's backup goalkeeper, Urbig, alongside Backhaus and Atubolu — though only as and when Urbig plays regularly at club level. And, given his standing at Bayern, that's bound to come down to how long Manuel Neuer chooses to continue to play. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: DW exclusive: Zelenskyy offers to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.86
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit scheduled for December. Zelenskyy replied enthusiastically when DW's correspondent Misha Komadovsky posed the question on Friday. "Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," he said. Zelenskyy added that what he was going to say to Putin mattered less than results. "It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That's it." Zelenskyy and Putin have not met in person since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbor in February 2022. The Kremlin has so far declined to say whether Putin would go to Miami for the meeting. The Russian leader has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019. Last month, Russia's Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was however invited by the US to attend a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina in a move that upset European officials. 100-year partnership declaration with Canada First up, however, Zelenskyy spoke of the deals he signed on Thursday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, including a 100-year partnership declaration. Zelenskyy underlined the importance of the deal, which he said covered numerous sectors, "from security, financing, energy, very important energy, veteran policy, and culture, and relationships and humanitarian issues." "So it's a global decision, a really historic decision, and I'm happy that we have it," he said. Zelenskyy said he had also signed a deal on collaboration on drone production with the Canadian leader involving a number of Ukrainian companies. Zelenskyy pushes for more Patriot missiles ahead of winter Zelenskyy's interview with DW comes as summer is nearly over and Ukraine is gearing up for the cold months of winter. The Ukrainian president has conceded that his country has been struggling to counter flying jet-propelled drones that Russia has been increasingly deploying. "They [US] have political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big. So it means that stocks is a variant," he said. "Will Americans be ready to give us (Patriots)? I don’t know. We will see." Patriot missiles are powerful weapons that are currently the most effective defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks. What Zelenskyy needs from US and European allies "Russia [currently] produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need a 1-to-2 [ratio], 280 missiles," Zelenskyy told DW. "You will never have 280 missiles per month, and between us, it’s a huge challenge to have [even] 100 missiles per month. This is what I want. I want to have 100-120 for these difficult months, especially the cold months." Germany earlier this week said it was going to send Patriot missiles from its national stock, without specifying how many missiles that would be. Zelenskyy called on Kyiv's European allies to provide more support. "They have to give as much as possible. With all respect to them, they have to give to Ukrainians to save their lives." Zelenskyy also spoke of having secured agreements with several European companies to develop a Ukrainian-led anti-missile system called Freya. He said he was hoping that the first test phase would begin by the end of December, stressing that time was short. Ukraine in 'good position for negotiations' Zelenskyy said that it was a "good signal" that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier this week, and not just Moscow. He said he had made clear to them that his country was well-placed for negotiations on ending the conflict, with Russia estimated to be losing more than 30,000 soldiers a month. Zelenskyy said this meant that Moscow was paying a "big price" for small gains on the battlefield. "So that’s why we think that we have now good position for negotiations," he said, adding that his country was stronger than last year. Grain and energy top priorities The other concern that has been coming up steadily over this summer is the shipment of grains through the Black Sea, with Moscow and Kyiv currently targeting each other's ships and hindering exports. Russia's de facto blockade of Ukraine's Black Sea ports in the Odesa region has led to a 76% fall in Ukraine's grain exports year-on-year so far in August. Zelenskyy said he had spoken with the two envoys about an energy and grain ceasefire that could provide a starting point for peace. "What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," he said. Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

item.title: News helicopter crashes in LA, killing 3
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.79
A news helicopter in Los Angeles crashed and burst into flames while covering a deadly bus accident on Tuesday evening. At least three people were reported killed and a fourth was injured. The helicopter crashed near a storage building in the Chatsworth neighborhood, northwest of downtown Los Angeles. A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said at least one person was killed in the parking lot next to the building, adding it was currently unclear if the other two victims were on the ground or inside the aircraft. He said officials were combing the wreckage. "We're trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter," said spokesperson Branden Silverman. Cause of crash unknown The local affiliate of US broadcaster NBC confirmed the helicopter was NewsChopper4, which had been en route to cover a deadly collision between an SUV and a city bus that killed two people. There has been no immediate confirmation of the identity of those on board the helicopter, however, NBC reported it has been unable to contact the crew. Reporters at the scene of the bus accident said the helicopter crashed about a mile (1.6 kilometers) away. The fire department said dozens of firefighters had been dispatched to the incident and quickly extinguished the flaming wreckage. Aerial footage showed remains of the tail and rotor among storage containers and vehicles. The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have launched an investigation into what caused the crash. Helicopters are frequently used in Los Angeles to provide live aerial coverage of news events in the second largest city in the US. Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.36
Any and all ships may pass, at least at first. That was how the spokesperson for Yemen's Houthis rebel militia put it. Transit through the Red Sea would be safe, with one exception: According to the Houthi spokesperson, ships from Saudi Arabia would not be allowed to pass this stretch of the sea. The comments came during a time when the Houthi militia has been fighting to increase its presence at the southern entrance to the ocean passage. The Houthis now control the tiny volcanic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, at the entrance to the Red Sea, as well as other parts of the Yemeni coast and some small islands. With these moves, pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia, the country that opposes the Houthis and previously fought a war (unsuccessfully) with them. But pressure is now also increasing in Egypt. Every decrease in shipping traffic through the Red Sea also impacts one of that country's most important sources of national income, the Suez Canal. As yet, maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has not been significantly reduced. According to news agency Reuters, last Saturday 24 ships passed through it and on Sunday, 27 did so. That is around the same as the 10-day average. The Houthis appear to want to signal that their plan is not stop traffic altogether. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a chokepoint between Yemen and and the Horn of Africa. Ships have to pass it to enter the Red Sea. In general though, maritime traffic has decreased here, according to maritime intelligence organization Kpler. On Monday, 21 ships went through the strait. But in the middle of July, the average number of ships passing through was 47. How will things develop from here? "The Houthis could actually interrupt, or at least significantly disturb, the connection between Asia and Europe," says Stephan Roll, a senior fellow with the Africa and Middle East division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, or SWP, in Berlin. "So first we have to wait and see how big the actual disruption to the Suez Canal will be." Even complete control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait doesn't automatically mean control of the Suez Canal. But it does give the Houthis a further opportunity to indirectly threaten traffic. For Egypt, this new disruption comes at a particularly unwelcome time. Houthi attacks at the end of 2023 had already disrupted business at the Suez Canal. According to the International Monetary Fund, earnings at the canal in 2024 fell by around $6 billion (€5.2 billion). Before the current security crisis, Egypt had been making between $9 billion and $10 billion from the Suez Canal annually. More recently things had actually been improving again. "The situation is certainly problematic compared to 2023," Roll told DW. "But it is not so clearly negative compared to the situation one, two or even three months ago." Thanks to rising oil prices and the resulting higher cost of circumnavigating Africa, shipping companies had been using the Red Sea as they travelled between Asia and Europe. The Suez Canal's finances had recently improved. The Suez Canal Authority, which manages the passage, reported that during the 2025-2026 fiscal year, revenues had risen by 23% to $4.67 billion (€4.5 billion). Despite the various conflicts in the region, this actually represented a recovery for the Suez Canal. Houthi offensive could change all that There is also a second critical factor. After recent drone attacks that the Saudis blamed on Iraqi groups, Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline to the coastal city of Yanbu will be out of service for at least several weeks. Between 4 million and 5 million barrels of oil were going through the 1,200 kilometer pipeline per day as the Saudis attempted to circumnavigate the Strait of Hormuz, blocked due to the US-Iran war. This latest damage could put as much as 4% of global supply at risk, according to Reuters. An analysis by Qatar-based think tank, the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, warns of a scenario where the Persian Gulf and Red Sea are both likely to become more precarious. The East Asia Institute, a think tank based in Korea, has also written about the dangers of dual choke points. Neither route can be seen as an independent alternative because flows of oil and trade depend on secure connections at several points. Certainly for Egypt, this will increase economic pressure. What can Egypt do about this? In geopolitical terms, there is not a lot that Egypt can do. The Houthis in Yemen have only impacted the country indirectly. "Egypt's military capabilities are very limited," Steffen Krüger, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's Cairo office, explained. Egyptian interventions in Yemen in the 1960s are still remembered in Cairo — back then, the country sent thousands of troops to support a new government in Yemen, in a war that would eventually last years — so Egypt would prefer to exercise restraint there. "Although Egypt formally remains a member of the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, its participation is largely symbolic," Krüger told DW. And there is no doubt that Egyptian officials have noted the lack of success other countries like Saudi Arabia and the US have had in their attempts to rein in the Houthis. "The Egyptians simply have no real alternative," argues the SWP's Roll, adding that Egypt is likely to try diplomacy first. "Basically they have to try to put a positive spin on a bad situation and somehow negotiate appropriate arrangements with the Houthis." London-based media outlet The New Arab wrote that the Houthis offered to talk directy to Cairo about shipping security via the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) in London. But the ICS rejected that claim and said that "no such request was ever made to ICS" and that the chamber hasn't had direct communications with the Houthis. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabian leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Cairo to try to get Egypt's support against the Houthis. "The Egyptians are likely to wait and see," says Roll of the SWP about the next steps for Cairo. Egypt has a difficult balancing act to perform. The country is closely allied with Saudi Arabia but is also bound to suffer economically in any further escalation between the Saudis and the Houthi group. A decisive factor will depend on if, and how, the Houthis restrict maritime shipping, and if they go beyond vessels with Saudi Arabian ties, or whether they are just using their currenty improved military position to exert pressure on their enemies. This story was originally published in German. Editor's note: A previous version of this article mentioned a story in The New Arab that claims the Houthis offered to speak with Egypt via the International Chamber of Shipping. The ICS has rejected this claim; we updated our story accordingly.

item.title: US charges 5 people over Russia-backed plots
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.32
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has charged five men with working for Russian intelligence to carry out surveillance and plan targeted killings in the United States and Europe. "The men were recruited to carry out attacks and assassinations around the world, including the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment. Yuri Khrameev, 63, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, both Russian nationals; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela, 22, were charged with conspiracy to commit financial terrorism. Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. All the individuals are still at large. The DOJ announced the unsealing of charges against the five individuals one day after DW published an investigation looking into one of the members of the murder plot. The DW investigation identified Romagoza Durruthy as a salsa teacher in Russia who recruited a number of people in 2024 to carry out sabotage across Europe. The agents were mostly from Spanish-speaking countries and had been sent across Europe to commit arson attacks on businesses and military equipment destined for Ukraine. The investigation found that Romagoza Durruthy had been the person who directed them and organized their travels. What else did the DOJ say? Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the plans included attempts to assassinate a Russian dissident in Washington, DC. According to the DOJ, several people were recruited in the US alone to surveil Russian dissidents, in addition to monitoring civilian and military infrastructure in European countries such as Lithuania. The Justice Department also reported that one recruit was allegedly offered "$40,000 to 'eliminate' or 'disappear' a US resident." Last year, another recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania. Russia has previously denied carrying out such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States. The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Edited by: Natalie Muller

item.title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.27
A decade after the deadliest jihadist attack in Germany's history, a new six-part TV series looks at the institutional failures that allowed it to happen. "Blindspot Berlin," which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, follows the year-long police investigation that failed to stop Anis Amri — a Tunisian whose asylum applications had been rejected, and who was already known to German security services — from driving a hijacked truck into a crowded Christmas market at Berlin's Breitscheidplatz on December 19, 2016. Twelve people died, including Lukasz Urban, the Polish driver Amri shot before seizing his vehicle. Dozens more were injured; a 13th victim died of their injuries in 2021. Amri fled the scene and made his way across Europe before being shot dead four days later by Italian police, near Milan, during a routine identity check. "What happened behind the scenes of that attack is in many ways just as disturbing," says "Blindspot Berlin" director David Nawrath . "[It's] a picture of overwhelmed institutions, systemic failure and a staggering blindness to the threat that was developing right in front of our eyes." Inside the Salafist network Set in the year before the attack, the series follows police investigator Frank Laudin (Albrecht Schuch, of "System Crasher" and "All Quiet on the Western Front") and Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla), a young officer and Arabic-language translator, as they try to infiltrate the Salafist network around Abu Walaa, the Iraqi preacher based in Hildesheim who recruited for extremist group "Islamic State" (IS). Frank recruits Murat (Tamer Trasoglu), who risks his life as an undercover informant. Inside the network, they find Amri: volatile, and getting more dangerous. But despite repeated warnings, their bosses refuse to take the threat seriously. They dismiss Amri as a possible terrorist, in part because he is also a drug dealer, something the authorities see as incompatible with being a radical Islamist. Fiction built on the parliamentary record The series writers and production team closely based "Blindspot Berlin" on the facts of the Amri case, and the years-long parliamentary investigation into the institutional failures that made the attack possible. The main characters in the series — Frank, Isra and Murat — are fictionalized, but the events play out as they did in real life. "We tried to keep as close as possible to what is known about the attack and what led to it," producer Simon Amberger told DW. "There is still a lot that isn't known, that is speculation. There we tried to leave things open." Border authorities stopped Amri from leaving Germany before Berlin attack The facts of the case are damning enough. The parliamentary inquiry committee found that the criminal division investigating Amri and other suspects was grossly understaffed, that judicial and security agencies failed to coordinate the exchange of information, and that officials made serious errors of judgment. Amri's asylum claims were rejected, but he was never deported. At one point the bureaucracy tipped into farce. Amri tried to leave Germany to rejoin his family and was stopped at the border, where police confiscated his passport on the grounds that he lacked the correct papers to go. Not only a German story The producers knew from the start that the story reached beyond Germany. The Breitscheidplatz attack came at the end of a run of assaults across Europe: the Bataclan and coordinated shootings in Paris in 2015, the suicide bombings at Brussels airport and Maelbeek metro station, and a similar truck attack in Nice, in 2016. Despite the lessons learned in the past decade, threat levels remain high. On July 25, 2026, a man drove a van into the crowds of Christopher Street Day Pride celebrations in Berlin, killing one and injuring dozens. The Breitscheidplatz attack also continues to resonate today, as it raises questions on "how far a free democratic society is willing to go, how much of its freedom it is willing to sacrifice for security," says Amberger. Fears of political misuse He's aware, however, that a story of Islamic extremism, and the failure of the German state to protect its citizens, lands differently now, in the wake of recent elections that have seen a surge of support for the anti-immigrant, Islamophobic far-right AfD party. "There is a danger that this story, this series, could be misused to support a simplistic, populist political agenda," Amberger admits. "But it isn't that simple. [In the series] we show how extremism arises in marginalized groups that feel isolated, unseen and powerless. The solution isn't 'stop immigration.'" "Blindspot Berlin" premieres in Germany on public broadcaster ARD in October; international distribution is also planned. Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

item.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.21
Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media.
