A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK. She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain. What did Greer's husband say about her death? Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life." Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness. He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together. "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated. Who was Bonnie Greer? Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers. Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings. She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career. Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer. Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities. She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play. Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time". Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time. She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

item.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.16
On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions. But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage and possibly drone operations and related disruptions." Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party. In a recent interview with DW, she complained, "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table." She accuses the German government of failing to take action. "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong." Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel. Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior." In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations. Russia's threats: just a bluff? It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint aims to avoid escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war." Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded. "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said. "Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely avoided confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels." After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through." Armed Russian crews on board Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk. "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation." Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way. "It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel." Inspections would raise costs for Russia While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it." He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy." This article has been translated from German. What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

item.title: How hotter weather is making us poorer
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.10
The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world. According to a 2026 study by the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in 10 US counties. These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example. "Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers . How climate change is already hitting incomes A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy $38 trillion a year by 2050. But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets? "If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario. Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains. "Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW. Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price. "As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down." Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River, the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe, could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July. Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany. Compounding existing economic pressures One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output. Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the report showing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974, $15,000) per person in 2024. "The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty." The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to 10 billion Australian dollars due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance. These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance. In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality. Can climate adaptation limit costs? "Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study. Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things." However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital to head off much worse future economic impacts. The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis. Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted. But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively. Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says. Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets. "Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Russia's drone war comes to Moldova and Romania
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.00
For Ukrainians, Russia's air war has been a bitter, bloody reality for years. People in Ukraine are being killed every day by missiles, bombs, and drones. But the country's central and southeastern European neighbors have also found themselves affected, albeit on a smaller scale: Missiles and drones sometimes invade their air space, and occasionally even crash on their territory. Now the Russian drone war is coming dangerously close to two of Ukraine's neighbors: Romania and the Republic of Moldova, where drone incidents are now an almost daily occurrence. The drones often explode, leaving people injured, and there have also been recent attacks on Ukrainian checkpoints at the Moldovan and Romanian borders. The attacks have now escalated to such a degree that many observers believe they can no longer be considered unintentional. They suspect the Kremlin is deliberately trying to bring the war to Ukraine's neighbors. The latest drone incursion and crash on Tuesday caused a furore as it prevented a plane with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on board from taking off in the Moldovan capital Chisinau. A Russian Geran drone, which can fly as fast as 500 kilometers per hour (311 mph), took off in Crimea, then flew through Ukrainian airspace and eventually crashed in a sunflower field near the Moldovan city of Riscani. The drone also flew over Romania, where two fighter jets were scrambled from NATO's Kogalniceanu airbase near the Black Sea port of Constanta, though it remains unclear why they did not shoot down the drone, as they had on other occasions. More and more incidents in Moldova and Romania The most serious aspect of the incident was that it showed how limited Moldovan air defense is in its ability to protect the country's air space. The drones were detected and tracked by air traffic control, but it was not possible to shoot them down. According to publicly available information, the country possesses only a small number of Polish Piorun anti-aircraft missiles, and these are only able to protect certain specific targets. There have been around three dozen drone incidents in Romania and Moldova since the beginning of August this year. The majority were airspace violations, but there have also been crashes and explosions, while debris has also been found. In Romania, several drones have also been shot down. According to official data, 17 drones crashed in August in Moldova alone – as many as in all of 2025. Deaths at border crossings There was also a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and southeastern Moldova on the night of September 8. The crossing, situated around a kilometer from Moldovan territory, and was damaged in the attack. Two people were killed and two others wounded, one of them a Moldovan citizen. The Moldovan leadership has strongly condemned the drone attack. President Maia Sandu said on Wednesday that Russia's war had arrived at the Moldovan border. "It is hard to understand, given this reality, that there are still voices who try to convince Moldovans that Russia is not the aggressor, or that the war in our part of the world has nothing to do with us," Sandu said. The president of the Moldovan parliament, Igor Grosu, wrote on Facebook that these were incidents "we can no longer view as something remote." The threat from Russia, Grosu said, was not a "specter," and not propaganda: "It is a daily reality." Moldova's Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatii said that the deaths of Moldovan citizens could no longer be ruled out in future. Vladimir Bolea, the minister of infrastructure, warned that Giurgiulesti, Moldova's port on the Danube, could become a target after the Russian Foreign Ministry accused Romania and Moldova of using the port as a "transit hub" for arms shipments. 'Planned operation' by Russia? Moldovan military and security expert Rosian Vasiloi, a former head of the Moldovan border police, wrote on Facebook in response to Tuesday's drone crash in Moldova: "This is a planned operation by the aggressor state." He also referred to the drone's peculiar flight path: After flying from Ukraine over Moldova into Romania, it made an about-turn and flew back to Moldova. Vasiloi concluded: "We can no longer view our airspace as separate from Ukraine's and Romania's. Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Romania already form an interconnected operational area as far as air threats and their impact on regional connectivity are concerned." The Romanian leadership has not yet reacted to the latest incidents. But in July, the Romanian government made a political and military change of course: After a long period of restraint, it started to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace. Former Romanian General Virgil Balaceanu, a regular analyst in the country's media, has urged Romania's leaders to accelerate the enhancement of Romanian air defenses. Balaceanu also believes that the drone incident on Tuesday was a deliberate maneuver. Following this latest incident, the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a leading public think tank for analysis of Russia's war against Ukraine, wrote that while there was no evidence that the airspace violations were intentional, it could be said that Russia benefited from such actions. In particular, it wrote, the incursions using Russia's latest, extremely fast Geran drone model "aim to further test NATO and Moldovan defenses and the response of the entire NATO alliance." This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthis target Mecca, warns of 'red line'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.80
Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed a drone allegedly launched by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis before it entered restricted airspace over Islam's holiest city Mecca. The Houthis denied targeting the city, which is the destination of the annual Muslim hajj pilgrimage. The claim was announced by the Joint Forces Command of what is still called the Saudi-led coalition. The multinational alliance formed in 2015 has largely fragmented, leaving current operations dominated by Saudi Arabia and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said the security of Mecca and its pilgrims was a "red line" and warned that the command would take "necessary and deterrent measures." According to the statement, the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone "launched by the Terrorist Houthi Militia." Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and in the kingdom's southern region which borders Yemen. How did the Houthis respond? The Houthis were quick to reject the coalition's claims as a "lie." "The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone," Hazem al-Assad, a high-ranking member from the Houthi movement, wrote on X. Pakistan's prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous attack on Mecca." "The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he wrote on X. Meanwhile, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a bloc of 57 Muslim nations, also condemned the "henious" attack. The OIC General Secretariat "stresses that the violation of the sanctity of the holy sites is an unacceptable and intolerable transgression that requires deterring the perpetrators and blocking the path of anyone who dares to infringe upon these sites," it said in a statement. Why are Saudi forces in conflict with the Houthis? Saudi Arabia is being increasingly affected by the rapidly escalating conflict across its southern border in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia injured 13 people on Monday night, bringing the total number of people injured since the conflict escalated in July to about 100. In July, the Houthis also blocked Saudi oil shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz. With the kingdom under attack, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday reached out to Egypt for support against Yemen's Houthi rebels. The leaders called for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. The growing escalation has opened up another front in the Middle East, which is already grappling with the US war on Iran. Amid the latest development, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday issued an advisory asking its citizens to "reconsider travel" to the kingdom. It warned of the "risk of Iranian drone and missile targeting American interests, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans and local laws regarding social media activity." Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.51
Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland. After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat. "Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday. "Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war. Poland prepares response Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details. "Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening. On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe. "There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security. Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time. Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack. Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train. "Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do." "The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said. Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster. Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine. Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest. But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion. In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up." Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment." "In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added. Polish media sound alarm The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm. "Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line." "These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote. Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door." "The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski. Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat. "We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: China’s Purges Are Working as Designed
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.28
For two decades, scholars believed that the main reason Chinese communist rule endured into the twenty-first century—whereas every communist regime in Europe collapsed—was that it had built sturdy, long-lasting institutions. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had moved away from the unpredictable personalist dictatorship of the Mao Zedong era and established the foundations of a modern state. It set term limits on its leaders, embraced collective leadership, and increasingly promoted officials based on merit, which made it resilient enough to bounce back from the external and internal shocks that had felled other socialist systems. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, however, has spent the past decade demolishing nearly every institution that supposedly kept the party strong. He abolished presidential term limits in 2018, hollowed out collective leadership, and has declined to designate a successor. Xi has also purged high-level officials at will, especially in the most sensitive domain: the military. In January, only months after party leaders expelled nine senior military officers, the country’s Ministry of National Defense announced that General Zhang Youxia and General Liu Zhenli—until that point the People’s Liberation Army’s most senior uniformed officer and top operational commander, respectively—had been placed under investigation. Since 2022, according to data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the party has formally purged three dozen generals and lieutenant generals, and many more are conspicuously missing. In Washington, many observers see these purges as evidence of China’s weakness. They see a powerful leader consumed by suspicion and obsessed with maintaining his own grip on power. If the party’s strength were indeed based on the freestanding institutions that China had built in the post-Mao era, then Xi’s purges would be a warning sign of fragility and even a potential crackup. But the party has not shown any signs of falling apart. If anything, as these purges have continued, Xi and the party appear to have only gotten stronger. Far from weakening its rule, the way the CCP cleans its ranks can explain part of what makes it durable. A purge is not an event but a process—one that the party has run in nearly identical form for a century. It regularly targets, evaluates, and forces cadres to seek clemency to retain their standing within the system. The goal is to reform them rather than get rid of them entirely, which strengthens the party by encouraging obedience and dedication to the party’s cause. CCP leaders believe it’s working, too: Xi has embraced “self-revolution,” or continuous and permanent rectification, as the means by which China will escape the unhappy fate of the Soviet Union and other socialist regimes now residing in the dustbin of history. What could threaten the party’s longevity, then, is not the count of how many officials have been purged but the one problem that such a strategy cannot solve and can even make worse: how to handle succession. A regime of self-revolution will rise and fall on that question, no matter how hard it tries to avoid internal decay. CURE THE SICKNESS, SAVE THE PATIENT China’s history of purges predates the founding of the People’s Republic, in 1949. In some cases, as has been true in similar regimes, the CCP launches violent purges to remove cadres from its ranks. The type of purge now synonymous with the actions of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union aims at eliminating someone from the party, whether through incarceration, exile, or death. The victim of such a purge does not come back. Mao employed this tactic as early as 1930, when he executed more than 700 army officers in a show of total control. But what the CCP has also done, and what is unique to its continued rule, is not a purge in the traditional sense. CCP leaders often turn to a different method of discipline: rectification. Rectification aims to keep a person inside the party, even if sometimes at a greatly diminished status. Whereas the traditional idea of a purge seeks to eliminate enemies in the ranks (the Chinese term qingdang means to “cleanse the party”), rectification aims to retain and remold cadres while keeping them in the party’s orbit. Throughout its history, the CCP has sought to rectify cadres far more frequently than it has sought to eliminate them. In December 1929, in the village of Gutian, in Fujian province, Mao put forward a resolution called “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party” that asserted the party’s control of the military. The resolution also included clues as to how the party understood internal discipline: it described its targets not as enemies but as people who had deviations in their thinking. Cadres might suffer from ailments such as having a “purely military viewpoint” (a perspective untethered from politics), promoting ultrademocracy (a political system lacking party authority), and supporting individualism. Mao’s resolution treated each of these as a sickness that could sometimes be cured through a regimen of criticism and self-criticism in front of peers. And it attached a promise to the cure: if party members submitted to the process, the CCP would retain them rather than destroy them. In the northern Chinese area of Yan’an, where Mao and his followers set up a wartime base camp starting in the mid-1930s, leaders turned rectification into doctrine. Party membership exploded from roughly 40,000 in 1937 to 800,000 by 1940, which meant that almost everyone in the organization was new and not yet trustworthy in the eyes of party leaders. The Rectification Movement of 1942–45 was the solution. Every cadre wrote an autobiography, measured his or her life against printed self-examination outlines, confessed before his or her party branch or work unit, and was examined, graded, and sorted by the party’s personnel department. In February 1942, Mao summarized the approach in a famous line: “Cure the sickness, save the patient.” Rectification aims to retain and remold cadres. None of this was gentle. The Yan’an campaign was brutal: many were tortured, and thousands died. Subsequent campaigns were often even harsher. But Mao’s approach separated Chinese communism from its nearest relatives. Stalin quickly executed unreliable cadres, and Pol Pot sent them to mass graves. In China, in many cases, the strategy was to keep cadres and try to remold them while also building permanent files detailing their every mistake. The basic procedure remains nearly identical today. A person is singled out for deviating in some way and made to write an account of his or her shortcomings. The account is checked against what his colleagues say about him and against what the organization’s records (in that individual’s personal file) already hold. The cadre is placed on a graded scale of possible sanctions, ranging from no action at one end to expulsion from the party at the other. (Most sanctions fall in the middle, including issuing a serious warning or putting someone on probation.) When a verdict on how to deal with a cadre, official, or campaign target is issued, that person, if deemed to have confessed sufficiently, is kept in the party but on terms that are revocable and conditional on the political winds. And every piece of paper the process generates goes into the cadre’s official file, permanently. It is the process used in 1952 against a village storekeeper who skimmed off the top of procured grain. It is also the process used today for China’s Politburo, whose members—the country’s most powerful men—read self-criticisms aloud to one another once a year and have their confessions written down and permanently attached to their files following the same template that was used in Yan’an. Even as Xi has expanded the scope of who can be targeted, the machinery has not changed. The ongoing case of the purged military officers under Xi likely fits this model, too. Zhang and Liu have been placed under investigation, not shot, and there is a chance that they remain on the party’s books, even if they are saddled with a thicker personal dossier and given a meaningless post or sidelined from public life altogether. In 2023, the diplomat Qin Gang, for instance, was removed from his position as foreign minister; news investigations reported that he had kept his party membership but had been reassigned to a low-level desk job at the foreign ministry’s publishing house. And even if Zhang and Liu are expelled from the party, purging remains the exception rather than the norm, as has been the party’s longstanding practice. Of the 101 generals and lieutenant generals that the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified as purged or potentially purged, only 14 had been officially kicked out of the party as of February. SINGLE FILE Rectification rarely, if ever, changes cadres’ beliefs. Eighty years of evidence, much of it the party’s own, shows cadres parroting the scripts given to them, performing the required contrition, and then reverting to their earlier behaviors the moment the campaign ends. It is a process so ritualized that participants learn to say exactly what examiners want to hear. Yet the main goal of the process is not to reform belief but to create a document to put into a dossier on file. Such a file contains objective personnel data as well as observable assessments of a cadre’s political shortcomings. It is this paper trail that enables the regime to maintain discipline even if no cadres change how they act or think. For cadres and others subject to rectification, the process sorts who is in and who has fallen out of the good graces of party leaders. As cadres constantly jockey for status, a purge is exceptional and devastating. For most party members, surviving a rectification process with minimal punishment is grounds for relief (and often accompanied by a desire to recommit to a forgiving regime) combined with a sliver of fear that the next campaign is always just around the corner. Expanded to 100 million party members, this process produces an internalized discipline in each person that strengthens the organization’s grip on power. Each cadre wakes up every day knowing the dossier exists and that it can be used against them at any time. The permanent, standardized, reopenable record of every party member’s history, associations, and vulnerabilities is also an information system that gives party leaders immense power. Autocratic rulers need information to head off threats to their power; the CCP’s personnel file system, filled with information about the party’s cadres, is an irreplaceable channel of information for China’s rulers. Most cadres are willing to go along with the party’s wishes, but for the small minority that does not express the proper attitude in the face of a discipline campaign, the party can expel them or put them in jail, heading off any threat of revolt from within. High-level defection and dissent sometimes occur, but when they do they are rarely organized and quickly fizzle out. Such record-keeping might be expected to generate resentment among party cadres, but the process is designed to spread the blame and thus insulate Beijing from any backlash. There is no single person or entity that issues a rectification verdict. Instead, party task forces (known as work teams) are mobilized to draft the verdict, colleagues from their workplace endorse it, and then a committee at a higher level of administration ratifies it. It passes through enough hands in the process that authorship is aggregated and spread so that no individual leader or party entity can be said to be responsible. Even the cadre, through his or her own self-criticism, is a co-author in the verdict. Disciplining cadres with rectification is also a coordination device. The Chinese party-state is a sprawling network of bureaucratic agencies, regional power bases, and administrative offices that have their own interests and frequently have to bargain with one another. A rectification campaign is one of the few instruments that transcends these fissures. As with the party’s other massive campaigns, such as the one-child policy, cadres understand that compliance with rectification is mandatory and a high priority for leaders. Discipline campaigns offer unambiguous carrots and sticks, including leniency for cadres who show the right attitude and professional purgatory, even exile, for those who do not. Many cadres that normally benefit from taking advantage of the fragmentation in China’s political system know to drop everything else and go along with discipline campaigns, providing Beijing with a highly visible way to impose unified priorities and strengthen party control. WHAT DISCIPLINE CANNOT SOLVE Chinese history is rife with examples of once powerful dynasties weakening and eventually falling apart. To avoid this outcome, Mao’s solution was mass mobilization: only by letting the people supervise the government, he believed, would it not slacken. Xi’s answer, offered in 2021 and elaborated since, is the party’s self-revolution. In this framework, the cure for the party’s ills can only come from inside the party, not from any external force. Ongoing party rectification campaigns require all officials to discipline themselves, and the occasional outright purge of some cadres provides undeniable proof that failure to comply has consequences. It is the first time the party has explicitly located the mechanism of its own survival inside itself. The choreography has been equally explicit. In the fall of 2014, with investigations that felled two senior military leaders underway, Xi summoned some 400 senior officers to the same hall in the village of Gutian where Mao had issued “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party.” State media called it the “new Gutian conference.” In 2024, Xi convened the military to discuss political work (that is, ideological loyalty) at Yan’an—a clear reminder that the party sees a direct line from past rectification campaigns to its present strength. Beneath the symbolism is Xi’s fear that China could end up like the Soviet Union, whose own Communist Party, Xi believes, let its internal disciplinary mechanisms atrophy and thus was the architect of its own demise. Beijing believes that the purges and rectification must continue permanently if the party is to remain in power. Whether or not the analysis of Soviet collapse is accurate, the CCP’s continued strength suggests that the party’s method of disciplining cadres may indeed explain its durability. Xi’s purges should not be measured by how many cadres they ensnared but whether they continue to produce files, verdicts, and party retention that keep the party firmly in control. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. But what strengthens the party also weakens some of China’s instruments of power. Senior military commands sit vacant or are staffed by less experienced officers, and future officers learn that the safest career record is a thin one. When forced to choose, political control is always more important to the party than operational effectiveness. This is a tradeoff that the party has been willing to make for a century and will continue to make. And China’s method of purges cannot solve the danger of succession. Rectification produces no mechanism for choosing the next ruler—if anything, by ensuring that no subordinate accumulates independent standing, it makes the emergence of a credible successor even harder. Succession, not discipline, is where the system is weak. The older generation of CCP leaders, including Mao and Deng Xiaoping, overcame the challenge of succession by drawing on their unassailable authority as revolutionaries who had fought for the party’s survival, and subsequent leaders relied on the institutions—term limits, collective leadership, and regularized succession rules—that Xi has summarily destroyed. Xi has neither, which makes the succession problem especially acute. The moment to worry about Chinese stability is not when generals disappear amid an investigation, but when the man who reads their files begins to age out of the role without an answer as to who will follow. The CCP is not going to collapse: the file system exists precisely to prevent elite fracture, and it has worked. What is likely to emerge instead is a state that is militarily weaker and politically stronger than most assessments suggest. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. Beijing’s own theorists are watching this, too, because they know that even a well-engineered system of rectification that has kept the party strong for a century has no answer for an elite power struggle over who comes next. item.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.21
Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships. Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet. The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually. Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault. SITTING DUCKS Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues. Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war. In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes. Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz. SMALL IS BEAUTIFUL As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force. Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion. These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion. A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective. RIGHTING THE SHIP The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices. But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them. After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion.
