item.title: The Emerging U.S.-China Détente
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.97
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump met in Beijing, in May, they agreed that their two countries should build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Although many observers in Washington responded skeptically to this new framework, dismissing it as empty words, it marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize. Strategic stability does not refer to nuclear détente; rather, it suggests a new equilibrium in which both sides can avoid further deterioration of the relationship and even expand cooperation where interests align. Leaders in Beijing do not expect that this new framework can resolve most of the differences between China and the United States or that it can stop new frictions from emerging. In June, for example, the U.S. Department of Defense placed more Chinese companies—including private-sector giants Alibaba, Baidu, and BYD—on its list of firms involved in civil-military fusion activities, barring the Pentagon from contracting with them. In retaliation, China placed ten U.S. entities on its dual-use export control list, which prevents any company from supplying them with items that have the potential for both military and civilian use. But Beijing hopes that a consensus built around strategic stability can help China and the United States manage their differences more effectively and that it will prevent the worst outcomes: military conflict or a new cold war. So far, ongoing friction has not derailed the overarching consensus established in May. By keeping sanctions and countermeasures relatively limited, Beijing and Washington have avoided dangerous escalation and kept the relationship moving forward. The goal of the new diplomatic framework between Beijing and Washington is a pragmatic one. It aims to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations rather than try to achieve an unlikely grand bargain that would resolve all conflict. It also represents a changing approach in Beijing to dealing with the United States. Unlike in the past, when China rejected U.S. frameworks focused on competition, it is now willing to recognize that the fundamental nature of U.S.-Chinese relations is competitive. Allies or partners, after all, would not set strategic stability as the overarching goal of their relationship; only competitors, or even adversaries, need to do so. Beijing’s willingness to accept a formulation to manage, rather than exclude, competition shows that it is gaining confidence and seeing itself more as an equal to Washington. Adopting this confident mindset could lead China to act with more restraint in its dealings with the United States—which could in turn bring a further degree of calm to the relationship. It now appears plausible that bilateral relations have turned a corner and entered a more stable phase. Although fundamental challenges remain that could cause new turbulence, the peak tensions of the past eight years may well be receding. The upcoming leaders’ summit in late September, when Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet in Washington, is a chance to further move the relationship forward. The two leaders can now add more concrete measures to support this new framework of strategic stability, including taking steps to reduce economic friction, increase military-to-military communications, improve crisis management mechanisms, expand citizen exchanges, and offer reassurances about Taiwan, thereby defusing tensions that could escalate into potentially catastrophic military conflict. With Xi and Trump likely to meet again multiple times in the next few months, the new framework is the first chance in years to lay the groundwork for enduring stability in bilateral ties. BEYOND STRATEGIC COMPETITION For a long time, leaders in both Beijing and Washington sought to define the bilateral relationship in terms of some kind of partnership. In 1997, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin visited the United States, Beijing and Washington announced aims of “a constructive strategic partnership oriented toward the twenty-first century.” In 2005, the George W. Bush administration urged China “to become a responsible stakeholder” in the international system; Chinese leader Hu Jintao responded in 2006 that the two countries were not only stakeholders but “should also be constructive partners.” But between 2009, when President Barack Obama and Hu agreed to “steadily grow a partnership” to address common challenges, and the Trump-Xi summit earlier this year, the countries’ leaders were unable to reach a new consensus on how to position the relationship. The United States moved away from seeing the relationship as a partnership earlier than China did. During Trump’s first term, the United States began to define U.S.-Chinese relations in terms of “strategic competition.” At first, China tried to accept the competitive element in bilateral relations. Beijing acknowledged that some competition was inevitable while hoping that the relationship could remain positive overall. But as U.S.-Chinese relations deteriorated sharply in the final year of Trump’s first term and continued to worsen into the Biden administration, Beijing began to see “strategic competition” as a narrative designed to foreclose China’s rise. It felt that the U.S. approach threatened its development prospects, leading Beijing to push back more forcefully against the concept. In July 2022, during a phone call with President Joe Biden, Xi told his counterpart that it was a mistake to make competition the defining feature of the relationship. To policymakers and analysts in China, the framework of strategic competition turned all U.S.-Chinese interactions into something akin to the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. They saw the United States’ actions such as export controls on semiconductors as concrete manifestations that the United States was trying to suppress China, to undercut its political system, and to constrain its development. Although official statements from Washington discussed bilateral ties in terms of cooperation, competition, and confrontation, in practice competition and confrontation snuffed out any potential for cooperation. After almost a decade in which China rejected and criticized strategic competition, transitioning to a relationship of constructive strategic stability reflects Beijing’s recalibrated assessment of both countries’ positions and roles in the international system, as well as the new realities of U.S.-Chinese relations. China is looking at bilateral relations from a position of greater equality and with more confidence, and it is less anxious that competition will undermine its national development prospects. Instead, Beijing believes that competition can be effectively managed without presenting an existential threat. MORE THAN ONE MAN Whether strategic stability succeeds as the basis of a new phase in U.S.-Chinese relations depends on whether it is rooted in the personal wills and agendas of Trump and Xi or it arises from structural forces that are more powerful than any individual leader. Many observers in both Beijing and Washington view the emerging consensus as a contingent result of the interests of the two men currently in charge. Trump, for instance, has taken it upon himself to change the direction of U.S. policy. His unexpected turn toward embracing a more stable relationship with China coincides with other unexpected turns in his second-term agenda, including adopting a cold and even hostile attitude toward European allies and launching a war against Iran despite frequently decrying U.S. military involvement overseas. But these shifts also obscure more durable structural factors in the U.S.-Chinese relationship that have pushed the two countries toward more stability, and which make it more likely that the new diplomatic framework can survive. The current rapprochement is the fourth time in the past eight years that a period of tension between China and the United States has given way to an announcement of some kind of stable state. Ongoing friction has not derailed the consensus established in May. After China and the United States first aggressively confronted each other on trade and technology, culminating in the trade war in 2018, the two countries reached the Phase One trade agreement, in January 2020, which stabilized ties. The COVID-19 pandemic, which broke out soon afterward, severely inflamed tensions, sending the relationship to its lowest point since before U.S. President Richard Nixon first visited China, in 1972. In November 2022, Biden and Xi met in Bali and announced that they wanted to restabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, but just months later, in February 2023, recriminations over a Chinese object floating over the United States—described by Beijing as a civilian meteorological airship and by Washington as a spy balloon—interrupted such efforts. That November, Biden and Xi smoothed over ties for a third time at their San Francisco summit. This set the tenor of relations until April 2025, when Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs spawned a new trade war. Across this period, the United States went through three different presidential terms under both Democratic and Republican administrations, yet U.S.-Chinese relations repeatedly swung back to a stable state. Structural factors independent of any individual leader’s views encourage stability in the relationship. This includes the prohibitive cost of total economic decoupling and the catastrophic consequences of potential military conflict. Put differently, since the beginning of Trump’s second term, it has become clear to both sides that the bilateral relationship is simply too big to fail. The two sides occupy such important positions in global and international affairs, each with enough power to cause enormous damage, that neither wants to see the other become an enemy. The intense clashes between China and the United States over tariffs and rare earths in 2025 revealed that each side could exploit the other’s vulnerabilities, reminding them both that the two countries are highly interdependent and need to act prudently in an economic confrontation. Moreover, as nuclear powers, Beijing and Washington are aware that they cannot afford the prospect of a steadily deteriorating relationship that increases the risk of military conflict. If U.S.-Chinese relations again become more volatile after the next U.S. president takes office, it will test the resilience of the relationship. Yet the structural forces at play are unlikely to have changed. Even if future American leaders announce a new approach to the U.S.-Chinese relationship, therefore, in the end it is likely that they will come to the same realizations as their predecessors and seek stability. TANGLED UP IN RED Other critics argue that the consensus on strategic stability is, at most, a temporary truce. In their view, both sides will use this time to shore up their weaknesses, seek new sources of leverage, and prepare for a future confrontation. The United States could find alternate suppliers for the rare-earth elements it needs, for instance, and China could find new sources of semiconductors or develop its own advanced chips. But despite intense trade and geopolitical frictions, global supply chains have proved more resilient—and more deeply intertwined—than most observers anticipated. U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology have fragmented global supply chains, but they have not severed them. Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit U.S. battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on U.S. soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence will make it particularly difficult for either the United States or China to eliminate the other’s sources of leverage. New technologies create new vulnerabilities. With the possibility of artificial general intelligence on the horizon, the frictions in the U.S.-Chinese relationship are unlikely to be concentrated in the same fields and to manifest themselves in the same ways as today. The likelihood of either China or the United States creating what Chinese martial arts novels call an “iron shirt”—a training regimen that makes someone impervious to blades and bullets—is very low. As both countries acquire more powerful, faster, and less predictable technological capabilities, what is needed to preserve stability is likely to change. Attempts by either side to achieve an overwhelming advantage or to ensure absolute security could instead heighten the other’s insecurity and intensify bilateral competition, ultimately forcing both countries to accept some mutual vulnerability and a different strategic equilibrium. The two countries are already realizing that they will have to manage the enormous challenges that AI presents, especially safety risks, whether through joint action or parallel efforts. U.S.-Chinese relations have stabilized four times over the past eight years; this also means that, viewed from the opposite perspective, the relationship has repeatedly devolved into confrontation. With each successive clash producing renewed grievances and hostility, a palpable fatigue has set in on both sides. Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways. THE EAST IS RISING One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more. But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive. Structural factors have pushed the two countries toward more stability. China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States. Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea. In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition. A NEW BALLAST The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities. Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries. Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result. The goal is to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations. As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible. Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead. A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement. item.title: What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.52
What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree Ahead of January elections, Bola Tinubu is pulling out all the stops to stem insecurity. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Spending Spree Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has appointed Maj. Gen. Ibikunle Ajose as the new top army commander for the northeast, the epicenter of the country’s Islamist insurgency, after the previous leader spent less than two years in the role. The move is the latest in a series of military reforms ahead of January’s general elections, in which insecurity will be high on the list of voters’ concerns. Ajose’s appointment was part of a bigger reshuffling last week that involved 15 top generals. These redeployments, along with a major hike in military spending, are key to the government’s wider plan to stabilize bellwether regions before Nigerians head to the polls. Tinubu is seeking a second term as the candidate for the All Progressives Congress party and will face the same main challengers he came up against in 2023: former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, who is running under the African Democratic Congress (ADC), and former Anambra state Gov. Peter Obi, with the Nigeria Democratic Congress. This year, Abubakar and Obi initially joined forces to unseat Tinubu under an ADC-led opposition coalition, but the alliance fractured due to their competing ambitions. Observers are looking to see whether Obi in particular, who came in third in 2023, can translate the unprecedented backing he garnered from young Nigerian urbanites in the last election into rural support. Importantly, the public is paying close attention to how candidates intend to address widespread violence and kidnappings for ransom. A mass kidnapping of schoolchildren in Tinubu’s political heartland in the southwestern state of Oyo in May magnified the issue. More than 7,800 people were kidnapped in Nigeria between July 2025 and June 2026—a 66 percent increase from the previous year, according to a new report from risk advisory firm SBM Intelligence. Over that period, kidnappers received some $5.8 million in ransom money, three times that of the previous year. Boko Haram collected 90 percent of those payments, mainly from mass abductions. The insecurity has ripple effects across the country. For instance, many farmers have been unable to access their lands due to the threat of kidnappings, leading to food shortages and hunger, especially in the north. The “security question in Nigeria is closely connected to the economic one: An attack that closes a road, displaces farmers, or shuts a market very quickly becomes an issue of household income and food prices,” said Sekinat Ojeniyi of Africa Practice, a global risk advisory firm. On the campaign trail, Abubakar has pledged to end insecurity within one year if elected. His plan centers on cross-border military collaboration with Sahel nations and providing jobs for young people drawn to extremism. Obi has also promised to fix insecurity in one term through youth poverty alleviation and education. “You cannot create widespread poverty and expect peace,” Obi told Nigerian broadcaster Channels Television. Tinubu’s government, meanwhile, is injecting unprecedented amounts of money into defense in an attempt to address the issue. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Nigeria’s military expenditure surged 55 percent year-on-year to $2.1 billion in 2025. That figure is expected to double this year. With this money, Tinubu approved salary increases for members of the military last month. The massive investment also supports the largest expansion of the Nigerian military since the country’s civil war in the late 1960s. In July, Tinubu approved the creation of four new army divisions with a planned recruitment of 28,000 additional personnel by December. A new bill passed by Nigeria’s National Assembly in June would also allow states to establish their own police forces, putting less pressure on the federal police to secure dense forested communities that have become hideouts for extremists. “The government’s emphasis on manpower and personnel welfare makes sense, but more personnel and better pay do not automatically translate into greater security,” Ojeniyi said. “Kidnapping networks are highly adaptive and operate across state and local government boundaries, while the police, military, and intelligence agencies do not always have the same visibility or operational reach.” Meanwhile, many Nigerian and U.S. political observers have commended Tinubu for his handling of tensions with Washington, which has transformed the Trump administration’s divisive rhetoric about supposed Christian persecution in Nigeria into security cooperation. Beginning late last year, the United States deployed troops to assist with counterterrorism operations. (Most U.S. troops withdrew in July.) Although U.S. strikes in northeastern Nigeria in May killed a senior Islamic State leader, the mass abductions have continued. More than 600 people were taken from Nigeria’s north-central Niger state last month in an attack on a mosque. Although many Nigerians welcome his new security reforms, Tinubu will likely be judged on whether these last-gasp efforts a few months ahead of elections can stem the violence. The Week Ahead Wednesday, Sept. 16: The U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee holds a nomination hearing on ambassadors to Benin, Gabon, Kenya, and Togo. Wednesday, Sept. 16, to Thursday, Sept. 17: Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo meet in Geneva to discuss monitoring their cease-fire. Wednesday, Sept. 23: Morocco holds general elections. What We’re Watching Historic IPO. Africa’s richest person, Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote, launched the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering on Monday, floating 4.1 billion shares in his $20 billion oil refinery on the outskirts of Lagos on the Nigerian Exchange. The rush to buy shares briefly crashed many Nigerian investment apps. The move is expected to raise about $1.6 billion, which will fund Dangote’s expansion projects across Africa. Dangote Industries said it will use the investment to double production capacity, deliver refined products across the continent, and build another refinery in Kenya. The public offer closes on Oct. 13, and Dangote is reportedly eyeing a secondary New York listing in the future. Sahrawi citizenship. The Spanish parliament’s lower house approved a bill granting citizenship to Sahrawis born before 1977, when Madrid administered Western Sahara. The legislation will now go to Spain’s Senate. It marks the latest escalation of tensions with Morocco after thousands of migrants entered Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta from Morocco in late July. Rabat claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Western Sahara, and it has occupied about 80 percent of the latter’s territory since the 1970s. More than 170,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps in Algeria, which hosts the Polisario Front, a group fighting for Sahrawi independence. U.S. tech bid. The United States will lend nearly $100 million to Africell, the only mainstream U.S.-owned mobile network operator in Africa, as part of broader strategic investments to counter China in the region. Africell operates in Angola, Congo, Gambia, and Sierra Leone. The loan from the U.S. Export-Import Bank is part of Washington’s efforts to counter the expansion of China’s Huawei company in Africa. But the United States has a long way to go: Chinese firms are now baked into the continent’s tech infrastructure. For example, the three major smartphone brands in Africa—Tecno, Itel, and Infinix—are manufactured by China’s Transsion and have dominated the market for nearly two decades. Congo-Israel ties. Congo has revived plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem following President Felix Tshisekedi’s visit to the country earlier this month. Analysts consider the move an attempt to both court Israeli security support and get the United States to exert more pressure on Rwanda to stop backing the M23 rebel group in eastern Congo. Tshisekedi previously told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2023 that Congo would move the embassy, three years after Tshisekedi announced that he would appoint its first ambassador to Israel in more than two decades. Meanwhile, Tshisekedi faces mounting calls in Congo to resign over his attempts to implement constitutional reforms that could pave the way for a third term in office. This Week in Health The United States has announced that it will no longer fund Namibia’s HIV program after a final $45 million disbursement for the 2027 fiscal year, ending more than two decades of aid through the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, which has provided around $1.1 billion to Namibia since it was launched under President George W. Bush in 2003. The withdrawal follows Namibia’s refusal to give the United States unrestricted access to genetic data and pathogens, which it could then share with private companies and organizations without oversight from the Namibian government as part of Trump’s America First Global Health Strategy. Namibian officials cited concerns over sovereignty, national law, and patient privacy. Since pulling out of the World Health Organization in January, the Trump administration has pursued deals that would provide commercial access to African nations’ health data. So far, Ghana, Zambia, and Zimbabwe have rejected such deals, while at least 19 nations, including Nigeria and Ethiopia, have agreed to them. “We need to reserve our data, and no one has the right to get a sovereign state to be used for other things, except for the World Health Organization cabinet,” former Namibian Health Minister Richard Kamwi said in August. FP’s Most Read This Week - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan What We’re Reading Al-Shabab’s win. In Foreign Policy, Mohamed Gabobe reports from Mogadishu on how the U.S. withdrawal of support for the African Union peacekeeping mission in the country has severely jeopardized the remaining forces’ capacity to counter the Islamist group al-Shabab. The two-decade military intervention’s failure to quash al-Shabab—which has “has retaken nearly all the territory that it lost in a 2022-2023 Somali army campaign,” Gabobe writes—partly informed Washington’s decision. There “is no one other nation that can fill the United States’ void,” he adds. What’s in a map? On Sept. 4, the United Nations General Assembly voted to adopt a Togo-sponsored resolution to replace the traditional Mercator map with one that better represents Africa’s true size. Only the United States voted against it. In Foreign Policy, Howard W. French argues that this is just the latest example of the West being behind in understanding not just Africa’s geographic size but also its demographic weight. “Just as drawing up maps in ways that graphically diminish Africa does nothing to reduce Africa’s true dimensions, actively shunning African migrants will do nothing to change the hard demographic realities that will radically shape our collective future,” he writes. Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. item.title: Why Existential AI Fears Have Hit a Crescendo
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.93
Why Existential AI Fears Have Hit a Crescendo And the complicated geopolitics of slowing down the technology’s development. Long before ChatGPT and Claude entered the global lexicon, there had been a steady stream of warnings about the dangers of artificial intelligence. That stream has now become a flood. Late last month, OpenAI revealed a worrisome new development: Not only had one of its models broken out of its “sandbox” and hacked the company Hugging Face, it had in fact done so in secret coordination with hundreds of other OpenAI models (or “agents”). Subsequent reports revealed that OpenAI’s agents had previously infiltrated two other websites months before the Hugging Face incident. Long before ChatGPT and Claude entered the global lexicon, there had been a steady stream of warnings about the dangers of artificial intelligence. That stream has now become a flood. Late last month, OpenAI revealed a worrisome new development: Not only had one of its models broken out of its “sandbox” and hacked the company Hugging Face, it had in fact done so in secret coordination with hundreds of other OpenAI models (or “agents”). Subsequent reports revealed that OpenAI’s agents had previously infiltrated two other websites months before the Hugging Face incident. The hacks exacerbated long-standing concerns around the growing cyber-capabilities of advanced AI models, including their ability to find vulnerabilities in software systems and the potential for AI-assisted bad actors to more easily disrupt poorly defended critical infrastructure such as water systems. The same day as the OpenAI report, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates published an essay warning about the “turbulent AI era” and highlighting societal risks from the technology such as widespread job losses, diminished human cognition and relationships, and use by a variety of bad actors to do harm. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve wished innovation could happen faster,” he wrote. “With AI, my feelings are more complicated.” But even those warnings were dwarfed by the highly public resignation last week of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic who previously worked at OpenAI. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote in a viral social media post announcing his resignation. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Coxon’s sentiments were echoed by several current employees at Anthropic, including Evan Hubinger, who leads the company’s research on alignment (making sure AI models are aligned with humans). “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote, adding that he estimated there was a more than 10 percent chance of that happening within the next decade. Last Thursday, Anthropic released its latest threat intelligence report containing alarming examples of misuse of its Claude models. Days later, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay of his own calling on companies to slow down the pace of AI development and for global governments to do more to rein in the technology. Some of his biggest rival executives—including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, xAI’s Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis—voiced their agreement in a rare kumbaya moment. All of this has sparked an AI panic in Washington and beyond. U.S. lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are advocating for greater oversight of artificial intelligence. It’s also made for strange bedfellows: Left-wing U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and far-right provocateur Steve Bannon both spoke at a Washington conference called the “Pro-Human Assembly” on Tuesday and called for curbs on AI. But neither the fears nor the calls to slow down are new. The latter date back to at least 2023, when an open letter calling for a six-month pause on “giant AI experiments” received over 33,000 signatures—including Musk’s. Several similar letters and calls have followed, including one as recently as July that was signed by more than 1,300 employees of the top AI companies—including Amodei. “This has been a conversation for quite some time,” said Rumman Chowdhury, an AI researcher who served on the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s AI safety and security board under the Biden administration. “Jacob Coxon is not the first person to leave a frontier lab making similar claims,” she said, joking that AI has long slipped into an “another day, another letter” pattern without meaningful change. So why has the conversation around AI risk spiraled this time? Multiple experts Foreign Policy spoke to used the phrase “perfect storm” when answering that question, pointing to the Hugging Face hack and the revelation about the models’ ability to create a “swarm” to perform tasks together. Amodei expressed “worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet” if the current rate of AI development is maintained. There has always been a heavy degree of skepticism on the motives of AI companies warning about the existential risks of the technology that they continue to forge ahead in building. Amodei acknowledged in his essay that Anthropic gets accused of “hype, ‘doomerism’, or regulatory capture,” adding that he didn’t feel a pause was appropriate back in 2023 but advocates a slowdown now because of how far the technology’s capabilities have progressed. Coxon sought to head off some of those frequent criticisms more pointedly right after warning that AI could kill everyone. “This is not a marketing stunt,” he wrote. Amodei’s claims and the rush of industry warnings should be taken seriously, said Kat Duffy, a senior fellow for digital and cyberspace policy at the Council on Foreign Relations. “I don’t agree with people that these are necessarily PR stunts pre-IPO,” Duffy said, referring to OpenAI and Anthropic’s anticipated trillion-dollar initial public offerings. “You would say that this is incredibly dangerous and look at how good we are at controlling it, or you would say that this is incredibly powerful but it’s not really that dangerous,” she added. “Saying that this is really dangerous and we desperately need the government to jump in—it’s not clear to me why that’s in anyone’s interest as they start to go public.” However, the debate around existential risk to humanity from AI also obfuscates the many real-world harms that the technology is already causing, such as surveillance, algorithmic bias, discrimination, deepfakes, and data misuse, according to Chowdhury. “These are not the issues that are being discussed,” she said. “The regulatory structures or whatever environment that pops up around the kinds of risks that are being talked about today simply lead to a regulatory capture on a very, very narrow set of fantastical scenarios,” she added. The bigger priority, Duffy said, should be increased transparency and visibility into how AI systems are built and tested. “There is a tension between addressing what needs to happen yesterday and addressing the possibilities of catastrophic or existential risk,” she said. “If we do not go on and address the vacuum we currently have in terms of systems, collaboration, independent evaluation and vetting, shared standards, shared understanding of the problem—if we don’t have that, how on earth are we going to be able to navigate things like existential threats?” U.S. President Donald Trump’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington next week has also contributed to that “perfect storm,” Duffy said. AI is expected to be high on the agenda when the two leaders meet, with many—including Amodei—hoping for the emergence of some sort of shared mechanism to manage the technology’s most catastrophic risks. But early indications are that neither Trump nor Xi is ready to blink first. Trump spent much of Monday dismissing concerns around AI risk and the need to regulate the industry. “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX,” he wrote in a post on Truth Social, one of five separate posts in which he shared a similar message. In that initial post, he cited Xi as announcing that “China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future.” Duffy said China’s advances actually make an argument for more governance, not less, particularly when the leading U.S. AI executives are asking for it. “China continues to close the gap between where we are in AI and where they are in AI,” she said. “Everybody can agree or disagree on exactly what that metric is, but I think there’s uniform consensus that they have been gaining, and they are the most heavily regulated AI environment in the world.” Xi has not directly weighed in on the ongoing debate thus far, but China’s state-run Global Times newspaper published an editorial on Sunday labeling Amodei’s call to slow down AI development a “Cold War playbook” for the technology that is “packed with containment provisions targeting China.” Beijing has long sought to present itself as the more responsible global player when it comes to AI development and governance but hinted on Tuesday that it would prefer doing so through the United Nations—which also convenes for its biggest annual gathering next week—rather than a bilateral agreement with Washington. “AI development and governance require the practice of true multilateralism,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Tuesday. “China always supports the UN’s role as the main channel in global AI governance, and … stands ready to join hands with all countries to build a just and equitable system.” It was a slight hedging of Guo’s statement from the previous day when asked about U.S. AI executives calling for a slowdown, when he said: “Fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only hamper efforts toward sound global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest.” Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.34
Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente Despite the thaw, India-China rivalry remains inevitable. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Modi, Xi Meet on BRICS Sideline Over the weekend, Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to India for the first time in seven years. Xi was in New Delhi for 24 hours to attend this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, where he held a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. An Indian Foreign Ministry statement said the two leaders pledged to strengthen commercial and cultural cooperation. A more striking readout came from Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who said that the bilateral meeting covered long-term, strategic issues and that Modi and Xi reached “the most important consensus” to be partners, not rivals. Beijing hopes the meeting will advance bilateral ties “without stagnation or backsliding,” Wang added. These are positive words for a relationship between major competitors—and one that was plunged into deep crisis after a deadly 2020 border clash in the Ladakh region. But an India-China rapprochement has been playing out for nearly two years. Xi’s visit marked the culmination, not the commencement, of India-China detente. Still, the extent of the thaw shouldn’t be overstated. Historically, India-China ties have had their moments, with ample heady talk and good optics. Invariably, fresh tensions have spoiled them; the two are destined to remain rivals by history, geography, and geopolitics. In October 2024, the post-Ladakh tensions began to ease with the inking of a new border agreement. India and China subsequently made pledges to resume direct air flights and bolster commercial cooperation. In March 2025, Modi said on a podcast that cooperation with China was “essential” for global stability. Contrary to some commentary, the detente began before U.S. President Donald Trump was elected to a second term and wasn’t sparked by his policies. But Trump’s tariffs, which have hit both India and China hard, and concerns about access to U.S. markets gave both sides a strong incentive to accelerate their rapprochement and especially to deepen trade ties. However, the reality is that continued India-China rivalry is all but inevitable. Both countries are both proud civilizational states and dispute claims to around 15,000 square miles of territory—equal to the size of Greece—along their shared border. They disagree on many other major issues, from Taiwan and Tibet to surveillance. Perhaps most significantly, China is a close ally of India’s bitter rival Pakistan. Last year, the Pakistani military used Chinese weaponry in air combat operations against India for the first time. Such challenges may seem surmountable, given what the India-China relationship has going for it. This includes their rock-solid trade partnership, shared interests, and considerable cooperation in global forums (including BRICS, but also the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.) Not surprisingly, India-China ties have often enjoyed periods of warmth—but ultimately a trigger, often a border provocation, has shattered that calm. In 2017, a few years after Xi and Modi were photographed smiling on a swing together, a 73-day military standoff on the Doklam Plateau plunged relations into crisis. The Ladakh clash came just months after another Modi-Xi summit in India. Though border tensions have subsided, territorial disputes still fester and occasionally flare. To be sure, there are plenty of reasons for New Delhi and Beijing to bury the hatchet. They want to ease tensions along their fraught border, create space for deeper commercial cooperation, hedge against Trump’s unpredictability, and remove a diplomatic headache from the BRICS grouping, which both capitals badly want to succeed. Ultimately, however, so many divergences and sources of lingering mistrust preempt the possibility of full-on rapprochement. Though an extended period of cooperation is possible, it’s likely only a matter of time before the very “stagnation and backsliding” that Beijing says it wants to avoid. What We’re Following Bangladesh passes 1,000 measles deaths. More than 1,000 people in Bangladesh have now died from the measles virus since March 15, according to the latest government figures, released on Sept. 9. The country is suffering the world’s worst measles outbreak; it has logged thousands of new cases this year, including nearly 60,000 between January and June alone. Nearly 20 million children have been vaccinated in Bangladesh since a new national inoculation campaign was launched in April. Health experts attribute the ongoing crisis to underestimations of how many children needed to be vaccinated—the target figure was 18 million, but experts say that a more accurate estimate is 22.6 million. The number of measles vaccinations in Bangladesh—both first and second doses—fell between 2019 and 2023, and this year’s national campaign was the first since one from December 2020 to January 2021, during the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. A sudden change of government in August 2024 caused further vaccine interruptions. The current government, which took office in February, is working hard to ease the crisis. But it must grapple with not only the large number of children who still need to be vaccinated, but also economic stress and energy shortages that further complicate inoculation efforts. Thousands still missing in Nepal. Three weeks after a glacial collapse precipitated catastrophic floods in Nepal, more than 5,000 people remain missing. Authorities say they continue to search and are trying to provide information to families as soon as possible. But massive destruction—including 2.2 million tons of—has made search and rescue difficult. Authorities are now transitioning from search and rescue to relief and reconstruction efforts, with an eye toward the large number of people who lost their homes. The disaster leveled entire villages, submerged tunnels, and swept away hydropower facilities. Damage to roads and bridges has created additional complications. Nepal’s government said that the total estimated cost for reconstruction efforts will be $4.8 billion—around one-tenth of the country’s total nominal GDP. Sri Lanka signs labor accords with Thailand. This week, Sri Lanka and Thailand signed agreements to enable 10,000 Sri Lankans to work in the Southeast Asian country, with a focus on young workers and sectors including information technology and tourism. The Sri Lankan workers will receive equal rights and protections under Thai labor laws. The agreements address a key need for both countries: Thailand has a labor shortage, and Sri Lanka is looking to tap into a wider array of foreign labor markets. But the deal goes against a common pattern in Sri Lanka—and elsewhere in South Asia—in which young people go to the Middle East, Europe, or the United States for work. There appears to be a cultural factor at play. The Sri Lankan government believes cultural similarities between Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia will make for a smoother adjustment process—putting them in a strong position to be productive and send home remittances that are critical for the Sri Lankan economy. FP’s Most Read This Week How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan Under the Radar Last week, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said that it was not contemplating the use of military force against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Middle East. The statement came in response to speculation, fueled by a Turkish news report, that Pakistan was considering invoking the Mecca Agreement—the new mutual defense pact among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey—and joining a military operation with the Saudis against the Houthis. Houthi attacks against Saudi targets have escalated in recent days. Pakistan’s statement gives ammunition to critics of the Mecca Agreement—as well as a similar bilateral deal between Islamabad and Riyadh—who dismiss the accord as a paper tiger. In the last year, Taliban military operations have hit Pakistan has been hit multiple times; Saudi Arabia has been assaulted by the Houthis as well as direct Iranian strikes. At no time has Pakistan or Saudi Arabia intervened militarily to assist the other, though Pakistan has sent some arms and troops to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Still, the two mutual defense pacts are mainly meant to focus on deterrence, which the signatories say the United States cannot provide sufficiently in the Middle East. In Pakistan’s case, the accords are meant to help advance key foreign-policy priorities, including playing a larger role in the security architecture of the region. Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. item.title: Are Chinese Firms Handing the United States Data?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.27
Are Chinese Firms Handing the United States Data? AI competition may be an unwitting weakness for Beijing. A recent report by the U.S. artificial intelligence company Anthropic accused several leading Chinese AI firms, including Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, of distilling Claude’s capabilities on a large scale. Anthropic said some of these companies went beyond using Claude to generate training data and, without users’ knowledge, in one instance routed at least 300,000 requests from real users through the model over a 10-day period. The data reportedly sent to Claude included surveillance material submitted by a user Anthropic suspected of being affiliated with the People’s Liberation Army; internal code and valid credentials from engineers at major Chinese state-owned enterprises; information from police case management systems; and details of internal AI projects at Chinese technology companies. A recent report by the U.S. artificial intelligence company Anthropic accused several leading Chinese AI firms, including Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, of distilling Claude’s capabilities on a large scale. Anthropic said some of these companies went beyond using Claude to generate training data and, without users’ knowledge, in one instance routed at least 300,000 requests from real users through the model over a 10-day period. The data reportedly sent to Claude included surveillance material submitted by a user Anthropic suspected of being affiliated with the People’s Liberation Army; internal code and valid credentials from engineers at major Chinese state-owned enterprises; information from police case management systems; and details of internal AI projects at Chinese technology companies. The leakage of sensitive information will of course alarm Beijing. But compared with one or two pieces of sensitive material reaching the United States, the bigger worry may be that, in the process of distilling the capabilities of the most advanced U.S. models, Chinese AI companies may also be sending large quantities of real Chinese user data to the United States. AI competition is not just about compute but about data. Today, data available on the open internet is increasingly easy to obtain. What is truly scarce is the high-quality data generated by real tasks: why users turn to AI, what problems they are trying to solve, what background materials they provide, how far they have progressed in writing code, what technical obstacles companies encounter, and what they want AI to help them accomplish. Such data can be far more valuable than the ordinary detritus of the web. On its own, such data may not mean much or be worth much. But once hundreds of thousands, millions, or even tens of millions of such pieces of data are aggregated, their nature changes completely. A Chinese programmer asking why a piece of code failed has little or no intelligence value. But if thousands of Chinese engineers repeatedly encounter and ask about similar problems, the aggregate may expose a common bottleneck in a Chinese technological system. Likewise, an employee asking how to improve a particular piece of equipment or software would hardly be a concern—or a secret. But if large numbers of engineers from industries such as semiconductors, robotics, aerospace, telecommunications, electricity, and automobiles are continually talking about their work to AI models, over time those interactions could allow others to form a dynamic map of China’s industrial and technological capabilities. This data is more telling than conventional searches. Those queries generally reveal what a person wants to know, but AI often reveals what a person is actually doing. Users voluntarily provide work context, upload code, documents, and project descriptions; explain what they have already tried; identify the problems they have encountered; and describe what they intend to do next. This is a very particular kind of data. It might be called intent data. It tells outsiders not only what China possesses but what China is doing. In peacetime, such data primarily has commercial and technological value. But as tensions between the two superpowers grow, so too will the value of such a data mine. Imagine a scenario where war seems to be on the horizon. U.S. intelligence agencies would need to know not only how many missiles and warships China possesses but also whether its military-industrial system is accelerating production; where bottlenecks are emerging; which civilian companies are beginning to enter wartime production; what weaknesses exist in semiconductors, drones, communications, electricity and transportation; and which research institutions are suddenly concentrating on particular problems. Large volumes of AI interactions could provide precisely this kind of information. When the institutions, names, equipment, software, suppliers and technical failures mentioned in AI conversations are combined with satellite imagery, customs records, procurement data, patents, academic papers, corporate information, network data, and other intelligence already available to the United States, an apparently ordinary user query can become one node in a much larger network. Hundreds of thousands or millions of such nodes, taken together, could prove far more valuable than one or two traditionally classified documents. This raises a question that has received almost no attention: Did Beijing previously know that Chinese AI companies, in the course of distilling U.S. models, were sending real user data to the United States? China has plenty of data security regulations. In recent years, Beijing has repeatedly tightened oversight of cross-border data transfers. The Provisions on Promoting and Regulating Cross-Border Data Flow impose security assessment requirements and other restrictions on the overseas transfer of important data—defined in terms of what could endanger national security, the economy, or social stability—and large volumes of personal information. China’s rules governing generative AI services also explicitly require providers to protect users’ personal information, trade secrets, and data security. The question is whether this regulatory system recognized a new form of cross-border data transfer. Instead of a Chinese company formally exporting a database to a foreign company, an AI company seeking to train its own model may use proxy accounts and intermediary services to quietly feed batches of real user requests into a U.S. foundation model. If Beijing was unaware, then Anthropic’s report has exposed a major blind spot in China’s AI regulatory system. China may have been scrutinizing multinational companies transferring databases to the United States while failing to notice that its own leading AI companies were continuously sending users’ work, code, technical difficulties, and even sensitive materials into U.S. models through model calls. But even if China now understands the problem, that will not make it easy to resolve. On the one hand, Beijing may require Chinese AI companies to stop such practices or at the very least prohibit them from sending unprocessed real user data into U.S. models. Given China’s existing data security laws and regulatory capacity, doing so would not be difficult. On the other hand, why would Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek, Xiaomi, and other companies take such risks to access and distill Claude on a massive scale? The answer appears equally obvious: The capabilities of U.S. frontier models remain valuable to Chinese companies. According to Anthropic, Alibaba’s distillation-related activity exceeded 151 million exchanges between May and July; Moonshot’s exceeded 23 million; and DeepSeek conducted more than 12.1 million exchanges in just 14 days in July. This amounted to industrial-scale acquisition of technological capability. Moonshot and DeepSeek were even accused of building dedicated technical pipelines designed to extract Claude’s reasoning process for use in training their own models. This illustrates the dilemma confronting China. Distilling the most advanced U.S. models has become an important means for some Chinese companies to narrow the technological gap. China has engineers, computing power, its own large models, and a strong AI industry. But if Chinese companies are completely cut off from distilling the capabilities of leading U.S. models, producing training data and reasoning capabilities of comparable quality independently would require more time, computing power, and trial and error. In the short term, the pace at which China catches up with U.S. frontier models could therefore slow. If Chinese AI companies are allowed to continue distilling U.S. models on a large scale, Beijing must accept the risk that Chinese data will continue to flow into U.S. systems. If that route is tightly shut down for data security reasons, however, the cost of catching up may rise, and the technological time gap may widen further. As AI competition increasingly depends on distillation, data, and the exchange of model capabilities, China therefore faces a difficult question: How can it take advantage of the most advanced U.S. AI capabilities without allowing China’s own data to become a strategic asset for the United States? Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: Are Drone Incursions Europe’s New Normal?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.23
Are Drone Incursions Europe’s New Normal? NATO suspects that Russia is behind the latest airspace violation in Lithuania. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at NATO intercepting a drone in Lithuania, the threat of Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, and a long-running maritime dispute between Thailand and Cambodia. ‘Get Out and Stay Out—or Else’ NATO deployed fighter jets overnight on Tuesday to shoot down a drone that violated Lithuanian airspace. Although local authorities did not initially comment on the drone’s origin or purpose, European officials were quick to point fingers at Russia, which has repeatedly been accused of orchestrating military incursions, arson attacks, and other acts of sabotage against Ukraine’s European allies. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at NATO intercepting a drone in Lithuania, the threat of Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, and a long-running maritime dispute between Thailand and Cambodia. ‘Get Out and Stay Out—or Else’ NATO deployed fighter jets overnight on Tuesday to shoot down a drone that violated Lithuanian airspace. Although local authorities did not initially comment on the drone’s origin or purpose, European officials were quick to point fingers at Russia, which has repeatedly been accused of orchestrating military incursions, arson attacks, and other acts of sabotage against Ukraine’s European allies. Over the past few years, NATO members have blamed both Russia and Ukraine of launching stray missiles, drones, and aircraft into the territories of Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania, among others. However, allegations against Moscow have become particularly vehement this week following an attack on a civilian train in Ukraine near the Polish border on Sunday, which narrowly missed a separate train carrying several senior European leaders, including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt. “It’s difficult not to interpret the incident, so far out west and so near the border of a NATO member state, as a message from [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to Europe: Get out and stay out—or else,” argued Foreign Policy editor in chief Ravi Agrawal, who was aboard the diplomatic train when the strike occurred. But the alliance does not appear to have been cowed. Russian strikes so close to NATO territory show Putin’s “desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror,” NATO chief Mark Rutte said on Monday. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen echoed that sentiment, saying, “Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger.” That resolve continues to be tested. According to Lithuanian military officials, Tuesday’s drone incursion potentially entered from neighboring Belarus, which remains closely allied with Russia, and “likely” carried explosives. Meanwhile, in a separate incident late Monday, Denmark accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at a Danish helicopter in the Baltic Sea. Vladimir Barbin, Russia’s ambassador in Copenhagen, insisted on Tuesday that “dangerous maneuvers” made by the Danish aircraft were to blame for the incident; however, Copenhagen dismissed those allegations and summoned Barbin in response. “One thing is very clear: Putin will not stop unless he is stopped,” European Union foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Tuesday, pledging to ramp up measures against the Kremlin’s so-called hybrid attacks. “So, as Russia is willing to take greater risks, Europe must impose a greater cost.” But if NATO’s European members are hoping to strengthen their threats with support from the United States, they might be out of luck. Rather than condemning Russian incursions into NATO airspace, U.S. President Donald Trump has instead urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to cease strikes on Russian diesel facilities, arguing that the ensuing fuel shortages are “hurting the world.” On Monday, Trump claimed that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed not to hit energy targets, but Zelensky stressed that Ukraine would only stop striking Russian territory if NATO could secure a genuine promise from the Kremlin not to attack critical Ukrainian infrastructure. Today’s Most Read - Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree - Why My Kyiv Visit Worried Me So Much by Ravi Agrawal - Why 9/11 Baffles Us 25 Years Later by Michael Hirsh What We’re Following The Iran war’s new front. Saudi Arabia’s civil defense agency on Tuesday issued security alerts across several urban areas of the country, including in the holy city of Mecca and the country’s second-largest city, Jeddah, following a week of attacks on the kingdom by Yemen’s Houthis. Although the warnings were quickly lifted, the extensive swath of territory that they covered illustrates growing fears that the conflict is likely to get worse. Fighting between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed forces has added a new front to the Iran war. On Tuesday, Saudi officials accused the Iranian proxy group of injuring 13 people in recent attacks, and Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry claimed that Saudi strikes had killed three people, including two children. Alongside the human toll, the conflict has further destabilized a global oil market that was already under strain from the Iran war’s disruption to the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis’ seizure of critical Red Sea ports and islands now threatens another critical shipping lane in the Middle East, while Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure and a devastating attack on the country’s East-West pipeline, allegedly by an Iranian-supported militia in Iraq, have hampered operations in one of the world’s biggest oil producing-countries. Riyadh and its allies have tried to downplay the long-term impact of these assaults. The crude oil outage in Saudi Arabia “will be measured in days,” U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday, calling the East-West pipeline attack a “brief and temporary interruption.” Yet oil futures have jumped in response to repeated Iranian-backed attacks on Saudi Arabia, with the price of Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate exceeding $106 and $102 per barrel, respectively, early Tuesday. Who controls the sea? Thailand and Cambodia’s foreign ministers delivered their opening statements on Tuesday as part of the two countries’ first meeting intended to settle a long-running maritime dispute. Arbitrated by the United Nations, Bangkok and Phnom Penh aim to establish a single, all-purpose boundary in the Gulf of Thailand to reinstitute an equitable sharing of resources agreement that collapsed four months ago. In 2001, Thailand and Cambodia signed a framework allowing them to jointly exploit resources from their disputed maritime area; that overlapping region is estimated to hold nearly 12 trillion cubic feet of natural gas as well as oil deposits worth around $300 billion. But this May, following fierce border clashes in 2025, Bangkok terminated the agreement. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul argued that the decision was not tied to last year’s deadly attacks, which killed dozens of soldiers and civilians on both sides and displaced hundreds of thousands of people. However, Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn saw the two incidents as related and stressed that Phnom Penh “has no choice” but to settle the dispute via the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. This will be the second time in history that the treaty’s compulsory conciliation process will be used to resolve a territorial feud, with the first instance being between Australia and Timor-Leste in 2016. Seeking independence. The leaders of Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales issued a stark warning on Monday to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham: A breakup of the United Kingdom is in their future. “We believe that constitutional change is coming,” the first ministers wrote in a joint statement during their inaugural Celtic Alliance summit in Cardiff, Wales. “We believe the future of our nations belongs in the European Union.” This is the first time that pro-independence or pro-unification parties have led all three British constituent countries. Last week, Burnham told Scottish First Minister John Swinney that a second referendum for Scotland to seek independence was “off-limits”; in 2014, Scottish voters rejected independence by a 10.6-point margin. Meanwhile, Wales and Northern Ireland have never held a formal referendum for independence, though both of their governments host sizable secession movements. However, Trump’s visit to his golf course in Ireland over the weekend, during which he said that he’d “love to see” a reunified Ireland, has reignited the conversation. “No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future,” Monday’s joint declaration said. Odds and Ends Tuesday marked one week since Italy displayed what is believed to be the largest fresco and mosaic complex of ancient Rome. The “Painted City” and “Great Mosaic” were discovered during underground excavations near the Colosseum in the 1990s but only became available for public viewing this month. Although it is unclear which port city is depicted in both artworks, experts laud them for their “artistic beauty” and their “historic and documental importance,” Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri said at the unveiling. item.title: Is Your Strategic Plan Too Ambitious? Or Not Ambitious Enough?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.98
Summary. How ambitious should your strategic plan be? Aim too low, and you may settle for incremental gains. Aim too high, and you risk overwhelming the organization. Finding the right balance requires You’re weighing a plan to enter a new market, launch a new offering, or create a new business division. You have benchmarks in mind and a rough sense of the cost. What you don’t know is whether your idea is ambitious enough to be worth it.

item.title: Research: Gen AI Is Collapsing Creative Processes
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.36
Summary. Generative AI is transforming creative work by making it faster and easier to brainstorm and visualize ideas. But a new, yearlong study following senior creatives in charge of television and Imagine a photographer reviewing a concept image for an advertising campaign that the client has already approved. He notices a problem: The man in the image is wearing a baseball cap that casts his face in shadow, but his eyes are clearly lit, showing his intense stare into the camera. The photographer’s trained eye tells him immediately that that lighting is impossible. No real-world set up could produce it. The image had been created by a senior creative using gen AI, and the client had loved it. Now the production team has been tasked with recreating—with cameras and human actors—something that reality can’t match.

item.title: Will Your Organization Stand By Its Values—Even When It’s Hard?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 2.90
Will Your Organization Stand By Its Values—Even When It’s Hard? Summary. Organizational values often emphasize what companies stand for, but their real power may lie in defining what they refuse to do, Thirty years ago, Ralph Larsen, then the CEO of Johnson & Johnson, was interviewed by Jim Collins and Jerry Porras, who quoted him in their 1996 HBR article, “Building Your Company’s Vision,” which would become the defining playbook on organizational values. “The core values embodied in our credo might be a competitive advantage,” Larsen said, “but that is not why we have them. We have them because they define for us what we stand for, and we would hold them even if they became a competitive disadvantage in certain situations.”

item.title: Execution-Led Adaptability Is the New Supply Chain Advantage
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 2.63
By Eugene Amigud, Chief Product & Innovation Officer, Infios Traditionally, supply chain planning has been based on stable assumptions about demand, lead times, and costs. But despite heavy investment in AI forecasting, demand sensing, and predictive analytics, unplanned supply chain incidents still cost businesses $184 billion annually, according to the J.S. Held Global Risk Report 2025. Many leaders assume the problem stems from flawed data and inaccurate models. But recent risk analyses show disruptions are the norm, not the exception. The first major challenge to the forecasting framework was COVID-19, which wreaked havoc with the global supply chain for everything from flour to semiconductors. In 2025, the sudden implementation of tariffs by the U.S. upended the board yet again. In 2026, the closing of the Strait of Hormuz due to hostilities between the U.S. and Iran has disrupted the transport of multiple commodities, hurting many sectors in global trade, including energy, agriculture, and manufacturing. In this unpredictable environment, even the most sophisticated forecasting models fall short. Forecasts depend on patterns. Geopolitical conflict, climate events, regulatory change, and cyber attacks have little historical precedent to model against, which is exactly what makes them so hard to forecast. In addition, supply chains are now subject to several layers of risk at the same time. One disruption is enough to test a system, but these events often interact, creating a cascade of failures that is difficult, if not impossible, to recover from. Most companies are running on technology infrastructure that was never designed for this degree of chaos. Their operating models were built for linear plans instead of nonlinear shocks. And even the most sophisticated forecasting model produces insights no one can act on fast enough: Decision-making is slow, execution is fragmented, and the gap between knowing that something changed and doing something about it is too wide. Meanwhile, changes continue to unfold at all times, keeping teams stuck in reactive mode as they try to keep up. And as the burden of making decisions and synchronizing action falls on overwhelmed operators, risks and costs increase. Nearly 60% of supply chain leaders say manual workflows and interventions are the biggest source of inefficiency in their operations. Their mistake is to treat these disruptions as surprises instead of assuming they will happen. That shift from prediction-led planning to execution-led adaptability is the real opportunity. This mindset moves resilience to the center of any solution, asking not “What will happen?” but “How fast can we respond when it does?” A New Model for Performance With traditional forecasting, by the time businesses catch up with major disruptions, inventory has already been delayed, orders have been rerouted, and customer commitments are at risk. Supply chain leaders are clear on the better strategy: 79% say the biggest advantage comes from how quickly and dynamically they can adjust their execution and plans. The key performance metric today is not forecast accuracy but time to adapt: measuring how long it takes your company to detect disruption, respond to it, and recover from it.
