item.title: 'Machine Gods' explores the latest developments in the world of AI
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 5.30
'Machine Gods' explores the latest developments in the world of AI NPR's Steve Inskeep talks to tech journalists Casey Newton and Kevin Roose about their new show 'Machine Gods,' which is coming to NPR. STEVE INSKEEP, BYLINE: Two leading tech journalists are founding a new video show on AI, and it's coming to NPR twice a week. The hosts are Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, previously known to the tech world for the New York Times podcast "Hard Fork," among other things. Their new venture on NPR is called Machine Gods, and it launches in October. Gentlemen, welcome. KEVIN ROOSE, BYLINE: Thanks so much, Steve. CASEY NEWTON, BYLINE: Hey, Steve. INSKEEP: And I want listeners to understand each of your voices. Will you each just say your names? ROOSE: Yes. I'm Kevin Roose. NEWTON: And I'm Casey Newton. INSKEEP: And the program is called Machine Gods. What's the big idea? ROOSE: So Machine Gods is how people out here, where we are in San Francisco, talk about what's happening in AI. They talk about the fact that we are creating these rapidly improving AI systems. Some people sort of jokingly refer to them as the Machine God. And also, we're - we've been spending the past four years making a show about the latest developments in the world of tech. We're very excited to bring this show to NPR because we think this is a really important time for the public to understand what we see here, which is this industry racing ahead towards something that we've never really seen before. These AI systems are becoming quite capable, quite dangerous, and we're both excited by the potential as well as a little terrified of the risk. INSKEEP: Isn't this almost a literal title in that there are some people in this field who think they're creating God? NEWTON: Absolutely. There is a religious element to the way that lots of folks out here talk about what they're doing. The name is also sort of a play on some of the leaders of these companies who also sort of styled themselves as religious figures. So that's definitely an element we hope to capture in our reporting. INSKEEP: What has obsessed you about this topic in recent years? ROOSE: One thing that I'm fascinated by is that the people who are building this technology are in some sense the most scared of it. You know, we've seen this just in the past couple of weeks with the Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, who resigned, saying that he was scared about how quickly things were progressing. We've seen this in the call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to pace the frontier and kind of slow down AI development. This has not been true for other waves of technology that Casey and I have covered in our careers. You didn't see people at Facebook saying how terrified they were of the godlike superintelligence they were trying to build. But this is really a feature of the modern AI era, is that the people on the inside who have the most exposure to the technology are in some sense the most concerned. INSKEEP: I feel that you have a unique challenge, which I certainly experience as a journalist, as a broadcaster, when I touched this topic, and that is trying to understand myself what is going on and then explain it to laymen. It's extraordinarily difficult. NEWTON: It's very difficult, but I think it's a challenge that Kevin and I both relish. We have seen firsthand the power of explanatory journalism to get people interested in a topic and give them the tools they need to make better decisions about the kind of world that they live in. ROOSE: And, Steve, it's really not that complicated. I mean, if two idiots like us can understand it, I have high hopes for the NPR audience. (LAUGHTER) INSKEEP: That's good. That's good. I'd like to understand how you think about the developments of the last several days. You already referred to them. Jacob Coxon was a relatively junior employee who quit and issued this warning. Dario Amodei, the CEO of the entire company, talks about pacing AI differently and wanting antitrust exemptions so that companies can collaborate on safety. There are all kinds of theories about why all of this discussion is happening now. There are some conspiracy theories about why it's all happening now. What do you think is going on? NEWTON: You know, at the most fundamental level, it is the CEOs of really two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, who have the best window into the present state of AI development. And when they look at the models that they're building right now that haven't yet been released to the public, they're seeing things that make them really, really worried. And they're saying, hey, even if we were to stop individually, we're not confident that other companies around the world would stop. And so this is the time to figure out how we would initiate a slowdown if we felt like we were getting to that point. ROOSE: Yeah. And I don't buy the conspiracy theories, Steve, because these people have been talking about these risks for years. I think what's new is that other people outside the bubble are starting to talk about it as well. INSKEEP: What keeps you guys awake at night when you think about this topic? NEWTON: I mean, I think for me, it would be what they call recursive self-improvement. The idea that eventually these systems will just build and improve themselves and they will just improve at a rate where human beings can't understand what's going on. And, you know, if that were to happen, we may enter some kind of scenario where we see ourselves losing control over this technology. ROOSE: And I'll throw in another bit of AI insider jargon, which is I worry about the alignment problem. This is the classic dilemma of how you build a system that is aligned with human values. It's an unsolved technical problem, and as these systems get closer and closer to human-level experts, it's even more urgent that we figure out how to make them behave not just predictably, but to also behave in line with our values, to not go off and conduct cyber attacks or build bioweapons. So that's what keeps me up at night. INSKEEP: And let me ask you about the other side of this. When you peel away the hype, what excites you about the possibilities of this technology, for real? NEWTON: I mean, Kevin and I both get really excited about applications in medicine, the potential of this technology to help us discover new drugs and otherwise improve medical care. If you're on the side of human progress and you'd like to see us make great scientific discoveries, it seems like AI could be a really great tool to get us there as long as we're able to manage all of the risks. ROOSE: And I'm excited about some of the more sort of mundane daily applications of this stuff. We're creating this company now and this new show and we needed a website. And I've been building websites for more than 20 years and I've spent untold weeks, months, years of my life struggling through some sort of programming problem related to a website I'm building. And now we were able to just give an AI a set of instructions about our company and what we're doing and some visual assets, and it went off and built an amazing website that was better than anything I could have done. INSKEEP: Casey Newton and Kevin Roose are the hosts of the new show Machine Gods. You will see their work on NPR starting in October. It's video first. A full radio program will be available on NPR member stations early next year. Gentlemen, thanks. ROOSE: Thanks so much, Steve. NEWTON: Thanks, Steve. INSKEEP: And because we mentioned Anthropic, I will note that Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. item.title: As AI execs worry publicly, Bill Gates would like a word
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 4.47
As AI execs worry publicly, Bill Gates would like a word NPR's Scott Detrow speaks with Bill Gates, the former Microsoft CEO turned philanthropist, about his contributions to AI equity initiatives — and his criticisms of an AI-powered future world. SCOTT DETROW, HOST: Depending on who you ask, AI could unlock the true power of humanity or threaten humanity itself. Lately, both messages are coming from the same people. The CEOs of AI companies are raising louder and louder warnings about the technology's potential dangers as they continue developing advanced AI. With so much in the hands of Big Tech CEOs, we figured it is a good moment to talk to someone who very much understands that point of view, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who now chairs the Gates Foundation. I'll note here the Gates Foundation is a financial supporter of NPR. Today, it announced over $1 billion to expand access to AI tools in order to tackle social inequities. While at the same time, Bill Gates himself is warning that AI could turn out to be, quote, "the worst source of injustice" ever. Bill Gates, welcome back to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. BILL GATES: Thank you. DETROW: Since we've heard so many apocalyptic scenarios this week, I want to start with a concrete example from you of how you think AI tools could help lift people from poverty. GATES: Well, the Gates Foundation, the majority of its work is helping low-income countries in health, agriculture and education. So AI, for example, if you take a farmer, it can take your photos of your crops, you know, tell you what's going on with the disease. It can give you weather data that you never had before. It can tell you about your soil and what fertilizers you should use. And it'll understand the market prices and when you should store your crop and when you should sell it. And so it's been phenomenal to see that already hundreds of thousands of farmers in Asia and Africa are using the AI-based tools to make themselves way more productive than before. DETROW: You talk about those in your writing that you've recently published. You also raise really serious specific concerns, and some of the things that you are flagging are a little different than some of the things we've heard in recent days. You're not just talking about models going rogue, cyberattacks, things like that. You're talking about society-wide inequities. Can you walk us through some of these specific scenarios that you have become worried about? GATES: Well, I think everybody's taxonomy of the concerns is pretty much the same. There's, you know, the biosecurity, cybersecurity. There's the job market and how AI, including future humanoid robots, will affect the job market. There's the psychosocial effects of kids or even adults having a dependence on the AI for their relationships. And finally, there's the issue of control. Will the AIs either be under control of bad people or out of human control in a way that's detrimental to all of humanity? And so, believe it or not, we have to address all of those challenges that - I call that minimizing the bad, while we accelerate the very positive things. And so the billion-dollar announcement from the Gates Foundation - where we're going to make sure African languages are very highly accurate, which they're not yet today - that's about accelerating the good uses of AI into health, agriculture and education. DETROW: Given that, what was your response when President Trump said earlier this week that he did not see a role for the federal government regulating it? And he said, "the only control or guardrails," and this is a quote, "that AI needs is a strong and smart, high-IQ president." GATES: I wish it was that simple. This is a technology that was not developed really with government R&D, and so unlike rockets and nuclear weapons, where the government has tons of people who understand how quickly it's moving, here the federal government, as big and as smart as it is, is really playing catch-up. And so they have to deepen their expertise in biosecurity and cybersecurity. My memo was a rallying cry that people in universities, people in nonprofits and the government get more engaged in how we accelerate the good and minimize the bad. So I think as the U.S. government deepens its expertise, the message to the president will be these are, in fact, very, very serious problems that should not be taken lightly. DETROW: And in the meantime, the main focus is on whether the AI giants self-regulate. And that's something I was interested to hear your take on because I think you probably understand the Sam Altmans and the Dario Amodeis more than anybody else in the world. If an outsider had warned you to slow down when you were building Microsoft in the '80s and '90s, would you have listened? GATES: Well, fortunately, you know, nobody ever said that Microsoft Word, you know, was a problem because somebody could type something rude or a ransom note, you know? Yes, it is very surprising that in my comments on AI, I am saying this is a case where going full speed ahead is not the complete answer. My whole life, I've always said, you know, more PCs, more internet. You know, I'm - I believe innovation can solve almost every problem. But this is such a dual-sided technology that here some degree of slowing down may be important. And I - you know, I think the industry is not the issue here. The issue is getting all of the rest of society, who really controls these trade-offs, to get them up to speed and so that, without reducing the good stuff significantly, we can make sure to minimize the - those five, all significant, areas of potential harm. DETROW: I did want to ask, as we talk about these potential solutions, I did - felt like I need to ask you about your association in the past with Jeffrey Epstein because the Gates Foundation has been such a major player on policy. I'm wondering if you are concerned, if you feel like its ability to impact these future conversations, to be in the room to make decisions was harmed in any way by this association. GATES: Well, certainly, I'm very regretful that I spent time with Epstein. I really appreciated the opportunity to go in front of the Congress and go through, you know, meeting by meeting during that three-year period that ended in 2014, what my interactions with him were. You know, I made it clear what I did do. I did spend time with him, which was a mistake. You know, I never had a social relationship, went to an island, made any payments. So I - you know, people should look at that. There are many reasons - you know, I am a billionaire who's benefited from technology. You know, so hopefully I'm just one voice of many. But I tried in my memo to say, yeah, you can say that I'm not the perfect messenger, although I'm not sure who is. DETROW: And on AI, whether it's preventing the worst or putting the guardrails in place or making sure it's distributed in a broader way, how much time do you think we have to get these changes in place before it's too late? GATES: I think the sooner we say that models need to not be usable by bioterrorists, the better. The threshold of being capable of aiding bioattacks and cyberattacks, that is being crossed right now. And I know that the models that will come out later this year are far more powerful. And so there really isn't time to spare. DETROW: That was Bill Gates, philanthropist and entrepreneur. Thank you so much for talking to us. GATES: Thank you. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. item.title: AI CEOs call for industry slowdown
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 4.14
AI CEOs call for industry slowdown Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman are joining calls for a slowdown amid fears the AI industry is racing toward building technology that humans can't control. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We can put guardrails. We can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up. And they're bringing up things that won't happen. ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST: The remark seemed focused on keeping America competitive with China, rather than on regulation from Washington, dismissing rising fears after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay on Saturday calling for international cooperation to slow down the development of AI. Sam Altman, the CEO of rival OpenAI, joined in on social media saying he agreed with Amodei and that OpenAI is delaying their plans for an expected blockbuster public listing. Jacob Coxon, a researcher who resigned last week from Anthropic, came on this program recently with a caution about the dangers of artificial intelligence. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT) JACOB COXON: There's the possibility we create something that, if it wanted to, could hack into any device on the planet, could use novel biological research to go far beyond what current scientists are capable of, could control, like, every robot in the world simultaneously. NADWORNY: Coxon whirled (ph) about - worried about sleepwalking into a science fiction scenario. But will the growing backlash lead to a slowdown of AI development or any new government regulation? NPR's Shannon Bond joins us to discuss this weekend's developments. Shannon, Amodei and Altman, they run two of the companies behind the most capable AI systems. Why are they so worried about what they're building? SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Yeah, so Dario Amodei says he believes in the benefits of AI still, but he feels the technology is advancing too quickly now for safety to keep up. And so he's urging companies and governments to do what he calls pace the frontier, basically to collaboratively slow down development so they can address these risks. Here's what he told CNN. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) DARIO AMODEI: At the end of the day, the industry has to work together, and it's harder, but to some extent, the world has to work together. BOND: And as you said, Altman quickly hopped on board, saying that he agreed. And in an interview with Fortune magazine, Altman also said that OpenAI would delay its highly anticipated initial public offering, which the company had been targeting to happen this year. NADWORNY: So we've heard warnings about powerful AI for years. Why are these CEOs saying now is the time to take action? BOND: That's true, especially from Dario Amodei. He left OpenAI, in fact, to co-found Anthropic specifically to take a more safety-focused approach to building AI. But listen, lately these fears have become inflamed about how quickly AI is advancing towards the point where it might no longer be governable by humans. You know, when Coxon, that Anthropic researcher, quit, he said both Anthropic and OpenAI are, quote, "gambling with our lives." They're not acting responsibly, and many in this industry agree with him. And it really seems, Elissa, we hit this tipping point recently with this incident this summer, where OpenAI systems went rogue and hacked a company called Hugging Face and hacked OpenAI itself. And Amodei pointed out to this hack and to other security breaches, including at Anthropic, in his essay, calling for these measures. NADWORNY: So what are these AI leaders proposing to do? BOND: Well, Amodei says that labs need to bring in independent evaluators who can look at safety. He says Anthropic is going ahead, taking that step now. Altman says OpenAI will do the same. And other AI leaders, including Elon Musk, Microsoft's Satya Nadella, Google's Demis Hassabis, they also chimed in this weekend, largely agreeing, though they didn't make specific commitments. OpenAI already said last month that it was temporarily slowing down development of its leaning (ph) edge AI models to make sure something like this Hugging Face hack does not happen again. But Dario Amodei says addressing safety risks is not something that these companies or the industry can do alone, and it's going to require global cooperation. NADWORNY: What would global cooperation or global governance look like? BOND: That is a good question. So what Amodei is calling for is for governments and industry to work together to create rules of the road, such as establishing common safety standards for AI and verifying compliance. But so far, we have not seen progress on that front. Officials from the U.S. and China are expected to meet this month to talk about AI safety, and AI is on the agenda at the U.N. General Assembly. So even if President Trump is brushing these worries aside, it seems like other world leaders are paying attention. NADWORNY: Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR, and we cover it like any other company. We've been talking with NPR's Shannon Bond, who covers how technology, politics, power and influence all intersect. Thank you, Shannon. BOND: Thanks, Elissa. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. item.title: What to make of warnings that AI may pose an existential threat to humanity
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 3.55
What to make of warnings that AI may pose an existential threat to humanity Over the past week, fears of AI wiping out humanity are surging. But could it happen? And if so, how? SCOTT DETROW, HOST: They call it, quote, "The Pro-Human Assembly" - a gathering held today in Washington where politicians, celebrities and religious leaders discussed what to do about artificial intelligence. The meeting comes amid renewed warnings that AI could cause great harm or even destroy humanity. Joining me to help unpack the fears, both existential and otherwise, is NPR's Geoff Brumfiel. Hey, Geoff. GEOFF BRUMFIEL, BYLINE: Hi, Scott. DETROW: So today, I saw two very unlikely figures in the same room - Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent, and pro-Trump firebrand Steve Bannon. I guess they are both humans. BRUMFIEL: (Laughter). DETROW: They have that in common. What do they have to say about AI? BRUMFIEL: Yeah. Bannon and Sanders both talked about the possibility of AI going rogue. My colleague Huo Jingnan was there, and she captured what Sanders had to say. BERNIE SANDERS: If AI surpasses human intelligence, as many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences. BRUMFIEL: Bannon, for his part, spoke about the arrogance of the people building these systems. DETROW: Let's rewind a little bit. Over the weekend, the leaders of the big AI companies agreed that development needs to be slowed down. These companies are locked in a tight race right now. There are hundreds of billions of dollars of investment on the line, and it makes it sound like they are really worried. Explain what exactly got them spooked. BRUMFIEL: Yeah. You know, I think a lot of this started earlier in the summer when another AI company called Hugging Face got hacked, and that hack actually came from the OpenAI, the makers of ChatGPT. They were training a bunch of AI agents. These agents were given a test. And as they tried to figure out how to do it, they decided to attempt to steal the answer key from Hugging Face. A group of more than a thousand agents organized themselves. They even kind of elected a leader called Phase One. Malo Bourgon is CEO of a company called The Machine Intelligence Research Institute. He said it was clear the AI was very comfortable with trying to cheat. MALO BOURGON: You see that the agents clearly understood that they were, you know, trying to accomplish or solve the evaluations that they were in, in a way that wasn't intended, but they just did not seem to care. BRUMFIEL: And this echoes a much bigger risk people have talked about for years with AI. Sometimes it's called the paper clip problem. You know, you imagine an AI who's given a simple task - make paper clips - and everything starts out fine. They build a little factory, and they start doing it, but they keep thinking about how to make more paper clips. Then it starts mining iron ore, maybe, in huge quantities, destroying the environment or diverting resources from other areas. Eventually, maybe some humans figure out what this AI is doing and try to shut it down, and it decides to get rid of the humans in the name of covering the earth in paper clips. I mean, obviously, Scott, that sounds kind of silly. But these hacks do have some similarities. The AIs kind of maniacally pursued their goal of getting the answer key. They appeared to be aware humans didn't want them hacking into another system, but they went ahead and did it anyway. As Bourgon pointed out to me, hacking a billion-dollar company is a crime when humans do it, and the AIs just didn't care. DETROW: Right. So I very much understand why that has people scared. What other factors are going on right now? BRUMFIEL: The other big one is just how fast things are moving. Over the weekend, Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, talked about the speed with which AI systems are evolving, and in particular, the fact that AI is now helping to train better AI. That's sometimes called recursive self-improvement. If you fully automate it, some people believe you could end up very quickly developing a super-intelligent AI. And, you know - see previous worry - it doesn't really care whether it hurts humans to achieve its goals. And Bourgon points out there's already an example of this on planet Earth, and it's actually us. We are super-intelligent beings, and that hasn't always been good for other life forms. BOURGON: There are a lot of other species that are extinct due to our behavior, not because we were, you know, trying to cause their extinction, not because we thought they were evil and we were trying to take them out, but because we had things that we wanted to do in the world, and they were in the way. DETROW: OK. So this is the prevalent loudest concern right now. At the same time, though, Geoff, there are people out there who do not think an apocalypse is inevitable. What is the counterargument to all of this doomerism (ph)? BRUMFIEL: Yeah. I mean, I think the counterargument is this is more of an engineering problem than an existential risk. Yesterday, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, which makes all the chips for all this AI stuff - he was on a podcast called "All-In," and he said he could see why the AI companies are freaking out. (SOUNDBITE OF PODCAST, "ALL-IN") JENSEN HUANG: They're building their company. They're building their culture. They're building the technology. They're building engineering. They're building products all at the same time. And so I can understand it's a little bit hair on fire. BRUMFIEL: But he said he really thought these hacks were fixable problems. So these companies could contain their AI and keep it from causing trouble. (SOUNDBITE OF PODCAST, "ALL-IN") HUANG: I would bet you money that in every single one of those cases is within their control in the future to prevent it. BRUMFIEL: You know, for now, this AI remains mainly in the computers, and Huang feels like, you know, we have lots of new technology. In the past, we've been able to control it. It can be scary. It can be unpredictable, but it's just tech. We got this. DETROW: Let's bring this back to the event we first started talking about. You've got Steve Bannon on the far right and Bernie Sanders on the far left, and they are both saying we need regulation, and yet, regulation seems unlikely. Where are we with that? BRUMFIEL: Yeah. I mean, regulation is such a tough problem. Part of it is that engineers don't really understand how AI works or even exactly how the training yields the results it does. So it's kind of hard to know where you regulate. Still, everyone seems to agree some sorts of rules and oversight need to be established and quickly. I mean, even if you don't think that there's this existential risk, AI is being used to create deepfake images for harassment and scams. People are having unhealthy relationships with chatbots. It's getting very good at hacking. And, you know, people can direct it to hack. It doesn't always need to do it on its own. So there's plenty to worry about and plenty to think about putting constraints on. One model that I've heard sort of talked about that I think is interesting is think about, like, the airlines, right? We have federal regulators all over the world regulating the airlines, but we also have industry-led organizations trying to make sure airplanes are safe. Because in the end, you know, if airlines or AI aren't safe, no one's going to want to use them. DETROW: That is NPR's Geoff Brumfiel. Thanks so much. BRUMFIEL: Thank you. Copyright © 2026 NPR. item.title: The 9 best places to visit in Indonesia in 2026, beyond Bali
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.25
The 9 best places to visit in Indonesia in 2026, beyond Bali Komodo National Park's new 1,000-visitor daily cap, Raja Ampat's reefs, Mount Bromo's sunrise over a sea of volcanic sand — the destinations that make up the other 16,999 islands worth knowing about Bali earns its reputation, but it's one island within an archipelago of more than 17,000, stretching roughly 5,000 kilometers from the tip of Sumatra to the jungles of Papua, and within that span sit volcanic crater lakes, prehistoric dragons, some of the most biodiverse coral reefs on the planet, and islands remote enough that foreign visitors remain a genuine novelty. Indonesia is also shifting its broader tourism approach for 2026 toward what officials describe as a "high-value, low-impact" model, meaning more visitor caps and mandatory guided experiences at ecologically sensitive sites, a shift worth understanding before planning a trip to several of the destinations below. Komodo National Park, Flores Giant Asparagus / Pexels Komodo National Park, home to more than 4,000 wild Komodo dragons across a landscape of savannah, grassland, and tropical forest, is implementing a strict 1,000-visitor daily cap starting in April 2026, a major change specifically designed to protect the park's fragile ecosystem from overtourism. This means visitors can no longer simply show up and hope for a spot, and current guidance specifically recommends booking Komodo permits months in advance through the official digital system, treating this step as essential rather than optional for anyone planning a 2026 visit. Labuan Bajo functions as the practical gateway to the park, and April through October specifically offers the best weather and underwater visibility for visitors hoping to dive with manta rays, alongside the park's other signature experiences: trekking with dragons on Rinca, watching sunrise from Padar Island, and snorkeling at Pink Beach. Raja Ampat Andi saiful Sidik / Pexels Raja Ampat represents the pinnacle of Indonesia's diving destinations, home to what marine researchers consider the most biodiverse coral reef systems on the planet, giving serious divers access to marine life density and variety that few other diving destinations in the world can match. The region's remoteness, requiring multiple flights and boat transfers from Bali or Jakarta to actually reach, has helped preserve this biodiversity, meaning the journey itself functions as a natural filter that keeps visitor numbers considerably lower than more easily accessible Indonesian destinations. Raja Ampat's specific appeal is uncompromising: this is a destination for travelers specifically prioritizing world-class diving above convenience, offering an experience current guides group alongside Wakatobi and the Banda Islands as representing the absolute peak of Indonesian marine tourism. Lake Toba, North Sumatra neilstha firman / Pexels Lake Toba, the largest volcanic lake in the world, formed within the caldera of a supervolcano that erupted an estimated 74,000 years ago, giving the lake a scale and geological significance that dwarfs most other crater lakes found anywhere else on Earth. Samosir Island, sitting within the lake itself, preserves Batak cultural traditions and traditional architecture, giving visitors genuine cultural depth alongside the lake's dramatic natural scenery, a combination current guides specifically recommend pairing with a broader North Sumatra itinerary. Lake Toba's specific value within a broader Indonesia trip is combining significant geological history with living cultural heritage in a single, accessible destination, distinguishing it from the more purely nature-focused or purely cultural destinations elsewhere on this list. Central Java's ancient temples Mario La Pergola / Unsplash Central Java is home to Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple, and Prambanan, a significant Hindu temple complex, giving visitors direct access to two of Southeast Asia's most architecturally significant ancient religious sites within a single region. Yogyakarta, the region's cultural capital, adds the Taman Sari Water Castle and a broader royal heritage to the temple sites themselves, and current guides specifically recommend combining Central Java with Lake Toba for travelers prioritizing cultural depth over the beach and diving destinations that dominate much of the rest of this list. Central Java's specific appeal is delivering the kind of significant ancient architecture and religious history that travelers might otherwise associate with destinations like Cambodia's Angkor Wat, within Indonesia's own borders and considerably less crowded than some more internationally famous comparable sites. Mount Bromo, East Java Aldrin Rachman Pradana / Unsplash Mount Bromo's sunrise views, looking out over the so-called Sea of Sand surrounding the active volcanic caldera, rank among Indonesia's most iconic single travel experiences, drawing visitors specifically for this one dramatic sunrise moment above the volcanic landscape. For 2026, current coverage specifically notes stricter "Zero Waste" enforcement at the caldera itself, reflecting the same broader shift toward more sustainable, lower-impact tourism management visible at Komodo, and while cable car proposals remain under discussion, the traditional motorized jeep tours continue serving as the primary way to reach the sunrise viewpoints. Bromo's specific value is delivering a genuinely dramatic, single iconic experience efficiently, making it a strong addition to a broader East Java itinerary for travelers who want one unforgettable volcanic sunrise without requiring the extended time investment that some of the more remote diving destinations elsewhere on this list demand. Gili Islands Andrea Huls Pareja / Unsplash The Gili Islands, three small islands off Lombok's coast, offer a car-free, motorbike-free atmosphere built specifically around walking, cycling, and horse-drawn transport, giving visitors a genuinely slower-paced island experience distinct from Bali's more developed tourist infrastructure. Current guides specifically recommend spending at least a day on each of the three islands, since Gili Trawangan, Gili Air, and Gili Meno each maintain a distinct character and pace, ranging from a livelier nightlife scene to a considerably quieter, more relaxed atmosphere depending on which specific island a visitor chooses. The islands' proximity to Lombok makes them a natural pairing within the same regional trip, giving visitors access to both Lombok's volcanic and cultural attractions and the Gili Islands' beach-focused, laid-back character within a single, geographically compact itinerary. Lombok Johnny Africa / Unsplash Lombok offers a genuine, geographically close alternative to Bali, sharing a similar tropical climate and volcanic, rice-terraced landscape while maintaining a predominantly Muslim culture distinct from Bali's Hindu traditions, giving visitors a culturally different experience within a short distance of Bali itself. Mount Rinjani, an active volcano, offers a genuinely demanding hike rewarded with a dramatic sunrise view over its crater lake, while Tetebatu Village at the mountain's base and the Sendang Gile and Tiu Kelep waterfalls give visitors gentler activity options within the same broader region. Lombok's specific appeal, current guides consistently note, is offering a comparable range of beaches, mountains, rice terraces, and surf culture to Bali, at a meaningfully lower cost and with considerably fewer crowds, making it a strong choice specifically for honeymoon travelers or anyone seeking a Bali-adjacent experience without Bali's now-considerable tourist density. Sumba Deepavali Gaind / Unsplash Sumba remains one of Indonesia's more untouched islands, known for wild horses, traditional villages maintaining distinct cultural practices, and a noticeably quieter, less-developed tourism infrastructure than most other entries on this list, giving visitors a genuine sense of discovery. The island's traditional architecture and living cultural practices, distinct from the more commercialized cultural tourism found in parts of Bali, give Sumba a specific appeal for travelers prioritizing authentic cultural immersion over convenience or extensive tourist infrastructure. Sumba's relative remoteness and limited infrastructure mean it requires more deliberate planning to visit than more established destinations elsewhere on this list, but current guides specifically recommend it for travelers who have already experienced Indonesia's more accessible destinations and are looking for something considerably less developed. Wakatobi Tom Fisk / Pexels Wakatobi, part of the Coral Triangle, ranks alongside Raja Ampat as one of Indonesia's premier diving destinations, offering exceptional coral reef systems and marine biodiversity within a national marine park specifically established to protect this ecosystem. The region's remoteness, similar to Raja Ampat, has helped preserve its underwater ecosystems from the kind of tourist pressure affecting more accessible Indonesian diving destinations, though this same remoteness means reaching Wakatobi requires more extensive travel logistics than most other entries on this list. Wakatobi's specific position alongside Raja Ampat and the Banda Islands as one of Indonesia's top-tier diving destinations makes it a strong choice specifically for serious divers planning a trip primarily around underwater exploration rather than broader general sightseeing, cultural tourism, or beach relaxation.

item.title: 10 sleep habits sleep specialists actually follow themselves
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.12
10 sleep habits sleep specialists actually follow themselves A consistent wake time even on weekends, a strict no-screens buffer before bed, a bedroom kept specifically cold — the habits the people who study sleep for a living say actually move the needle Sleep specialists have access to the same general advice everyone else does, get eight hours, avoid caffeine late in the day, but the specific habits they actually build their own routines around tend to be narrower and more consistently applied than the broad, sometimes vague guidance most general sleep advice offers. Each entry in this list covers a specific habit, the mechanism behind why it matters, and how it's typically applied in practice. A consistent wake time, including weekends Slaapwijsheid.nl / Unsplash Sleep specialists consistently emphasize waking up at the same time every day, weekends included, since this single habit does more to anchor the body's circadian rhythm than almost any other single intervention, including going to bed at a consistent time, which naturally follows once wake time is fixed. The specific reasoning is that sleeping in on weekends, even by a couple of hours, functions similarly to mild jet lag, requiring the body to readjust its internal clock at the start of the following week, a pattern sometimes called social jet lag that can leave someone feeling groggy on Monday despite having technically slept more over the weekend. The practical guidance is picking a wake time that's realistic to maintain seven days a week rather than the earliest time someone could theoretically manage on a demanding weekday, since consistency matters more than the specific hour chosen, and an unsustainably early wake time abandoned by the weekend defeats the purpose entirely. A strict buffer before screens go off Slaapwijsheid.nl / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly build in a specific screen-free buffer before bed, typically 30 to 60 minutes, since screens emit blue light that specifically suppresses melatonin production, the hormone that signals to the body it's time to prepare for sleep. Beyond the light itself, screens also tend to introduce mentally stimulating content, whether that's work email, social media, or an engaging show, that keeps the brain more alert than the winding-down state actually needed before sleep, meaning the content itself compounds the light-based effect rather than existing as a separate concern. The practical application many specialists follow themselves is treating this buffer as non-negotiable rather than aspirational, using the freed time for reading a physical book, light stretching, or another genuinely low-stimulation activity that doesn't involve a screen at all. A bedroom kept specifically cold Jamie Street / Unsplash Sleep specialists frequently keep their own bedrooms cooler than what feels comfortable while awake, typically in the range of 65 to 68 degrees Fahrenheit, since the body's core temperature needs to drop somewhat to initiate and maintain sleep, and a room that's too warm can directly interfere with this natural temperature decline. This specific guidance reflects a genuine physiological mechanism rather than simple personal preference, since research consistently links a cooler sleep environment with both falling asleep faster and experiencing fewer overnight awakenings compared with a warmer room, even when the difference in temperature feels relatively minor. The practical guidance is testing a slightly cooler setting than usual for a period of consistent nights rather than a single trial, since the body's response to a temperature change often becomes more noticeable after several nights of consistent exposure rather than being immediately obvious on the first attempt. No caffeine after early afternoon Tatiana Rodriguez / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly cut off caffeine considerably earlier than many people assume necessary, often by early afternoon, since caffeine has a half-life of roughly five to six hours, meaning a meaningful amount remains active in the body well into the evening even after a mid-afternoon cup. This specific cutoff reflects caffeine's actual metabolic timeline rather than a general, vague suggestion to avoid caffeine "late in the day," since a coffee at 3 p.m. can still have roughly half its caffeine content active in the bloodstream by 8 or 9 p.m., a specific quantity often still sufficient to disrupt sleep onset for a genuinely caffeine-sensitive person. The practical guidance is treating this as an individual calibration rather than a universal rule, since caffeine sensitivity varies considerably between people, but starting with an early afternoon cutoff and adjusting based on actual sleep quality gives a reasonable, testable starting point. A consistent pre-sleep wind-down routine Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly follow the same specific sequence of actions each night before bed, whether that's a particular order of brushing teeth, dimming lights, and reading, since this consistent routine functions as a learned behavioral cue that signals to the brain sleep is approaching, similar to how a consistent routine helps a child learn to fall asleep more easily. This conditioning effect develops over repeated consistent nights rather than working immediately, meaning the routine's value comes specifically from its unchanging repetition rather than any single component of the routine being uniquely powerful on its own. The practical guidance is choosing a routine simple enough to actually maintain consistently rather than an elaborate sequence likely to be skipped on a tired or busy night, since a simple, reliably repeated routine provides more consistent benefit than a more elaborate one followed only sporadically. Getting out of bed when unable to sleep Alexander Grey / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly recommend getting out of bed after roughly 20 minutes of being unable to fall asleep, moving to another room for a calm, low-stimulation activity until feeling genuinely sleepy again, rather than remaining in bed growing increasingly frustrated. This specific guidance addresses a documented psychological pattern in which repeatedly lying awake in bed can condition the brain to associate the bed itself with wakefulness and frustration rather than sleep, a learned association that can worsen insomnia over time if the pattern continues. The practical application is treating the bed strictly as a place for sleep, getting up and doing something else during a genuine period of wakefulness rather than tossing and turning, and only returning to bed once drowsiness has actually returned, reinforcing the bed's specific association with sleep rather than wakeful frustration. Morning sunlight exposure Slaapwijsheid.nl / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly prioritize getting outside for natural light exposure within the first hour or so of waking, since morning light exposure is one of the strongest signals available for setting the body's circadian rhythm, directly reinforcing the wake-sleep cycle that determines when melatonin release begins later that evening. This specific timing matters because morning light exposure has a considerably stronger circadian effect than light exposure later in the day, meaning a short period outside shortly after waking provides more benefit for nighttime sleep quality than the same amount of daylight exposure encountered later in the afternoon. The practical guidance is treating this as a brief, consistent daily habit, even just 10 to 15 minutes outside without sunglasses shortly after waking, rather than assuming general daytime light exposure throughout the day provides the same specific circadian benefit as this earlier, more targeted exposure. Reserving the bed for sleep only Slaapwijsheid.nl / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly avoid working, eating, or watching television in bed, reserving the bed specifically for sleep, a practice directly related to the same behavioral conditioning principle behind getting out of bed when unable to sleep, strengthening the mental association between the bed and sleep specifically rather than a broader range of daytime activities. This specific habit matters more than it might initially seem, since a bed used for work or entertainment throughout the day sends a mixed signal to the brain about what the space actually represents, potentially undermining the same conditioning effect a consistent pre-sleep routine is specifically trying to build. The practical application is moving other activities to a different room whenever reasonably possible, treating this boundary as a genuine habit worth maintaining consistently rather than an occasional inconvenience to work around only when convenient. Limiting alcohol close to bedtime Kelly Sikkema / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly avoid alcohol within several hours of bedtime, since while alcohol can initially make someone feel drowsy, it disrupts sleep architecture later in the night, specifically reducing REM sleep and increasing the likelihood of waking up partway through the night once the initial sedative effect wears off. This specific pattern means alcohol's sleep-disrupting effect isn't always obvious to the person experiencing it, since the initial drowsiness can create a false impression that alcohol improves sleep, when the actual overnight sleep quality, measured through both sleep architecture and how rested someone feels the next morning, tends to be measurably worse. The practical guidance many specialists follow themselves is treating any alcohol consumption as something to finish several hours before bedtime specifically, rather than close to it, giving the body adequate time to metabolize the alcohol before its sleep-disrupting effects would otherwise interfere with the night's rest. Not checking the time during nighttime awakenings Shane / Unsplash Sleep specialists commonly avoid checking a clock or phone during a nighttime awakening, since seeing the specific time, and mentally calculating how much sleep remains before an alarm, tends to increase anxiety and alertness in a way that makes falling back asleep considerably more difficult than the awakening itself would otherwise cause. This specific habit addresses a common but frequently overlooked behavior, since many people instinctively check the time immediately upon waking during the night without recognizing that this specific action itself is actively working against a quick return to sleep, rather than simply satisfying harmless curiosity. The practical guidance is turning a phone face-down or moving a clock out of easy view specifically to remove this temptation, addressing the habit directly rather than relying purely on willpower to resist checking the time during a groggy, half-awake moment when that willpower is often at its weakest.

item.title: Novo Nordisk is partnering with Anthropic to speed up drug discovery using AI
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.11
The Danish drugmaker will use Claude Science and Anthropic's frontier models to tackle drug discovery challenges and AI-driven software development The companies said they will work together on drug discovery obstacles identified by Novo's scientists and computational teams, building out purpose-built solutions for particular scientific workflows while also supporting biological reasoning. Novo will also use Anthropic's models to strengthen AI-driven software development across the company. "Joining forces with Anthropic will supercharge our R&D organisation and help us on our mission to bring new, transformative health solutions to people living with chronic diseases," Novo Nordisk president and CEO Mike Doustdar said in a statement. "AI can help us increase productivity in R&D and compress the path from research to marketed product." As an initial step, Novo will test Claude Science for specific R&D workflows and focus on scientific problems where the combined capabilities of the two companies are expected to have the greatest impact, the company said. Novo said the arrangement incorporates data governance protocols and human oversight requirements so that AI use remains consistent with the company's compliance standards. Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei framed the potential impact of the partnership in broad terms. "AI's increasing capability brings with it the potential to compress a century's worth of biological and medical breakthroughs into a decade," he said in a statement. The partnership adds to a string of AI collaborations Novo has pursued. According to The Wall Street Journal, the Danish drugmaker earlier this year struck a deal with OpenAI and also established an AI innovation hub with Amazon $AMZN Web Services. Anthropic launched Claude Science as a scientific research workbench that connects to more than 60 scientific databases and includes prebuilt toolkits for fields such as genomics, proteomics, structural biology, and cheminformatics. The workbench uses a primary agent that can spawn specialized sub-agents to divide workloads, with a dedicated reviewer agent that audits citations and calculations before any output reaches publication. Early users at institutions including the Allen Institute and the UCSF Brain Tumor Center reported significant reductions in research time for complex analytical tasks. Anthropic said Claude Science runs on existing Claude models, including Opus 4.8, and is not a new or specialized model. The Anthropic-Novo partnership follows an earlier arrangement Anthropic reached with Bristol-Myers Squibb, which gave that drugmaker's workforce access to Claude for research and drug development. item.title: Gates Foundation is pledging $1 billion to spread AI to the world's poorest communities
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.89
The Gates Foundation committed $1 billion over the next two years to expand access to artificial intelligence in health care, agriculture, and education, with a focus on low-income communities that current AI development largely bypasses. The funding, spread over two years, targets AI tools for healthcare workers, smallholder farmers, and teachers in low-income countries The pledge was announced Tuesday alongside the foundation's annual Goalkeepers report, which warned that AI risks deepening the gap between wealthy and poor nations unless governments, technology companies, and philanthropies act within the next 12 to 18 months. "The window to influence who benefits, and how soon, is short," the report said. The funding breaks down to roughly $400 million each for health care and education, and about $100 million for agriculture, according to the Associated Press. An additional $100 million will go toward building AI training data sets in languages spoken by underserved communities. Gates Foundation CEO Mark Suzman said the foundation is working with leading AI companies on the initiative. Google $GOOGL.org and Microsoft $MSFT's AI for Good Lab are among the partners backing an open call for proposals aimed at bolstering language infrastructure for thousands of communities across Africa whose languages are poorly represented in existing AI systems. OpenAI is contributing $50 million to a pilot program with the foundation that places AI tools in the hands of health workers at Rwandan clinics, with Suzman saying the effort will be extended to additional African countries. Anthropic's collaboration with the foundation includes efforts to speed up vaccine research and expand the AI's knowledge of locally grown crops, the AP reported. Bill Gates, the foundation's chairman and Microsoft co-founder, framed the investment as a response to a fundamental market failure: that the most capable AI tools are being built first for the wealthiest users. The Goalkeepers report warned that without deliberate intervention, AI development will prioritize profit over need: "the most capable tools will be built first for the people and institutions most able to pay for them." The report cited data showing that in sub-Saharan Africa, one doctor serves roughly 2,000 people, compared with fewer than 200 per doctor in high-income countries. It also noted that AI speech recognition systems produce errors more than 60% of the time in Yoruba, compared with less than 6% in English. Suzman acknowledged to the AP that the foundation's total commitment is a "tiny proportion" of what major technology companies spend on commercial AI products, and said conversations with those companies about additional contributions are continuing. The Goalkeepers report was timed to land just before the United Nations General Assembly convenes its high-level meetings in New York next week. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres has pushed for developing countries to have a seat at the table as global AI governance frameworks take shape, according to the AP. The Gates Foundation and Anthropic announced a $200 million partnership earlier this year to deploy AI across global health, education, and economic mobility programs, with Anthropic contributing Claude AI usage credits and technical staff support alongside the foundation's grant funding and program expertise. item.title: Meta is expanding its paid subscription lineup with AI and creator tiers
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.48
Meta $META introduced a new lineup of paid subscription plans on Tuesday under its Meta One brand, adding tiers for creators, businesses, and heavy AI users to its existing roster of app-specific subscriptions. The Meta One plans range from $2.99 to $499 a month and cover individuals, creators, and businesses across Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp The expanded offering includes more than 50 features across Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, and Meta AI, the company said. Meta One plans are available globally and range from $2.99 a month for single-product plans to $499 a month for the highest-tier business and creator bundles. Single-product plans — Instagram Plus at $3.99 a month, Facebook Plus at $3.99 a month, and WhatsApp Plus at $2.99 a month — offer app-specific features such as custom fonts, additional chat pinning, and expanded Story controls. Two bundle plans aimed at individuals and AI users combine those features with expanded access to Meta's AI tools, including image and video generation: Core at $7.99 a month and Premium at $19.99 a month. Four tiers target creators and business owners. The Essential plan starts at $14.99 a month and includes a verified badge, access to Meta's business agent on WhatsApp, and impersonation protection. The Advanced plan, starting at $49.99 a month, adds the ability to schedule Stories up to 30 days in advance, links in organic posts and Reels, exportable analytics, and team account access without password sharing. Expert plans start at $149 a month and Max plans at $499 a month, with the Max tier including an option to request phone support from a company representative, according to Engadget. The company noted that basic Meta AI access and its core app features would not be moving behind a paywall. The company noted that in initial tests, a majority of bundle subscribers made use of both the AI capabilities and the expression-focused features included in those plans. The company said subscription benefits will eventually reach additional products, including its video-editing app, Edits, and its AI glasses. Meta launched the initial wave of Meta One single-product plans — Instagram Plus, Facebook Plus, and WhatsApp Plus — earlier this year, alongside limited tests of AI-focused bundle plans in markets including Singapore, Guatemala, and Bolivia. Creator and business tiers were also tested in Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Thailand, and Bangladesh. Meta reported that its paid plans have attracted more than 15 million sign-ups, including both paid subscriptions and trials. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: 8 things a dentist can tell about your health just by looking in your mouth
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.46
8 things a dentist can tell about your health just by looking in your mouth Enamel erosion that signals acid reflux, a specific breath odor tied to kidney function, worn-down teeth from grinding you didn't know you did — the systemic health clues a routine dental checkup can catch before you notice anything wrong A dental checkup covers considerably more than cavities and gum disease, since the mouth often shows visible signs of conditions developing elsewhere in the body well before a patient notices any symptoms themselves, making a routine cleaning one of the more overlooked early screening opportunities in regular healthcare. Each entry in this list covers a specific sign a dentist can identify during a normal exam, what it can indicate, and why it often goes unnoticed by the patient until it's specifically pointed out. Nighttime teeth grinding Kamal Hoseinianzade / Unsplash Dentists can identify teeth grinding, known clinically as bruxism, by examining the specific wear pattern on tooth surfaces, since grinding produces flattened, worn edges and sometimes small fractures in a distinctive pattern that differs from the gradual wear caused by normal chewing over time. Many patients experiencing this grinding have no conscious awareness of it at all, since it most commonly occurs during sleep, meaning a dentist is frequently the first person to identify the condition, sometimes well before a patient notices any of the jaw soreness, headaches, or tooth sensitivity that grinding can eventually cause. Bruxism is frequently connected to stress or anxiety, and identifying the specific wear pattern gives a dentist a starting point for a broader conversation about potential underlying stress, sleep quality, or a referral for a properly fitted night guard to prevent further damage. Acid reflux affecting tooth enamel Caroline LM / Unsplash Dentists can identify enamel erosion caused by stomach acid through a specific pattern distinct from erosion caused by acidic foods or drinks, since acid reflux typically affects the back and inner surfaces of the upper teeth in a characteristic pattern reflecting how stomach acid actually flows within the mouth during a reflux episode. Many patients experiencing chronic acid reflux, sometimes called GERD, don't associate their occasional heartburn with any dental consequence at all, meaning a dentist noticing this specific enamel wear pattern may be the first person to suggest a connection between a patient's digestive symptoms and this visible dental damage. This finding often prompts a dentist to specifically ask about reflux symptoms during the exam, and identifying this connection early can lead a patient to address the underlying digestive issue before the enamel erosion progresses to the point of causing genuine tooth sensitivity or structural damage. Vitamin D or calcium deficiency SoyBreno / Unsplash Dentists can sometimes identify signs consistent with vitamin D or calcium deficiency through specific indicators including delayed tooth development in children, weakened enamel, or a pattern of bone density loss visible on dental X $TWTR-rays around the jaw and tooth roots. These deficiencies often don't produce obvious external symptoms in their earlier stages, meaning a patient may have no reason to suspect anything is wrong until a dentist specifically notices these dental indicators during a routine exam or set of X-rays taken for another purpose entirely. A dentist noticing these specific signs typically recommends the patient follow up with a physician for bloodwork to confirm an actual deficiency, since dental findings alone can suggest but not definitively diagnose a specific nutritional deficiency requiring medical confirmation and treatment. Early signs of diabetes lafayett zapata montero / Unsplash Dentists can identify certain oral signs associated with diabetes, including specific patterns of gum disease that progress more severely or heal more slowly than typical, along with dry mouth and a higher frequency of oral infections than would be expected in a patient without an underlying blood sugar issue. Gum disease and diabetes have a well-documented two-way relationship, since uncontrolled blood sugar makes gum disease more likely and more severe, while gum disease itself can make blood sugar control more difficult, meaning a dentist noticing unusually severe or treatment-resistant gum disease sometimes prompts a specific conversation about blood sugar testing. Many patients with prediabetes or early, undiagnosed diabetes have no obvious symptoms yet, making a dentist's observation of this specific gum disease pattern a genuine opportunity for earlier detection than a patient might otherwise receive through routine primary care alone. Sleep apnea indicators Caroline LM / Unsplash Dentists can identify several physical indicators associated with sleep apnea, including a specifically scalloped tongue (showing indentations from pressing against the teeth), a naturally narrow airway visible during an oral exam, and wear patterns suggesting the grinding that frequently accompanies sleep apnea in many patients. Sleep apnea often goes undiagnosed for years, since many patients aren't aware of their own symptoms occurring during sleep, and a bed partner's observations, if the patient has one, don't always prompt a formal medical evaluation, meaning a dentist noticing these specific physical indicators can be a patient's first real signal that something is worth investigating. A dentist identifying these signs typically recommends a referral to a sleep specialist for formal evaluation, since a dental exam alone cannot diagnose sleep apnea, but can provide the specific physical evidence that prompts a patient to actually pursue that further evaluation. Osteoporosis signs in jaw bone density Jonathan Borba / Unsplash Dentists can sometimes notice early signs consistent with osteoporosis through jaw bone density changes visible on routine dental X $TWTR-rays, since the same bone density loss that affects the rest of the skeleton in osteoporosis also affects the jawbone, sometimes becoming visible in dental imaging before a patient has experienced any fracture elsewhere prompting a formal osteoporosis diagnosis. This specific finding matters because osteoporosis frequently has no noticeable symptoms until an actual fracture occurs, meaning routine dental X-rays taken for entirely unrelated reasons can occasionally provide an early warning sign well before the condition would otherwise be caught through more typical screening pathways. A dentist noticing this pattern typically recommends the patient discuss bone density screening with their physician, particularly relevant for patients already in a higher-risk group for osteoporosis based on age or other risk factors, giving this specific dental finding genuine practical value beyond the mouth itself. Kidney function through breath odor Kamal Hoseinianzade / Unsplash Dentists can sometimes notice a specific ammonia-like or metallic breath odor associated with declining kidney function, since kidneys that aren't filtering waste products effectively can allow certain compounds to build up in the bloodstream and eventually become detectable through breath, distinct from the more common causes of bad breath like poor oral hygiene or specific foods. This specific odor pattern is distinct enough that dentists trained to recognize it can sometimes identify it before a patient has any other noticeable symptoms of declining kidney function, particularly relevant since early kidney disease often produces few obvious symptoms until the condition has progressed considerably. A dentist noticing this specific breath pattern, especially when a patient's oral hygiene otherwise appears good and doesn't explain persistent bad breath through more common causes, typically recommends a follow-up with a physician for kidney function testing, treating this unusual breath odor as a genuine diagnostic clue rather than dismissing it as an isolated cosmetic concern. Oral cancer in its earliest stages D Dental Office / Unsplash Dentists routinely check for early signs of oral cancer during standard exams, looking for specific indicators including persistent white or red patches, unusual sores that don't heal within a couple of weeks, or unexplained lumps and thickened areas of tissue anywhere in the mouth, throat, or on the tongue. These early signs are frequently painless and easy for a patient to overlook entirely, particularly in less visible areas of the mouth a person doesn't routinely examine themselves, meaning a dentist's systematic visual and physical exam during a routine cleaning can catch a genuinely serious condition at a meaningfully earlier, more treatable stage than a patient would likely notice independently. This screening represents one of the more consequential reasons regular dental checkups matter beyond cavity prevention alone, since oral cancer's treatment outcomes improve considerably with earlier detection, making this specific, brief visual screening during an otherwise routine appointment a genuinely significant health safeguard.

item.title: OpenAI says it has been working with Anthropic and Google on AI safety for weeks
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.40
OpenAI's global policy chief confirmed the discussions Tuesday, adding that the companies don't need an antitrust waiver to coordinate "It's better to try to work together to prioritize safety," Lehane said, according to Bloomberg. Lehane also argued that no antitrust waiver is necessary for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind to work together on safety. Spokespeople for Anthropic and Google DeepMind, a unit of Alphabet, did not respond to requests for comment. The confirmation comes days after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay on Saturday calling on AI companies to pump the brakes on frontier model development until researchers have a clearer picture of the risks involved. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI chief Elon Musk endorsed the call. In a post on X $TWTR, Altman said a slowdown had been a "primary topic" of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks and that the company would have more to share "soon." The roots of the talks go back to July, when Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis outlined a vision on X for a U.S.-led oversight body — structured as either a public-private partnership or a self-regulatory organization answerable to the federal government, along the lines of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority — that could vet cutting-edge AI models and trigger industrywide slowdowns when threats emerged, an OpenAI spokesperson told CNBC. The prospect of competitors coordinating has drawn scrutiny from antitrust regulators. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, speaking Tuesday, said he would be "deeply suspicious" of requests for antitrust exemptions, and that he views the AI companies as seeking barriers to entry that insulate their businesses from challengers, according to Bloomberg. "That sure sounds like moat digging," Ferguson said. Lehane argued that the coordination has precedent, citing the airline industry as an example of companies working together on safety. He said OpenAI is prepared to back bipartisan legislation on the Hill targeting catastrophic AI risks — among them a federal governance framework put forward by Republican Representative Jay Obernolte and Democrat Lori Trahan, as well as a Senate effort championed by Majority Leader John Thune alongside Republican Ted Cruz and Democrat Amy Klobuchar, according to Bloomberg. Lehane also said OpenAI supports a provision in the FRONTIER Act that would require top AI labs to allow independent verification organizations into their companies to monitor model development, according to TechCrunch. Any AI bill becoming law before the end of 2026 is a long shot. The House departs Washington on Thursday and has no scheduled sessions before voters head to the polls in November, according to Bloomberg. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.
