item.title: 9 Oktoberfest-style beer festivals worth traveling for, from Munich to Argentina
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.39
9 Oktoberfest-style beer festivals worth traveling for, from Munich to Argentina Stuttgart's 4.5 million annual visitors, a free daytime celebration in Ontario with its own Thanksgiving parade — the Oktoberfest-style festivals worth building a trip around, in the Northern and Southern Hemisphere alike Oktoberfest began in 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Bavarian Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese, and the celebration became such a beloved civic tradition that Munich has held some version of it nearly every year since, a legacy that has since inspired genuine, large-scale celebrations on nearly every continent rather than staying confined to Germany. This list covers nine of those celebrations worth building an actual trip around, from the 191-year-old original to alpine villages in the Southern Hemisphere celebrating the same tradition in spring sunshine rather than autumn chill. Munich, Germany Manuel Joseph / Pexels Munich's Oktoberfest remains the original for a specific reason: 2026 marks its 191st year on the same Theresienwiese fairground where it has been held, with only a handful of historical gaps, since 1810, and current coverage specifically credits this unbroken lineage with producing an atmosphere no replica anywhere else in the world fully replicates. The 2026 festival runs September 19 through October 4, drawing an estimated six to seven million visitors across 14 massive tents, with residents themselves arriving in traditional dirndls and lederhosen and Munich's mayor ceremonially tapping the first beer barrel to officially open the festival each year. Entry to the festival grounds and tents is completely free, though table reservations inside specific tents are strongly recommended for weekend evenings and must be booked directly with individual tent operators, a detail worth planning around given how far in advance popular tents typically fill up. Stuttgart, Germany Bastian Riccardi / Pexels The Cannstatter Volksfest, founded in 1818, ranks as the world's second-largest folk festival and draws more than 4.5 million visitors annually, making it the closest genuine rival to Munich's own Oktoberfest in both scale and historical pedigree within Germany itself. The 2026 festival runs September 25 through October 11, giving visitors a specific alternative to Munich with a comparable folk-festival atmosphere, traditional Swabian food, and large beer tents, but without needing to compete with Munich's considerably larger crowds and correspondingly higher demand for table reservations. Stuttgart's specific advantage for travelers is offering essentially the same core Oktoberfest experience, tents, traditional dress, folk music, and beer, at a scale still massive enough to feel like a genuine major event, without requiring the months-of-advance planning that securing a table in Munich increasingly demands. Cincinnati, Ohio Brett Sayles / Pexels Oktoberfest Zinzinnati has grown into one of the largest Oktoberfest celebrations outside Germany itself, drawing crowds well into the hundreds of thousands across a single weekend and transforming downtown Cincinnati into a city-spanning festival rather than a single fixed venue the way most European celebrations operate. The festival's specific signature attractions, including the Running of the Wieners, in which dachshunds dressed as hot dogs race down a designated course, and the World's Largest Chicken Dance performed simultaneously by the entire crowd, give it a distinctly American, high-energy character that differs meaningfully from the more traditional folk-festival atmosphere found in Munich or Stuttgart. Cincinnati's specific value for American travelers is proximity, offering a genuinely large-scale Oktoberfest experience without requiring international travel, though the festival's popularity means downtown hotel capacity fills quickly once dates are confirmed each year. Denver, Colorado Colin Lloyd / Unsplash The Great American Beer Festival, the flagship event of the Brewers Association, takes a genuinely different approach from the traditional Oktoberfest format covered elsewhere on this list, centering on American craft beer specifically rather than Bavarian lager tradition and folk-festival programming. Current guidance specifically recommends arriving before tents or session doors open, typically around 9 a.m. on weekends, for the best chance at finding space and working through the event's considerable selection of craft beers before the busiest afternoon and evening crowds arrive. Denver's festival is the strongest choice on this list specifically for travelers whose primary interest is craft beer variety and brewing innovation rather than the folk-festival costumes, brass bands, and carnival rides that define the more traditional Oktoberfest experience found in Munich, Stuttgart, or Cincinnati. Blumenau, Brazil Atlantic Ambience / Pexels Blumenau's Oktoberfest, held in a city founded by German immigrants in southern Brazil, ranks as one of the largest Oktoberfest celebrations in the world outside Germany itself, and current 2026 coverage specifically highlights it as free to enter, with beer available at a fraction of Munich's cost per liter. The festival's specific character reflects Blumenau's genuine German immigrant heritage rather than a purely commercial import, with traditional Bavarian architecture throughout the city's historic district providing an authentic backdrop that current travel coverage credits with feeling considerably more genuine than many other non-German celebrations on this list. Blumenau's specific value proposition is affordability combined with authenticity, giving budget-conscious travelers a way to experience genuine German-heritage Oktoberfest programming without paying Munich's considerably higher prices for beer and food throughout the festival grounds. Villa General Belgrano, Argentina Brett Sayles / Pexels Villa General Belgrano, a genuine alpine-style village in Argentina's Sierras founded partly by German and Swiss immigrants, holds one of South America's most significant Oktoberfest celebrations, and current 2026 coverage specifically notes that few travelers outside South America are even aware the town or its festival exists. Because Argentina sits in the Southern Hemisphere, this Oktoberfest takes place during spring rather than the autumn timing every Northern Hemisphere festival on this list follows, giving visitors a genuinely different seasonal atmosphere, warm spring sunshine rather than the crisp autumn chill that defines Munich's or Cincinnati's celebrations. This reversed seasonal timing makes Villa General Belgrano a specific, strategic option for travelers wanting to experience Oktoberfest-style programming during a part of the year when every Northern Hemisphere celebration on this list has already concluded for the season. Kitchener-Waterloo, Canada Brett Sayles / Pexels Kitchener-Waterloo's Oktoberfest is Canada's largest, and current 2026 coverage specifically highlights its Willkommen Platz gathering space and accompanying Thanksgiving parade as free, daytime, and genuinely family-friendly, distinguishing it from the more adult-oriented, evening-focused beer tent atmosphere that defines Munich and several other entries on this list. This family-friendly positioning reflects a deliberate community focus rather than an attempt to replicate Munich's scale or intensity, giving the festival a specifically different character suited to visitors traveling with children or anyone preferring a calmer, more daytime-oriented festival experience. The festival's Canadian Thanksgiving timing, which falls in early-to-mid October, means it runs somewhat later in the season than the German originals, giving travelers who missed Munich or Cincinnati's earlier dates a genuine later-season alternative within the same general Oktoberfest tradition. Qingdao, China Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels The Qingdao International Beer Festival, frequently described as Asia's Oktoberfest, ranks among the largest beer festivals in the world by attendance, reflecting Qingdao's specific brewing heritage as home to Tsingtao, one of China's most significant beer brands, itself originally established with German involvement in the early 20th century. This German brewing connection gives Qingdao's festival a genuine historical link to the same brewing tradition Munich's Oktoberfest celebrates, distinguishing it from purely imported or thematic Oktoberfest celebrations elsewhere in Asia that don't share this specific brewing heritage. Qingdao's specific value on this list is representing Asia's strongest and most historically grounded entry into the broader Oktoberfest tradition, giving travelers in the region a genuinely significant beer festival without requiring travel to Europe or the Americas. Brisbane, Australia Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels Brisbane's Oktoberfest celebrations reflect the same Southern Hemisphere seasonal reversal that defines Villa General Belgrano's festival, taking place during Australian spring rather than autumn, giving visitors warm, sunny conditions considerably different from the crisp fall atmosphere associated with the tradition's German origins. Current 2026 coverage specifically groups Brisbane alongside Villa General Belgrano as offering this reversed-season experience, giving travelers a specific, strategic reason to consider either destination if they're seeking Oktoberfest programming during a stretch of the calendar when the Northern Hemisphere celebrations covered elsewhere on this list have already concluded. Brisbane's specific appeal combines this seasonal advantage with Australia's own well-developed craft beer and festival infrastructure, giving visitors a comfortable, well-organized celebration that adapts the traditional format to a genuinely different climate and time of year than the tradition's original Bavarian context.

item.title: SK Hynix is in talks with Intel to make memory chips in the U.S. for the first time
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.22
The South Korean chipmaker could lease part of Intel's Ohio facility or form a joint venture with Intel and cloud firms In one scenario being discussed, SK Hynix could take over a portion of Intel's Ohio facility, which has been in the works for years, Reuters reported. Under another, the two companies could form a joint venture with major cloud firms seeking to secure memory chip supplies. One of the sources described the talks as exploratory and said no decisions have been made. In a statement, SK Hynix said it is "reviewing various measures, including establishing additional production bases, to strengthen the competitiveness of its memory business," adding that "no matters have been determined at this stage." Intel called the report speculation and declined to comment, though the company noted it remains committed to its Ohio investments as it prepares the site. Intel stock surged 5.2% in premarket trading on Wednesday, while SK Hynix stock finished 4.1% higher in Seoul. A deal could face significant hurdles. According to Reuters, producing chips domestically is considerably more expensive than doing so in South Korea, with U.S. facilities facing steeper wages and building expenses on top of the added costs of operating far from Asia's dense semiconductor supply chain. South Korean government opposition may also be a factor — any agreement involving advanced memory technologies such as high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, or DRAM could be subject to review under South Korea's Industrial Technology Protection Act, the country's trade ministry said. South Korea's trade ministry added that while any production decision would be at SK Hynix's discretion, technologies classified as "national core technology" would require regulatory review. SK Hynix's chairman, Chey Tae-won, said in July that building a factory in the United States had become necessary given pressure from customers and countries to supply more chips. SK Hynix currently has a chip packaging facility under construction in Indiana, but has no wafer fabrication presence in the U.S. An agreement would also provide financial relief to Intel, which is part-owned by the U.S. government. Intel's Ohio ambitions date to 2022, when the company pledged as much as $100 billion for what was envisioned as a massive chipmaking campus, though the two planned plants are now not expected to be finished until 2030 and 2031. SK Hynix is one of the world's leading suppliers of HBM, a key component in AI processors. The company's CEO, Kwak Noh-jung, warned earlier this year that 2027 will bring the most severe memory supply crunch the industry has ever seen, with customer demand expected to outpace production capacity beyond 2030. SK Hynix last month broke ground on a $4 billion facility in Indiana aimed at making the state a key HBM production base by 2030, according to CNBC. According to Reuters, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has warned that South Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers could face tariffs as high as 100% if they do not move to build more manufacturing capacity in the United States. The talks between SK Hynix and Intel are unfolding as South Korea and the U.S. wrangle over a broader investment commitment, with $200 billion of a proposed $350 billion package still undecided. item.title: Salesforce suffered a global outage just as its Dreamforce conference got underway
item.description:

Salesforce $CRM suffered a widespread service outage on Wednesday, the second day of its annual Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, leaving customers unable to access parts of its cloud software suite. Issues began around 3:50 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, leaving customers unable to access some services across all regions The trouble started at roughly 7:50 a.m. UTC (3:50 a.m. Eastern), based on Salesforce's status page incident tracker. Customers across all three of the company's operating regions, mainly in the U.S., may experience severe delays, intermittent errors, or an inability to access some services, the alert read. By 6:56 a.m. Eastern, Salesforce reported that its engineering team had pinpointed a fix, put it through testing in a controlled environment, and verified that it resolved the problem. The company said it was deploying the fix across all regions, according to Barron's. The outage coincided with Dreamforce, Salesforce's flagship annual technology conference held in San Francisco. First held in 2003, the conference has grown into one of the company's most important commercial and marketing platforms, according to Barron's. The outage comes as Salesforce has been deepening its push into artificial intelligence. The company announced a partnership with Anthropic to embed Salesforce customer data and workflows into Anthropic's Claude chatbot through a new plugin aimed at sales teams. That announcement coincided with Salesforce's fiscal second-quarter earnings release, in which the company posted revenue of $11.35 billion, up 11% year over year, and raised its full-year revenue guidance by $200 million. item.title: Walmart is partnering with a nonprofit insurer to sell Medicare Advantage plans
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.97
The co-branded plans will be available to more than 2 million Medicare enrollees in two states when open enrollment begins Oct. 15 The plans, pending regulatory approval, may include pharmacy, vision, food, and over-the-counter benefits, the companies said. Open enrollment for Medicare Advantage begins Oct. 15, according to MarketWatch. A central feature of the partnership is Walmart's Everyday Health Signals platform, an AI tool designed to provide personalized nutrition and wellness guidance based on members' shopping preferences and self-reported wellness goals. The companies said they plan to make that capability available to participating plan members as part of broader coaching and wellness support. "By combining Walmart's technology capabilities and consumer retail expertise with SCAN's Medicare product experience, we have an opportunity to develop products that translate those insights into meaningful support that helps members make more informed choices about their health and well-being," said Zack Myers, national general manager of SCAN Health Plan, in a statement. Walmart Group Director for Consumer Health and Data Solutions Pravene Nath said the collaboration is distinct because of Walmart's role in customers' everyday lives. "Because customers regularly turn to Walmart for groceries and other everyday essentials, we have an opportunity for those who choose to participate, to use insights from their shopping experiences to make nutrition guidance more relevant and actionable," Nath said in a statement. Walmart has offered in-store insurance support for more than a decade and launched Walmart Insurance Services, its licensed insurance agency, in 2020, the companies said. SCAN Group is a nonprofit organization whose health plan serves nearly 460,000 members across 33 counties in California, Arizona, Nevada, Texas, New Mexico, and Washington, with about half a million members and patients across all of its affiliated entities. The Walmart deal follows a similar move by SCAN with another major retailer. SCAN and Costco $COST Wholesale announced a partnership to sell Costco-branded Medicare plans, marking that retailer's first entry into the Medicare market. That arrangement covers two states for Medicare Advantage products and a third for a Medicare supplement plan, with a combined pool of around five million Medicare enrollees. The companies declined to name the target states, citing restrictions while plans await regulatory approval. The two companies did not disclose the financial terms of Wednesday's deal. item.title: The E.U. is inviting Canada to become its first associate member as U.S. trade war deepens
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.76
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the European Union's first associate member on Wednesday, a move that would bring the two sides closer as Canada's trade war with the United States deepens. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made the offer during her annual State of the Union address, with Canadian PM Mark Carney in attendance "I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the E.U.," von der Leyen said to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in her annual State of the European Union speech, delivered at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. Carney, who attended the speech and is due to address E.U. lawmakers on Thursday, rose from his seat and embraced von der Leyen as lawmakers gave a standing ovation, according to NPR. NPR noted that von der Leyen left unanswered the practical questions of what associate membership would entail and where it would leave nations currently pursuing full E.U. membership. The proposal would build on an existing partnership that already encompasses CETA, the E.U.-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, a deal that scrapped tariffs on 99% of all goods categories when it took provisional effect in 2017. Von der Leyen said the two sides would move beyond CETA toward an "Alliance for the Future" aimed at creating "a common prosperity and economic security space," with areas of cooperation to include advanced manufacturing, defense production, Arctic affairs, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and cybersecurity. According to NPR, Carney's office responded positively, framing the closer relationship as part of Canada's effort "to strengthen our sovereignty." The overture comes as Canada faces 50% U.S. tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on American goods matching U.S. duties dollar for dollar after trade negotiations between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month. The two countries have not resumed talks, and Canadian officials see little chance of negotiations restarting before the U.S. midterm elections. Roughly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States, according to NPR. Canada's entry this year into the E.U.'s 150-billion-euro SAFE defense program marked the first time a non-European nation had been admitted, opening the door for Canadian firms to participate in joint purchasing. Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding described the proposal as "a big step," telling CNBC that the push reflected Europe's broader effort to build alliances with democratic peers as a hedge against its exposure to both Washington and Beijing. item.title: Stock futures edge higher ahead of pivotal Fed rate decision
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.75
U.S. stock futures edged higher Wednesday as investors braced for a Federal Reserve interest rate decision widely expected to deliver the central bank's first hike since 2023. The S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%, with Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 futures climbing 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures added 77 points, a gain of 0.2%. The 10-year Treasury yield was hovering near 5%, and the 30-year stood at 5.374%. According to the CME $CME FedWatch tool, traders assigned 92.5% probability to a quarter-point hike at Wednesday's 2 p.m. ET decision. Markets put the chances of another quarter-point increase at 45% for October and 30% for December. The current target rate range is 3.5% to 3.75%. The anticipated move comes against a backdrop of stubborn inflation and rising energy costs. Annual CPI stood at 3.4% in August, retreating from a peak of 4.2% reached in May. On a monthly basis, CPI increased 0.4% as forecast, but core inflation, which strips out food and energy, came in at 0.3%, topping estimates. For the first time, U.S. diesel prices reached $6 per gallon on Friday, driven by supply constraints linked to the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran. Brent crude slid 0.7% to $107.92 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, dropped 1.2% to $104.55 per barrel. Brent Wilsey, chief investment officer at San Diego-based Wilsey Asset Management, argued that a decision by the Fed to leave rates unchanged would pose substantial risks. "That could surprise stocks, and surprises are rarely received well in markets, and it could also damage the Fed's credibility, and reignite concerns that the central bank is caving to political pressure to keep rates steady," Wilsey said in an emailed note, according to CNBC. The Fed's decision arrives amid pressure from the White House to leave rates unchanged. Tuesday's session ended in the red, with the S&P 500 off 0.45% and the Nasdaq Composite down 0.78%. The tech sector came under pressure after weekend conversations among leaders of major large language model firms raised the prospect of pulling back on how quickly new products reach market, according to CNBC. Overseas, Asian markets were mixed on Wednesday. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.34%, while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.24% and South Korea's Kospi added 0.12%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng slipped 0.18%. European stocks were broadly higher, with the regional Stoxx 600 up 0.4% and London's FTSE 100 rising 0.4%. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Pokémon is launching its biggest trading card set ever — and scalpers are already driving up prices
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.79
The Pokémon Company International launched the 30th Celebration expansion for the Pokémon Trading Card Game on Wednesday, releasing products at participating retailers worldwide to mark 30 years of the franchise. The expansion includes a guaranteed Pikachu rare in every booster pack and 30 reprints of classic cards Every card in the set is a foil card, the company said. The expansion also introduces a new card rarity called Futuristic rare, with artwork by Japanese artist YOSHIROTTEN. Each booster pack is guaranteed to include one of 30 Pikachu rare cards, and the set includes 30 reprints of classic Pokémon cards. Six products are available at launch. The Elite Trainer Box, priced at $89.99 through Amazon $AMZN, includes nine booster packs along with a foil Nidorina promo card and gameplay accessories. Amazon is offering an invite-only discounted price of $83.44 for the box, according to Mashable. Other launch-day products include the Poster Collection, Tech Sticker Collection, Pokémon ex Box, Two-Pack Blister, and Tin. Secondary market prices for some products are already running well above retail. On TCGplayer, the Elite Trainer Box carries a minimum listing of $150 against the $89.99 Amazon retail price, according to Mashable. The Pokémon ex Box, which comes with four booster packs and a promo card at retail, has TCGplayer listings opening at $67.32 for Greninja ex and $76.82 for Sylveon ex. Individual booster packs are going for $18.97 on TCGplayer. Additional products are scheduled for release later in 2026, the company said. Those include a Booster Bundle and Mini Tin in early October, a Battle Deck on October 30, and a Ditto Premium Collection, Figure Collection, and Ultra-Premium Collection on November 6. The Ultra-Premium Collection, which bundles 29 standard booster packs with one Classic Collection booster and various accessories, was already fetching $604.32 on TCGplayer before its November launch, according to Mashable. The 30th Celebration expansion is also available digitally through the Pokémon TCG Live app on iOS, Android, macOS, and Windows. Players who log in receive a themed deck accessory set and a 30th Celebration Battle Pass deck featuring Mew ex, the company said. An additional Sylveon ex deck can be unlocked through further play. item.title: Senate sank the Clarity Act, dashing the crypto industry's hopes for new rules
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.75
The Senate voted Tuesday to block the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act from advancing, with the motion to invoke cloture failing 50 to 49, well below the 60-vote threshold required to open floor debate on the bill. The procedural vote fell 11 votes short of the 60 needed, leaving the industry without a regulatory framework heading into midterm elections Every Democrat voted against the measure, joined by four Republicans: Senator Susan Collins of Maine, Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, Senator Jerry Moran of Kansas, and Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina. Senator Chris Coons of Delaware did not vote. According to CNBC, the legislation would have divided crypto regulatory oversight between the SEC and the CFTC, created registration requirements, and bolstered protections against money laundering. The central sticking point was an ethics provision intended to prevent presidents and other elected officials from profiting from crypto ventures while in office. Democrats challenged the provision as toothless, pointing out that the Justice Department — headed by Todd Blanche, who previously served as Trump's personal lawyer — would bear responsibility for policing a sitting president's own conduct, according to NPR. Those concerns deepened once Trump revealed that he and his family had taken in $1.4 billion from crypto ventures over the past year, according to NPR. Over the weekend, Republican bill sponsors — Senator Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, Senator John Boozman of Arkansas, and Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina — released revised language that would bar the president and other senior officials from issuing digital assets and give state attorneys general authority to bring enforcement actions. The sponsors said the updated text incorporated 126 substantive changes Democrats had requested. The revisions were not enough to break the impasse. "The compromise we had was a good ethics compromise that would have bought a lot of Dem votes," Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona, a Democratic negotiator, told CNBC before the vote. Gallego said Republicans cared "more about making sure the president keeps making money than actually bringing regulations." In the aftermath of the vote, bitcoin dropped 3%, and shares of Coinbase and Circle fell 8% and 10%, respectively. Senator Lummis had warned before the August recess that failure to pass the bill in this Congress could delay the legislation until 2030. Reviving the legislation faces a compressed timeline: the Senate is set to recess in early October, and with midterm elections arriving just seven weeks after Tuesday's vote, there is little room to maneuver, according to CNBC. Senator Lummis told reporters before the vote that "it's over" if the procedural motion failed, according to CNBC. Senator Tillis entered a procedural motion preserving the possibility of returning the bill to the floor at a later date, according to NPR. A version of the bill had already passed the House. item.title: OpenAI's CFO says the company will pace AI development if safety requires it
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.48
"We do need to take safety seriously," Friar told CNBC. "And if it means we have to pace the frontier and slow down, absolutely, we're going to listen to our researchers and do that." Friar said she was not concerned about the prospect of a slowdown, noting that even a pause would leave a substantial base of AI capability in place. "Even if we stop today, the amount of intelligence that's available in the world is massive," she said. She added that OpenAI would base investment decisions on a "strong ROI" even if development had to be paced. The comments came as debate over AI safety has intensified following warnings from a former Anthropic researcher who left the company and said the technology could cause catastrophic harm. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei weighed in Saturday with a blog post making the case that pulling back on the pace of AI development would lower the odds of a catastrophic outcome, a position OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Tesla $TSLA and xAI CEO Elon Musk each signaled agreement with over the weekend. Friar acknowledged Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang's view that speed and safety are not in conflict, but said OpenAI needed to be "pragmatic about the fact there are real risks here." Huang, appearing Tuesday at Salesforce $CRM's Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, pushed back on the premise that speed and safety are at odds, contending that market pressures already provided adequate guardrails against AI risk without the need for new rules. The broader industry debate has drawn in a wide range of voices. Altman warned that AI's rapid pace of development could go "very badly" if humans lost control of AI systems or if a single entity used AI to concentrate power. He called for a federal framework setting consistent safety requirements for frontier AI and said companies should not wait for government legislation before putting their own safety controls in place. President Donald Trump has rejected calls for caution, saying the fears represent a "hoax" and a "scam." On the question of a public offering, Friar said OpenAI still has a strong balance sheet and emphasized that the company will run its own timeline. In a Saturday interview with Fortune, Altman described a 2026 IPO as "ill-advised." Friar, meanwhile, told employees last month that OpenAI is on track to go public in 2027, though an earlier debut remains possible if market conditions are favorable, according to CNBC. item.title: AI data centers are devouring America's electric grid. It's all based on guesswork
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.25
The data centers powering artificial intelligence are eating the electric grid. Energy consumption by these facilities jumped 80% from 2020 to 2025, according to the International Energy Agency. Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta poured over $200 billion into AI infrastructure in 2024 alone, a 62% increase year over year. It's the fastest infrastructure buildout the power sector has seen in decades. Tech CEOs are reviving shuttered nuclear plants, installing gas turbines on farm land, signing deals that lock in electricity for years. The race to build artificial general intelligence has turned electricity into the most contested resource in tech. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy. The infrastructure buildout is real. The AI demand driving it is guesswork. Data center electricity demand in the U.S. sits around 176 terawatt-hours annually, roughly what Texas uses. By 2030, credible projections range from 200 terawatt-hours to over 1,000 terawatt-hours. "There's just enormous uncertainty about what the future business models of AI actually look like," says Brendan Pierpont, the electricity director at Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan energy and climate policy think tank. That uncertainty has created chaos. In both Northern Virginia and Texas, utilities are fielding power requests tripling what the entire state uses. Across the country, utilities designed for predictable growth are being overwhelmed with speculative requests, according to Andy Cvengros, who leads JLL's U.S. data center practice. “Anybody who owns land next to a power line is saying, 'Do I have power capacity available? Can I sell it for seven times what I got it for?'” Cvengros says. Utilities are trying to filter out the noise. They used to charge developers a few thousand dollars to study whether power could be delivered. Now some require million-dollar deposits upfront. When Texas utility AEP required developers to commit to paying for 85% of their requested power, which can be millions of dollars, applications dropped from 30 gigawatts to 13 gigawatts overnight. Projects are also getting blocked by local opposition, with communities worried about the impact on their environment and energy bills. According to Data Center Watch, more data center projects were delayed or blocked in a single quarter last year than in the previous two years combined. But the chaos is already affecting electricity prices. Grid operators are approving natural gas plants and locking in capacity prices based on projections of data center growth. The tech companies that make it through the filters are so desperate for power they'll pay whatever it takes. Gernot Wagner, who researches energy policy at Columbia Business School, said that willingness to pay premium prices is raising costs for everyone. The hyperscalers are so rich and the race so intense that they'll pay far more than traditional industrial customers ever would. Because everyone draws from the same grid, when utilities raise prices to meet data center demand, those costs get passed to all customers. The power market is heavily regulated, which means there's a choice to be made. "Should we allow hyperscalers to simply pay more for electricity, and all of our rates go up?" Wagner said. The grid operator covering the mid-Atlantic has already started revising its near-term data center forecasts downward. But capacity prices were set based on higher projections. "We've locked in high prices based on an already outdated load forecast," Pierpont said. "And customers are going to be paying those high prices for at least the next three years."

item.title: The 10 best cities in the world for nightlife in 2026, ranked
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.00
The 10 best cities in the world for nightlife in 2026, ranked From rooftop bars and underground clubs to street-side venues and queer nightlife, these cities offer diverse ways to experience a night out Reports of nightlife’s death have been considerably exaggerated. Sure, the specific way people go out has shifted noticeably, with rooftop raves and street parties replacing some of the old reliance on one or two big-name venues, but the underlying appetite for a great night out hasn’t gone anywhere. If anything, cities everywhere are getting considerably more creative about how they deliver it. Hotter summers have pushed much of that creativity outdoors too, with curbside drinking and open-air events becoming genuine fixtures of the modern going-out calendar instead of rare seasonal novelties confined to just a few warm weeks each year. This creativity shows up everywhere from historic club buildings getting cultural-heritage protection to entirely new nightlife districts springing up outside a city’s traditional going-out zones. Local governments and communities have fought to preserve legendary venues in several of these cities, proving that a great nightlife scene doesn’t simply happen on its own. It takes real investment, both financial and cultural, to keep the party truly alive decade after decade. Affordability and safety matter as much as the venues themselves, since a genuinely great night out means little if it’s priced out of reach for most locals or feels unsafe to enjoy after dark. The 10 cities below all appear in Time Out’s survey of more than 24,000 locals worldwide, combined with scores from a panel of Time Out’s own nightlife experts. Each entry below covers the specific venues, districts, and broader cultural shifts that earned the city its spot on this list. Only the single highest-scoring city from each country made the final cut, giving the ranking genuine global spread instead of clustering around a handful of famously party-heavy nations that might otherwise crowd out smaller destinations entirely. 10. Amsterdam spreads its nightlife beyond downtown Artem Shuba / Unsplash Amsterdam has long carried one of Europe’s most established nightlife reputations, but in 2026 that reputation feels considerably more local than it once did. The city has notably moved past its old party-town image, with the best nights now spreading well beyond the historic center into neighborhoods like Noord, Oost, De Pijp, and Jordaan. Noord has emerged as the city’s actual after-dark epicenter, home to warehouse clubs like Garage Noord alongside waterfront favorites such as Pllek. Several venues throughout the neighborhood blur the line between clubbing, art, and live music entirely, giving visitors a considerably different experience than the more traditional club format found elsewhere in the city. Elsewhere in Amsterdam, listening bars like Loop 51 and cocktail spots including Door 74 reflect a broader shift toward more adventurous, considered ways of going out. This shift away from purely high-volume partying toward properly curated experiences speaks to a maturing scene that’s found real depth beyond its historic reputation for simple, straightforward hedonism. WorldPride 2026 has brought fresh attention to Amsterdam’s already inclusive LGBTQ+ nightlife scene, with venues like Club Raum leading the charge throughout the city. Time Out’s expert panel gave the city a 60 percent approval rating, while 67 percent of locals rated the quality of their nightlife scene highly and 77 percent said finding community after dark comes easily. Clubs and casual pubs tied for the top spot when locals were asked what Amsterdam does best. The city’s canal-lined layout also shapes how nightlife unfolds, since many venues sit within easy walking or cycling distance of each other, letting visitors bar-hop across neighborhoods without needing to plan around public transit schedules. De Pijp in particular has quietly built a reputation for cozy, unpretentious bars that draw a genuine mix of locals and visitors instead of catering purely to tourists passing through the city center. 9. Beijing hides its best nights outside Sanlitun Christian Lue / Unsplash Beijing’s nightlife has always rewarded people who actually know where to look, and the Sanlitun district remains a natural starting point for many evenings out. Latin dancing at La Social or rooftop cocktails at Casa Bacardi both deliver a solid night, but the city’s actual best experiences tend to unfold somewhere else entirely. Great Leap Brewing offers craft beer tucked into a quiet hutong, a considerably calmer alternative to Sanlitun’s busier strips, while Shifter serves sustainably minded cocktails for a more considered evening out. Modernista, meanwhile, has kept crowds coming back downstairs to catch live indie bands for nearly 15 years running, a genuine institution by Beijing nightlife standards. Techno fans gravitate toward Groundless Factory, often nicknamed Beijing’s answer to Berlin’s legendary Berghain, alongside venues like Zhao Dai, Solo, and Pillbox. Collectives including Rave AM and Yinyang Productions have pushed the scene even further, hosting daytime coffee raves and house music events in truly unexpected spaces like churches, parks, and even hotpot restaurants. Beijing’s reputation for safety and walkability at night adds real practical appeal on top of the venues themselves, making bar-hopping across different neighborhoods part of the actual fun instead of a logistical headache. Locals rated the city the cheapest on this list, with a 77 percent affordability score; 72 percent rated nightlife quality highly, and 80 percent said the city delivers real community connection after dark. Beijing’s scene also benefits from a genuinely wide range of price points sitting comfortably alongside each other, letting visitors move from an affordable street-side beer to a considered cocktail without needing to switch neighborhoods entirely. This flexibility gives Beijing real appeal for travelers on tighter budgets who still want access to the city’s more polished venues on occasion, without feeling priced out of the broader scene. 8. Brighton keeps queer nightlife at its center T / Unsplash Brighton’s status as the UK’s LGBTQ+ nightlife capital continues to define much of what makes the seaside city special after dark. Staples like Revenge, The Queen’s Arms, and Bar Broadway provide notably safe, inclusive spaces for the city’s queer community, anchoring a scene that’s remained consistently strong for decades. Patterns hosts resident DJ MIMI, whose sets fuse Jungle with Mauritian Sega for a properly distinctive sound found nowhere else on this list. Casablanca, the city’s oldest club, delivers a different kind of energy entirely, with live soul, funk, disco, and pop performed by rotating local bands instead of relying purely on DJ sets. Brighton’s whimsical side shows up clearly in themed nights like Party in your Pants, an inclusive feminist paint rave, and Fairytopia, which blends pop music with high-fantasy costume culture. For visitors after a slower pace, venues like The Lion and Lobster, The Bees Mouth, and Patio offer more relaxed evenings, while Crossbar, the UK’s first dedicated women’s sports bar, opened its doors just this year. Brighton earned the highest community score of any city surveyed, with 84 percent of locals saying it’s actually easy to make connections there. The city also tied with Seoul for the second-highest nightlife quality rating overall, at 83 percent, and ranked as the most likely city after New York to be described as lively and inclusive by the locals who actually live there. Brighton’s compact size genuinely works in its favor too. Most of the city’s key venues sit within easy walking distance of the seafront and each other, making an evening of bar-hopping considerably more relaxed than in larger, more spread-out cities. This walkability, paired with the city’s long-standing reputation for tolerance and inclusivity, gives Brighton a genuinely welcoming atmosphere that extends well beyond its famous LGBTQ+ scene into nightlife more broadly. 7. Johannesburg reinvents itself one dance floor at a time Vije Vijendranath / Unsplash Johannesburg’s nightlife has thrived on constant reinvention since at least the legendary Carfax warehouse parties of the 1990s, and that restless creativity still defines the city today. Few destinations anywhere in Africa manage to stay this consistently exciting for a late-night out, decade after decade of shifting trends and venues. Gwigwi Mrwebi Street, named after a pioneering South African jazz musician who carried local sounds well beyond the country’s borders, hosts four iconic venues standing shoulder to shoulder within one of the city’s last true nightlife precincts. Club A.M., AND Club, Bad Manors, and Carfax together showcase exceptional DJs moving fluidly between deep house, techno, afro-house, gqom, drum and bass, and truly experimental sounds. Melville and Rosebank offer a considerably different pace for visitors who prefer lively cocktail bars to dance floors. Neighborhood favorites like Six Bar on 7th Street and A Street Bar Named Desire on Bolton Road deliver live music and performance in more intimate settings. This range gives Johannesburg real versatility depending on what kind of night someone’s actually after. Locals rated Johannesburg among the more affordable cities on this list, with a 66 percent overall score, while a properly impressive 80 percent said finding community after dark comes easily throughout the city. Clubbing, casual pubs, and cocktail bars all earned strong votes as the city’s best after-dark activities, reflecting how broad Johannesburg’s nightlife really is. Braamfontein has also emerged as a genuine draw for younger crowds specifically, with student-friendly bars and live music venues clustering around the University of the Witwatersrand and drawing a considerably younger energy than the more established Melville and Rosebank scenes. Security remains a genuine consideration for visitors moving between venues after dark, and most locals rely on rideshare services or organized transport between spots instead of walking long distances between neighborhoods late at night. 6. Medellín lets reggaeton rule its clubs Joel Duncan / Unsplash Medellín sits at the genuine heart of reggaeton’s global rise, having produced stars like Karol G, J Balvin, and Maluma, and that musical dominance shows up clearly across the city’s biggest clubs. Dulcinea and Tutaina remain longtime favorites, while newer hotspots Medallo Club and Medussa have quickly built their own devoted followings among locals and visitors alike. Beyond the reggaeton-driven megaclubs, Medellín has developed a notably intimate alternative scene over the past several years, with more than a dozen speakeasies, listening bars, and lo-fi spots scattered throughout the city. Mad Radio, which also operates locations in Miami and New York, brings that same considered approach to Medellín, while the newly opened 55 dB Listening Bar adds another properly low-key option for quieter evenings. Laureles and Poblado remain the city’s established after-dark hotspots, though Poblado’s center of gravity has shifted noticeably in recent years, moving away from the once-dominant Parque Lleras toward the neighboring areas of Provenza and Manila. This shift reflects a broader maturing of Medellín’s nightlife scene, spreading energy across a wider footprint instead of concentrating it all in one increasingly crowded plaza. Medellín earned the highest local quality rating of this entire ranking, with a remarkable 87 percent of residents calling their city’s nightlife good or amazing. It also ranked as the second-cheapest city surveyed, with a 67 percent affordability score, and 71 percent of locals specifically named clubbing as the single best thing about going out in Medellín. Medellín’s year-round, spring-like climate supports outdoor nightlife in ways colder cities simply can’t replicate, with rooftop terraces and open-air patios staying comfortable enough to use year-round instead of just a handful of warm months. This climate advantage, combined with the city’s relatively low cost of living compared to other major Latin American destinations, helps explain why Medellín consistently draws such enthusiastic ratings from the very people who actually live there. 5. São Paulo climbs onto historic rooftops to party Joao paulo m ramos paulo / Unsplash São Paulo has firmly established itself as an after-dark playground for Latin America’s largest metropolis, and much of that reputation now centers on a growing trend of nightclubs opening inside historic buildings, particularly on their rooftops. Matiz ranks among the hottest of these spots, having even landed on Dua Lipa’s personal list of favorite places worldwide, offering panoramic views from the 11th floor alongside renowned vinyl DJs and notably excellent cocktails. Ephigenia stands out as another genuine rooftop standout, spanning two floors, each with its own dedicated dance floor, hosting lively house music nights alongside more relaxed vinyl afternoon sessions. The iconic Edifício Martinelli, recognized as São Paulo’s first skyscraper, throws notably diverse rooftop parties, from samba to electro, on its rooftop, situated an impressive 25 floors above the street below. A Balsa offers a considerably cozier alternative for visitors specifically seeking rooftop dinners that naturally transition into dancing later in the evening. Tokyo has also become a beloved fixture of São Paulo’s nightlife, famous for its karaoke offerings, complete with private rooms where friends can belt out favorite songs away from a larger, more public crowd. Locals rated São Paulo highly across several key categories, with 74 percent calling the nightlife quality good or amazing and 71 percent saying a night out remains actually affordable. Time Out’s expert panel gave the city’s after-dark scene a solid 70 percent rating, while an impressive 72 percent of locals said finding real connection and community throughout São Paulo comes easily. São Paulo’s sheer scale works to its advantage here, since a metropolis this large supports dozens of distinct nightlife pockets across neighborhoods, each with its own character and regular crowd. Vila Madalena remains a longtime favorite for bar-hopping on foot, while Jardins caters to a slightly more upscale crowd seeking polished cocktails over the rowdier club scene found elsewhere in the city. 4. Melbourne turns nightlife into an adventure Alexis / Unsplash Melbourne’s nightlife truly feels like a choose-your-own-adventure exercise, offering distinctly different experiences depending entirely on what kind of evening someone’s actually after. Visitors happy to settle in with friends over a pint and some live music will find no shortage of welcoming pubs scattered throughout the city, each with its own particular character and regular crowd. Anyone wanting to dance for hours instead will find Solace Bar and Coil both deliver properly impressive audio systems built specifically for serious club nights. Pride of Our Footscray caters directly to the city’s LGBTQIA+ community, hosting regular drag bingo, trivia, and comedy nights that have become genuine neighborhood institutions in their own right over time. Nightlife trends inevitably come and go, and Melbourne has said goodbye to plenty of once-beloved fixtures over the years, including the golden age of dedicated club photographers documenting every big night out. Despite those shifts, the city’s broader after-dark scene has remained notably eclectic, consistently surprising, and reliably fun for like-minded people looking to let loose together. Melbourne ranked third among Time Out’s expert panel of nightlife specialists, while locals gave the city consistently strong marks across the board. Seventy-seven percent rated Melbourne’s nightlife as good or amazing, and 59 percent specifically praised the city’s sense of community after dark. When asked what Melbourne does best, locals pointed to cocktail bars and casual pubs, backed by 61 and 72 percent of respondents respectively. Melbourne’s laneway culture spills directly into its nightlife too, with narrow alleys throughout the CBD hiding small bars that are genuinely easy to walk past without knowing they exist. This tucked-away quality has become something of a signature for the city, rewarding visitors willing to actually explore instead of sticking to the more obvious main strips lined with visible signage and street-facing front entrances. 3. New York City adapts to a sleepier crowd Zac Ong / Unsplash New York’s nightlife scene has gotten a touch quieter in recent years, with early dinner reservations becoming far more coveted than they once were in a city famous for never sleeping. This shift doesn’t mean the scene has gone entirely to bed, though, since New York’s after-dark culture remains as diverse and adaptive as everything else that defines the city. Options genuinely span every possible mood and preference throughout the five boroughs. Raving beneath one of the city’s formerly overlooked bridges remains an option for dedicated night owls, as does finally catching a pulsating set at Pacha following its considerably soap-opera-like history of ownership drama and venue changes over recent years. A gentler pace comes courtesy of millennial-friendly dance parties that wrap up by 10pm, alongside spontaneous dancing on Harlem stoops and wine clubs specifically built around centering BIPOC and queer communities. This range of genuinely different experiences, all coexisting within the same city, speaks directly to how thoroughly New York’s nightlife has adapted instead of simply shrinking under changing habits. New York received the third-highest local rating on this entire list, with 82 percent of residents calling their city’s nightlife good or amazing. It did receive the lowest affordability score of any city surveyed, though, with only 40 percent of locals agreeing that a night out remains genuinely affordable. New York was also the single city most likely to be described as exciting, diverse, and lively, and a strong 95 percent backing from Time Out’s expert panel helped secure its third-place finish. Brooklyn’s role in the city’s nightlife has grown considerably too, with neighborhoods like Bushwick and Williamsburg now rivaling Manhattan for genuinely interesting venues, often at noticeably more affordable prices than their counterparts across the river. This geographic spread means visitors increasingly need to think beyond Manhattan alone when planning a night out, since some of the city’s most talked-about newer spots now sit firmly outside the traditionally expected nightlife map. 2. Berlin fights to save its legendary clubs Stephan Widua / Unsplash Berlin’s nightlife currently sits at a genuine turning point, with rising rents and aggressive redevelopment fueling what local critics have started calling Clubsterben, essentially the slow death of the city’s once-untouchable club scene. There’s a real reason for optimism, though, since Germany is actively working to reclassify clubs as cultural institutions, making them considerably harder for developers to displace going forward. This regulatory shift builds directly on UNESCO’s 2024 decision to recognize Berlin’s techno culture as intangible cultural heritage, adding a new layer of protection beyond anything clubbers could achieve alone. Institutions like Berghain and Tresor remain genuine anchors of the scene, even as nightlife more broadly has splintered into nomadic collectives and pop-up parties operating on considerably shorter notice. Queer, sex-positive collective Lecken exemplifies that nomadic shift directly, moving venues from Kreuzwerk to OXI while selling tickets through Resident Advisor and building a dedicated following on Instagram. Other collectives skip social media entirely, revealing locations through Telegram just hours before doors open. Berlin’s established clubs haven’t lost their edge either. KitKat still runs on unapologetic fetish energy, and Renate narrowly avoided eviction in December before rejoining Sisyphos and Else for open-air day parties that melt into full weekend marathons. ÆDEN has been soundtracking summer 2026 with euphoric trance, groove, and techno. Berlin received a 78 percent approval rating from locals for its overall after-dark offering, while Time Out’s expert panel backed the city completely, at a full 100 percent. Interestingly, despite Berlin’s reputation for underground raves and famously impossible-to-enter clubs, the majority of Berliners, 62 percent, actually rated the city’s casual bars and pubs as its single best nightlife asset. This gap between Berlin’s international reputation and how locals actually experience their own city’s nightlife says something genuinely important about the place. Visitors often arrive chasing the Berghain door policy or the city’s storied techno scene specifically. Residents seem just as content with a neighborhood bar and good conversation, suggesting Berlin’s nightlife identity runs much deeper and is far more varied than its famous clubs alone. 1. Bangkok spills its parties onto the street Florian Wehde / Unsplash Bangkok’s nightlife truly has everything a night owl could ask for, from pokey street-side bars to sprawling mega clubs, 360-degree rooftop bars, and wild LGBTQ+ party spaces scattered throughout the city. What makes Bangkok special, though, is how naturally parties spill from bars onto the streets, blurring the line between venue and public space. Soi Nana in Chinatown captures that spillover energy perfectly, a narrow lane home to icons like G.O.D, Tep Bar, and Ba Hao, an old shophouse serving cocktails upstairs to a steady stream of regulars. Nearby, Bar Temp. runs almost entirely on genuine community spirit, hosting the city’s various collectives and resident DJs most nights of the week without fail. Sing Sing Theater adds real theatrical flair too, a red-lanterned cabaret megaclub that even appeared in the third season of The White Lotus. Bangkok’s after-dark culture extends well beyond partying alone, encompassing everything from genuine fine dining to eating pad kaphrao off a plastic stool at 2am with equal enthusiasm. Rooftop bars deliver some of the city’s best skyline views, particularly in the Thonglor and Silom districts. Silom specifically serves as the city’s hub for queer-led gay bars and clubs, while other dedicated spaces cater directly to trans and sapphic communities throughout the city. Bangkok’s infamous daytime heat also plays a real role in explaining why the city comes alive so thoroughly once the sun goes down. Seventy-three percent of Bangkok locals rated their city’s nightlife as good or amazing, while the exact same percentage said finding genuine community there comes easily. Time Out’s expert panel gave Bangkok a whopping 95 approval score, cementing the Thai capital’s position as this ranking’s clear favorite. Bangkok’s sprawling scale works in visitors’ favor once they get the hang of the city’s transit options, since the BTS Skytrain and river boats connect most major nightlife districts without requiring an expensive taxi ride between neighborhoods. This accessibility, combined with the sheer density of options packed into areas like Thonglor alone, means even a short trip to Bangkok can genuinely deliver a completely different kind of night out every single evening of the stay.

item.title: Treasury yields are hovering at a 19-year high as the Fed prepares to raise rates
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 2.31
U.S. Treasury yields held above 5% on Wednesday morning as investors waited for the Federal Reserve to announce its latest interest rate decision, which markets widely expect will be a quarter-point increase. The 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest closing level since 2007 on Tuesday, with traders pricing in a 92.5% chance of a quarter-point hike At 4:30 a.m. ET, the 10-year Treasury yield held steady at 5.004%, and the 20- and 30-year maturities sat at 5.409% and 5.372% in kind. The Federal Open Market Committee is set to announce its monetary policy decision at 2 p.m. ET. According to the CME $CME FedWatch tool, fed funds futures put the odds of a quarter-point hike at about 92.5%, a steep climb from approximately 33% just a month earlier. Should the Fed deliver the expected quarter-point increase, attention will quickly turn to what Chairman Kevin Warsh says at his post-decision press conference. "At this stage, it would be very difficult for the Fed to leave rates unchanged this week without eroding its inflation-fighting credibility," Vail Hartman, U.S. rates strategist at BMO Capital Markets, said in a note, according to CNN. Brent Wilsey, chief investment officer at Wilsey Asset Management, warned in a Wednesday note that a decision to hold rates steady could unsettle markets. "If the Federal Reserve were to keep rates steady Wednesday, that could surprise stocks, and surprises are rarely received well in markets," he said. "It could also damage the Fed's credibility, and reignite concerns that the central bank is caving to political pressure to keep rates steady." The 10-year yield climbed above 5% for the first time since 2007 on Tuesday, touching an intraday peak of 5.041% before closing at around 5%. Friday's August CPI reading put annual inflation at 3.4%, and the most recent personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's go-to price measure — showed a 3.7% year-over-year gain through July, while crude oil continues to trade north of $100 a barrel. The sharp bond market selloff that pushed yields to multiyear highs reflects a confluence of pressures: heavier issuance from both corporations and the federal government, oil prices inflated by Middle East tensions, and deepening worries about the country's fiscal trajectory. The Fed's rate-hike odds climbed to around 90% after the August inflation report and have continued to rise heading into Wednesday's decision. In a Wednesday note, Jonathan Pryor, co-head of FX dealing at Marex, argued that the Fed has entered a new phase. "Earlier in the year, it looked like we were entering into a rate cutting cycle that may last for six or twelve months, but now it feels like the tables have turned," he said, according to CNBC. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: Tours in Town: Thievery Corporation, Wave to Earth, Pierce the Veil
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 4.16
Thievery Corporation For over 20 years, Rob Garza and Eric Hilton have been expanding the dancefloor boundaries of EDM as Thievery Corporation. Though early efforts were paint-by-number exercises in straight dub and acid jazz, their evolution toward stadium spinning has been fueled by melding world music into their jams, particularly Middle-Eastern, Latin, and Indian sounds. Since the breakthrough release that landed them a worldwide audience, 2005’s The Cosmic Game, it’s not uncommon to find multiple languages represented on any given album, from Spanish and Italian to French, Portuguese, Romanian, Persian, and even Hindi. The band’s political and social stances are trotted out and propped up from time to time, as in “History” where Boston rapper Mr Lif complains about how “I can’t look at a cop without second-guessing.” The duo recently re-released their sixth studio album Culture Of Fear as a 15th Anniversary edition, and they’re currently on their 30th Anniversary Tour. Wave To Earth South Korean indie rock band Wave To Earth is known for their dreamy blend of lo-fi indie pop, surf rock, jazz-inspired percussion and drumming, and English-language songwriting. They create warm, melancholic, and atmospheric soundscapes with cinematic flourishes on tracks such as “light,” from their debut EP, which earned them early underground traction. They went viral on TikTok in 2020 with "seasons" from their album 0.1 Flaws and All, which surpassed 500 million streams, and their single "bad," which climbed to number one on Spotify's Viral 50 Global Chart. Promoting their work as "All Self-Made," members Daniel Kim (vocals, guitar), Cha Soon-jong (bass), and Shin Dong-gyu (drums) handle their own recording, mixing, mastering, visual art, and direct all of the band’s music videos. They have become one of the most-streamed South Korean indie acts globally, selling out major tours across North America, Europe, and Asia, and performing at major international festivals like Lollapalooza. Pierce the Veil Pierce the Veil was founded by singer/guitarist/songwriter Vic Fuentes and his drummer brother Mike, both former Mission Bay High School students who previously played with Early Times and Before Today. Their debut album Flair for the Dramatic - recorded in Seattle and in the studio that their parents had built for them in their home near Mission Bay - came out in summer 2007, during which the band took part in that year's Warped tour. In 2010, their album Selfish Machines debuted at number one on Billboard’s Heatseekers chart, and they toured that summer again with the Warped Tour, as the proggy metal band’s album racked up over 700,000 downloads. 2012’s Collide With the Sky became their biggest selling album, going gold and selling over 500,000 copies, while their fourth studio album from 2016, Misadventures, entered the Billboard Top 200 Chart at number four. Their most recent full-length, The Jaws of Life, dropped in 2023. This final date of the tour will be Pierce The Veil's only mainland U.S. headline appearance of the year.

item.title: Puddles Pity Party isn't just clowning around
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.34
Quick, name a comic-book clown who’s upset about the state of the world and who, for some reason, sings a lot. What’s that? The Joker from the godawful bite-the-hand-that-applauds-you sequel Joker: Folie a Deux? Well, you’re not wrong. But happily, that’s not who’s on stage tomorrow night, opening for Weird Al Yankovic at Rady Shell. No, the crooning clown of the hour is Puddles from Puddles Pity Party, seen here in full comic color on the cover of his new album No One’s Free. “I wanted a cover that invites people in,” writes Puddles. (Our interview was conducted via email; Puddles saves his spoken words for his songs.) “The imagery is like a little sugar to make the medicine go down. I think comic books have traditionally been a vehicle for imagining justice served in a perpetually cruel world. The thought bubble is basically my ‘wtf’ reaction to all the division and intolerance and violent rhetoric permeating our society lately.” The album title is also the name of its first song, and in case that bit about division and intolerance wasn’t enough, you can tell from the outset that we’re a long way from “Royals,” the Lorde cover that first made Puddles an internet phenom back in 2013. (Mainstream stardom came four years later, when he reached the quarterfinals of America’s Got Talent.) “Royals” is the story of a poor girl from a torn-up town who can’t help but notice the difference between pop-star life — jet planes, islands, tigers on a gold leash — and her own. But, she says, we’re fine with this; we didn’t come from money. “No One’s Free” has none of that serenity. Right away, the song warns, The world is getting’ much too small, and there’s really no room at all, and if one of us starts to fall, we all go down. No one’s free ‘til we can see ourselves in every stranger. It's almost unsettling, hearing such an earnest sentiment from an ostensibly comic figure. (One of his most popular stage bits is singing the theme song from Gilligan’s Island to the epically varied tune of “Stairway to Heaven.”) It’s one thing to listen to him cover Radiohead’s “Creep” in all its plaintive angst. It’s another to hear him sing something you haven’t heard before — the songs were written by longtime friend Andrew Douglas Quinn — that includes a sentiment as naked as In the end, my friend/ We all stall/ We’ll all fall/ Ya lose it all/ But you can have a ball/ In spite of it all. It put me in mind of "Cloony the Clown" from Shel Silverstein’s poem about a clown who can’t make people laugh — until he tells them how sad he is. “And after he finished his tale of woe/ Did everyone cry? Oh no, no, no/ They laughed until they shook the trees/ With ‘Hah-hah-hahs’ and ‘Hee Hee-Hees…and while the world laughed outside/Cloony the Clown sat down and cried.” I asked Puddles if he’d read Cloony, and wondered if there was a kind of dare to the audience at work: can you listen to this from a clown without wondering if you’re supposed to laugh? “Shel Silverstein is my jam,” replied Puddles. “Telling a compelling story in an uncomplicated, sincere way leaves room for wondering. But nobody is ‘supposed’ to laugh or not laugh. Reactions are personal to the listener, purely subjective. Some folks laugh when faced with uncomfortable or sad subject matter. It may be a nervous reaction, but it’s authentic to them.” Or maybe it’s enough to just turn our attention to a song that will likely show up in Weird Al’s setlist: the similarly sincere "Skipper Dan." I’ve never quoted a YouTube comment before, but this one from @TheAncientTale is worth it: “I was at a weird Al concert when he actually explained this song. He was on a Disney water ride, and the tour guy was talking about his failed acting career. Weird Al said to himself ‘that’s a song.’ And he went home that day and worked on this song tirelessly. This isn’t a joke, he actually said that.” Give it a listen: the chorus is an absolute banger. But that’s the exception for Yankovic; usually, he’s a little more layered, as when he gives us a peppy anthem about executing people on behalf of the Deep State with “Party in the CIA.” As Puddles notes, “Weird Al’s crowd is dialed in for a wild time. They appreciate absurdity. That said, there are a few poignant moments in my set that can catch some off guard. I’ve seen grown men in the audience get moved to tears. I’m sure they did not expect the feels to overtake them in such a festive environment while sporting a tinfoil hat.” On “No One’s Free,” the absurdity is that, like Cloony, the clown is quite sincere. Puddles: “I sing what I mean, and I mean what I sing. I like the Mark Twain quote, ‘When in doubt, tell the truth.’” The callback to Twain — another humorist with a strong moral bent — led me to ask Puddles about his heritage. Pagliacci? Bozo? Some other clown? “I’m descended from a long line of roustabouts and raconteur shrimp boat captains. Watching TV as a boy with my MeeMaw, I was inspired by the physical comedy of Carol Burnett, the absurdity of Monty Python, and the cringe antics of Andy Kaufman. And listening to the scratchy AM radio on PeePaw’s shrimp boat, I was always moved by the more dramatic vocalists, singers like Tom Jones, Freddie Mercury, and Shirley Bassey.” (It’s easy to hear Mercury’s influence on Puddles’ “Wasting Time.”) But despite the social concerns underlying Todd Phillips’ take on The Joker, the Clown Prince of Crime does not fit into Puddles’ pantheon. And "Creep" or no "Creep," he is not put off by the cultural ascendence of the Creepy Clown. “Joker and Pennywise are not real people. They don’t scare me. There are actual humans in real life who are far more sinister and frightening — many of whom are currently in positions of power and doing far more damage to the world than The Joker could have ever dreamed.”

item.title: Perry Mason's creator was a Baja nut
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 2.93
Perry Mason's creator was a Baja nut His Mexican pilot tells the back stories
Gardner and Muñoz. The two men decided to fly along the coast, about 180 miles south of Ensenada, to see if the rugged beaches could yield access to custom-designed trailers and dune bikes.
In early 1960, the man who created Perry Mason was introduced to an Imperial Beach resident named Francisco Muñoz. Erle Stanley Gardner had many friends, and he particularly liked Mexicans, but the friendship that developed between him and Muñoz appears to have ranked among the most cherished of both men. By 1962 Muñoz had become a main character in Gardner’s travel books and his abettor in adventures like this one, recounted by Gardner in The Hidden Heart of Baja. Erle Stanely Gardner on a Baja trip in the 1960s. “It was great fun flying at a height of 10 or 15 feet over the sand." Gardner had hired Muñoz, introduced to the book’s readers as a “quick-thinking, quick-talking aviator, who has been flying long enough to have developed an uncanny skill as well as an encyclopedic knowledge of the country over which he is flying.” The two men had decided to fly along the Pacific Coast, about 180 miles south of Ensenada, to see if the rugged beaches could yield access to custom-designed trailers and dune bikes in which the septuagenarian Gardner hankered to go exploring. “It was great fun flying at a height of 10 or 15 feet over the sand, with the plane throttled down so that we had just sufficient air speed to give the pilot good control,” Gardner recorded. Muñoz chats with passengers at Bahía de los Angeles. Muñoz moved his family to Imperial Beach in 1955 and began flying over Baja. For “mile after mile,” they traveled in this intimate proximity to the beach, with Muñoz touching down whenever it struck his and the writer’s fancy. They studied coyotes, including one “just preparing to feast on a dead baby whale which had been cast up.” They stopped at fishing camps to gossip with the Mexicans gathering lobster and catching totoaba. Later, realizing they were hungry, and seeing a clam camp, Muñoz “made a quick circle into the wind, came down on the sandy beach, landed, and taxied up to the place where the clam diggers were bringing in the huge clams.” ^^^^^^^^^^^ The Reader has started this series of its best stories from the past 52 years — 2600 cover stories and some remarkable interior features — to help make up for the loss of its physical edition, which was once large enough to hold whole oceans of print. These stories will feature all the original illustrations and photos (plus easy-to-read typography). ^^^^^^^^^^^ Receiving abrazos, Muñoz made his and Gardner’s hunger known, and “in no time at all a young lad was forthcoming with lemons and a large soup plate,” Gardner wrote. “One of the clam diggers, at a signal, brought up a sackful...and Muñoz and I stood by while the clam digger cut open the shells with swift skill and stripped out the meat....” The two men gorged themselves, then realized that the afternoon was waning. “It would be touch-and-go to reach Tijuana before dark.” Although Muñoz was unfazed, Gardner felt worried by the deepening gloom, and his alarm increased when it became obvious that the two were flying into a storm. Muñoz today lives part-time at Crest, east of El Cajon, where a second home overlooks rocky vistas. “[W]e were being borne along by a tail wind which increased until it was blowing at 75 miles an hour,” Gardner later wrote. “Below us the ocean was a churned mass of angry waters, and above us the clouds kept pressing down until we were forced to fly just over the tops of the waves.” Squinting through the torrential rains, Gardner shouted that Muñoz should land in Ensenada, but the storm swept them past the town. La Paz airport, 1950s. In 1964 Gardner had been invited to view some new cave paintings and fish-fossil beds near Santiago, so Muñoz flew him to La Paz. At times “gusts of wind would catch the plane and seem to lift the tail so that it took skillful handling to keep us from being blown over end to end.... We were now flying two or three hundred yards offshore, so low that headlights from the automobiles coming along the highway between Tijuana and Ensenada would dazzle me — darkness above and below, but over on the right there was a faint murky line of surf; a surf which was hitting the shore with terrific fury and sending great clouds of spray high into the air.” Finally Muñoz wrestled the plane down to a landing strip in Rosarito Beach, and the two men made their way, dripping, to the Rosarito Beach Hotel. Muñoz and Gardner stopped at fishing camps to gossip with the Mexicans gathering lobster and catching totoaba. Still the adventure hadn’t quite ended. As Muñoz called for a car to drive up from Tijuana, Gardner insisted on ordering stiff drinks and taking a room in which the two could await the ride north in comfort. “Muñoz insisted that as a customer I was entitled to the first shower, and after wasting some time in argument I stepped out of my wet clothes, leaving them in a soggy mess on the floor....” The mystery writer then entered the shower and turned on the wrong faucet, producing an icy blast. Twisting the alternate faucet, however, caused flakes of rust to jam the shower head; after a moment, only a few drops of warm water trickled out. Muñoz heard Gardner’s curses and came forward to help — not realizing that Gardner had already opened the faucet. “Suddenly he had the shower head off, and water...steaming hot, struck me full in the chest. I ducked, Muñoz jumped. We collided with each other and then the stream of water was pouring over both of us!” Francisco Muñoz and his Baja Airlines planes, c. 1950s. By 1962 Muñoz had become a main character in Gardner’s travel books. Today Francisco Muñoz roars with laughter at the memory. “He was in the nude, and I was dressed. And we both tried to get out at the same time!” Gardner died about 8 years after this incident, in 1970. But Muñoz, now 76, is still an active man with detailed memories of his life. He and his wife, Leysl, spend part of their time at a beach-front mobile home in the community of Bahía de los Angeles, about 100 miles south of San Felipe on the Sea of Cortéz. But every month or two, they drive to Crest, east of El Cajon, where a second home overlooks rocky vistas. “See this?” says Muñoz. He is standing in a jumbled storage area next to his Crest home, hefting a chalky white chunk of material. It’s part of a whale skull, including the ear bone, scavenged from Malarrimo Beach, near Guerrero Negro, on Baja’s Pacific Coast. Close at hand, other cardboard boxes, all labeled, are packed with more whale ear bones. Some of the pieces of Muñoz’s flotsam collection are unique. He shows off a wooden tool that looks like an archaeological artifact. Once, some shrimper used it to scrape his catch from the floor of his boat into an icebox. Along one side of his house, Muñoz has built shelves to hold his hundreds of bottles, once-hard-edged and glittering glass made subtle and milky by the work of seawater and sand and sun. Inside the house, the ceiling has been hung with huge glass balls that held up far-flung Pacific fishing nets and, over time, washed up on the shores of Baja, sea green, and turquoise, pale rose. Muñoz has a buoyancy that surges up through his stories, as when he recalls his first sight of an airplane. “My father subscribed to a magazine in Mexico City called Jueves de Excelsior. And they showed pictures of the Mexican air force. ‘Oh, God!’ ” he gasps, summoning a boy’s voice filled with longing. “ ‘I want to be a flyer!’ ” He was around eight years old. Raised on his grandparents’ ranch in Coahuila, Muñoz remembers going into the pecan orchard. “You had to climb the tree with a pole and you hit the branches, and then somebody picked up the nuts from beneath the tree.” Swinging on the branches, watching the flight of the birds, he says, enhanced his yearning to take to the air. But his parents were appalled by his ambitions. “First they send me to the seminary,” recounts Muñoz, whose still-accented English reflects a casual attitude toward grammatical tense. “They want me to be a priest. But the bishop kicked me out because I was asking too many questions.
