McCarthy’s writing began to shed some of its most ornate flourishes, taking on a stripped-down veneer. (Many of his later books were conceived as screenplays.) Critiques of the works as lightweight fare from the oracular McCarthy overlooked their hidden depths. This arresting insight, for example, comes to the young cowboy John Grady Cole in All the Pretty Horses: “He thought the world’s heart beat at some terrible cost and that the world’s pain and its beauty moved in a relationship of diverging equity and that in this headlong deficit the blood of multitudes might ultimately be exacted for the vision of a single flower.” Daugherty views McCarthy’s evolution in the Westerns as the pairing of a mature style with a genre framework. A similar combination has produced some of the best American movies of the past generation, by filmmakers such as Kathryn Bigelow and the Coen brothers, who directed an Oscar-winning adaptation of No Country for Old Men. Although he started over, McCarthy could not escape the past. His celebrated 2006 novel, The Road—a sort of postapocalyptic Western—is built on a tender father-son relationship that both reflects McCarthy’s experience as a late-in-life parent and implicitly rejects his own father’s heavy hand. Daugherty quotes wrenching correspondence in which McCarthy and his father tried to reconcile as grown men. “There was and is a strong artistic streak in me that I inherited from my mother’s family and it has caused me a great deal of anguish in my life but an even greater joy,” McCarthy wrote. “I think this was always suspect to you.” Another relationship that echoed in his fiction was one that endured longer than his three marriages combined. McCarthy met Augusta Britt several years after moving out west; they became lovers when she was 17 and he was 43. They remained close for 47 years, but she protested the way he kept using her in his books, including in plotlines that seemed to mirror her life. “Well, baby, that’s what I do,” McCarthy replied. “I’m a writer.” McCarthy attempted a second reinvention, a turn toward science. By the late 2000s, he was spending much of his time at the Santa Fe Institute, a multidisciplinary research center, where he hobnobbed with physicists, favoring philosophical conversations over writing books. The year before he died, he published a final pair of related novels, The Passenger and Stella Maris, which had been in progress for years; one of the main characters is a mathematics prodigy with a mental illness. In startling new reporting, Daugherty contends that McCarthy’s literary agent assembled the hodgepodge of pages and made the decision to break the mess into two books; McCarthy’s friends told Daugherty they suspected that the ailing writer had not even read the finished product. The result was unconvincing characters, mashups of McCarthy’s many interests, strange psychiatric sessions, and a lack of cohesion. Maybe we all have only one good pivot in us. Or perhaps it was just too late for McCarthy to change course again. Whatever the case, his turn west in the 1970s reveals not just a man escaping personal failures but a restless writer who sensed that a wide new horizon might require him to expand his vision if he was to find his voice and his audience. The small-town hustles and degradations of Tennessee were ultimately too provincial for such an epoch-spanning talent, which demanded plains, mountains, and an endless expanse of sky to bring out its full potential. After all, deep in the Appalachian woods, you can’t see the buzzards circling. This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Cormac McCarthy’s Midlife Crisis.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: The Year Great-White Sharks Took Over Maine
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.55
If you spend a lot of time in the ocean, it is hard not to think about sharks. I visit the beach near my home in southern Maine regularly with my family, and almost every night from spring to fall, I go surf fishing after dark. For a long time, I soothed my anxiety with statistics—in America, you are far more likely to be killed by a riding mower than a man-eating fish—and by reminding myself that, in all my years of beachgoing and striped-bass fishing, I’d never encountered a great white in the wild. But then, late one night a few weeks ago, I saw one. It was, as best as I could tell, a juvenile white, and the experience was wholly anticlimactic: A dark triangular fin appeared about 10 yards from where I was wading. It cruised the shallows at a 45-degree angle to the shoreline and seemed uninterested in me. I backpedaled out of the water. This would be the year that I finally spotted a shark. Maine’s great-white population has been growing for some time—the state had its first fatal shark attack in 2020—and this season, sightings have been unusually high. In July, beaches in Phippsburg were temporarily closed due to a shark sighting. Last month, Mile Beach, Half Mile Beach, East Beach, Wells Beach, and multiple Biddeford beaches were closed for the same reason. At one point, nearly a dozen sharks were reported at Pine Point Beach in a 48-hour period. Then, a longtime lifeguard at Scarborough Beach, Greg Wilfert, was dragged five or six feet underwater by a shark that grabbed his rescue torpedo. After the incident, Wilfert and his fellow lifeguards began monitoring the water with drones. He told me that they’ve seen as many as 15 great whites a day, which they chase off with Jet Skis. (Curious if they were exaggerating, I accompanied a drone-owning friend to check things out on a random afternoon: We saw four great whites in 30 minutes.) But if seemingly everyone agrees that more sharks have been around this season than in the past, even scientists are having a hard time pinning down what exactly is driving the spate of sightings, and what it means about the future of Maine’s beaches. Jérôme Pinti, a senior scientist at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute, attributed the rising number of great whites to a combination of factors: Climate change has expanded the species’ northern range; the effects of shark-conservation efforts begun in the 1990s are beginning to be felt; and, because the state is home to large biomasses of prey species including striped bass and seals, all the new great whites are finding ample food. Pinti also said, however, that ascertaining the true extent of the state’s white-shark increase is difficult without a formal stock assessment, which has yet to be done. He noted that the growing popularity of recreational drone use muddies the picture. “I believe we have more sharks,” Pinti told me. But also, “everybody and their brother has a drone right now. So if you have drones above the water all the time, you’re gonna see sharks a lot more.” Whether the rise in shark sightings is because of an actual increase in the number of sharks swimming in Maine waters, or because new technology simply makes the fish easier to spot, is an open question. Another open question is what, if anything, Mainers and those who visit the state’s beaches should now do differently. Ryan McDermott, a co-owner of the Black Point Surf Shop in Scarborough, told me that the sharks are making him and his fellow surfers choosier about when they go out. “It better be pretty good surf to get you out there when you know that there’s more than a handful of great whites just around the corner,” he said. I suggested that coastal Maine may soon become Cape Cod 2.0—another New England tourist destination that has had to negotiate its own rapidly expanding population of toothy ocean inhabitants. McDermott corrected me: “It’s already kinda happened.” When I tracked down Wilfert, an affable 71-year-old who bears more than a passing resemblance to Dog the Bounty Hunter, he was still manning his lifeguard post, flanked by a pair of massive Newfoundland water-rescue dogs. He walked me down to the water’s edge and showed me the frayed rope of his yellow rescue torpedo. He told me that he didn’t see the shark that came after him—he felt it. He thought his buoy had gotten caught on a boat propeller, until the fish dived and started dragging him down. “I’ve been here 55 years,” he said, “and I’ve never seen a shark.” When I asked Wilfert whether he’d changed his habits, he said he was still swimming, though he confessed that he was not going out as far and had recently relied on drone shark spotters. As our conversation ended, a pair of elementary-school-age boys ran up to the perma-tanned Wilfert to ask him if he was the lifeguard who had been attacked. They, too, wanted to hear about the shark. In the emptier-than-usual parking lot, a stone’s throw from the beach smoothie shack, I walked past a stylish woman unloading beach chairs while her teenage kids impatiently snapped their gum. I stopped on the way to my own car, identified myself as a journalist, and asked whether she was worried about the recent surge of great whites. “Not worried and don’t care,” came the reply. “My husband is a lobsterman.”

item.title: Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.26
Once, when I was 15 years old and as awkward and skinny-legged as a baby giraffe, I was idling in a department store in central London when I saw the novelist Jackie Collins standing at the register. Can you imagine the aura emanating from her, like Hermès-scented magnetic waves? She was wearing animal print and a tailored jacket and had the kind of steely composure I’ve never managed to pull off in adulthood without straining something. Faced with one of my true idols, all I could do was gawk. I learned about sex when I was 8, but it wasn’t until several years later, when my best friend yanked me upstairs to show me a particularly juicy paragraph from her mother’s neon-pink copy of Hollywood Kids, that I learned about pleasure. Jackie—with apologies, I will call her Jackie throughout, because “Collins” feels just too formal for a woman who impressed upon me the existence of the clitoris—once told The New York Times that she published her first novel “in 1968, when no one was writing about sex but Philip Roth.” Which wasn’t strictly true, but at a moment when second-wave feminism and sexual liberation were uneasy bedfellows, Jackie simply wrote her own revolution. The World Is Full of Married Men, her debut, was a caustic social satire in which a wronged wife emerges triumphant; The Stud, out the following year, was a flashy potboiler about a trophy wife and nightclub owner with a rapacious sexual appetite who treats men like toys and exalts in her social and financial clout. Jackie wrote 32 books in total, sold more than half a billion copies, and gained an indelible reputation as an airport novelist, the kind of writer whose books are equally devoured and disdained. But oh, what they did for me! In retrospect, I gained a slightly deluded understanding of what adulthood actually entailed. Jackie was a devoted Mickey Spillane fan, and her books tend to be stuffed with gangsters, serial killers, pornographers, and even freelance journalists who get paid in advance. But as an anatomist of Hollywood gender dynamics, no writer was sharper or more aspirational. Jackie’s heroines, as she wrote in an introduction to The World Is Full of Divorced Women (1975), “demand equality—sexual and otherwise.” She wrote about creative, ferocious women striving for power and getting it. Lucky Santangelo, a recurring character and a kind of alter ego, starts out as the neglected daughter of a crime boss and works her way up to become the head of a movie studio in 1990’s Lady Boss. Her characters carry on being fascinating and sexually active well past the age when other writers would have them tucked in bed with a crocheted blanket and a crossword puzzle. “In Jackie’s world, women’s real lives begin after forty,” the writer Helen Ellis observed of Hollywood Wives, the book that Jackie published at the age of 45, and that established her as a celebrity in her own right. Even if you hate women (many people do), hate explicit sex scenes, hate the kind of pulpy storytelling that has you still reading in a cold bath at midnight, you cannot help but admit that Jackie captured the entertainment industry like no one else. She seemed equally drawn to the business of movie production—the seedy dealmaking and kickbacks—as well as the rampant abuses of power embedded in the Hollywood system, both of which she exposed without hesitation. Writing in the heady 1980s, when movies were becoming brasher, dumber, and unrepentantly commercial, she scrutinized a creative industry at a notable low point, less in thrall to art than to profit. Although her novels made her a star, Jackie never considered herself fully part of Hollywood. Like a Reagan-era Margaret Mead, she took an anthropological approach. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told Vanity Fair in 1995. “I move in it. I’m an observer.” At parties, she would stalk the room listening for interesting tidbits, taking copious mental notes that she’d jot down later. Describing an A-list event in Hollywood Wives, Jackie drops in fragments of what one character calls “Hollywood conversation,” dialogue that evokes a world where money and desire meld: “ ‘He pays me, I think it turns him on,’ said the redhead in the mink-trimmed cape.” So accurate was her portrayal that when Hollywood Wives was published, Jackie noted, “The ladies of Hollywood had their drivers and housekeepers lining up at the bookstores to get an early copy,” both furious that their gilded sanctum had been breached and desperate to pinpoint which character was based on which real person. Hollywood, as a geographical term at least, is misleading: Jackie’s characters mostly work and play in Beverly Hills, a city of 30,000 or so extremely wealthy residents enclosed by Los Angeles. Formerly a lima-bean farm, then a failed oil field, Beverly Hills was developed into lots for housing around the same time that the movie industry headed west, in the early 20th century. When the silent-film stars Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks moved into a spectacular former hunting lodge on Summit Drive in 1920—the press immediately named it “Pickfair”—they helped establish Beverly Hills as a nexus of celebrity glamour and industry cachet. Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky, but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation. Early this summer, I traveled from London, where Jackie was born, to the enclave where she made her name. As a child of the ’80s, I was nostalgic for the maximalist era of shoulder pads, Giorgio perfume, and animal print. (Jackie loved big cats for their beauty and power, was convinced she’d been a panther in a previous life, and decorated her house and herself in leopard spots.) But as a cultural critic, I also wanted to revisit the era of moviemaking that Jackie had described in her novels. The ’80s saw a wave of corporate consolidation; venerable studios were gobbled up by behemoths from other industries. (Columbia Pictures was briefly a division of Coca-Cola.) This led to sillier, more crowd-pleasing movies. Even so, Hollywood was at the apex of its power, the global influence of filmmaking more potent than ever. Today, the center of cultural power and attention is shifting away from Los Angeles. Traditional storytelling has lost ground to what the consulting firm McKinsey calls “user-generated content”—TikTok and YouTube videos in which people talk enthusiastically about peptides and skinny-maxxing and the cruel feminization of the male life force. As a teenager, I had learned from Jackie’s books to expect that adulthood for women would be a series of hard-won triumphs that lead toward power. (She also suggested that midlife would involve a lot of stalking around restaurants while wearing crepe Halston jumpsuits and enough gold jewelry to sink a yacht, but I have long since made peace with neutral basics.) I am 43, roughly the age when Jackie’s heroines enter their prime, and when she herself did. I am very tired, having spent the past 14 months working, raising two 5-year-olds, promoting a book, and falling into existential mires of despair over the degenerating state of world affairs. A small, quiet part of my brain wondered whether tracing Jackie’s literary footsteps might reinvigorate my sense of what’s possible. Or at least demonstrate that her dreams for women—that they can have creative fulfillment, families, and happiness, as she did—might be somewhat more realistic now than they were 40 years ago. Hollywood Wives was published in 1983, a good two decades before reality television turned exposing the lives of the wealthy, married, and highly maintained into a Bravo gold mine. We’re accustomed to such excess now, but back then, Jackie’s gossipy revelations—$50 panties, discreet plastic surgeons in Palm Springs, society grandes dames who used to be French call girls—seemed otherworldly. The primary antiheroine in the book is the delightfully unlikable Elaine Conti (imagine a hornier, more desperate Becky Sharp), the 39-year-old wife of a movie star, Ross, whose last film bombed at the box office. There’s also a former gigolo on the brink of movie stardom, a buxom man-eater who wants to be taken seriously as an actress, and a serial killer who calls himself the “Keeper of the Order.” But for me at least, the book stands out for its portrayal of early-’80s Beverly Hills as a high-society Thunderdome, where everyone is scratching and clawing for status. In addition to the titular wives, who are drawn with both humanity and mild disdain, Jackie offers up a number of female characters operating in what she describes as the “Big Boys’ Club” of the movie industry: Sadie LaSalle, one of the most powerful and fearsome agents in town, and Montana Gray, a writer trying to save her screenplay from the clutches of a ruthless producer. This is a world where power-lunching demands tactical precision. Elaine’s mission throughout the book is to restore Ross’s A-list status, with buzzy parties the couple can’t afford and a standing Friday lunch reservation at Ma Maison, where “anybody who was anybody and in town invariably showed up.” Ma Maison closed in 1985, and so the first place I went to test out the current state of power-dining was the Polo Lounge, a clubby salon situated toward the back of the spectacularly retro Beverly Hills Hotel. In Hollywood Husbands, Jackie’s 1986 follow-up, the handsome and promiscuous talk-show host Jack Python regularly meets his best friends for breakfast there, where they occupy Table One, “a cosy leather booth directly facing the entrance.” Table placement, Jackie emphasizes, is everything—“The back of this restaurant is Siberia,” one model tells another late in the book. “Land of the underachievers. Don’t even glance in that direction.” I was not placed at Table One. I was seated just outside what seemed to be the main dining room, next to an elderly couple and a 12-year-old wearing a World Cup hoodie having pancakes by himself. Through the doorway, I could see men in button-downs and golf shirts conversing chummily; I started to feel slightly psychotic glimmers of envy and shame at being shut out from whatever they were brokering. The server’s eyes expressed gentle but unmistakable pity. A handsome Englishman was seated at a nearby table but immediately sensed defeat and asked to be moved to the terrace, where the sun shines regardless of a diner’s Variety profile, stock portfolio, or follower count. Failure is galvanizing, I tried to remember from Jackie’s books, as long as you don’t let it break you. For much of her early life, Jackie wasn’t known for her writing or her feline fixation. (A plaque engraved with a panther marks her place in the celebrity crypt at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery, where she was interred after her death, in 2015; the image is accompanied by the words SHE GAVE A GREAT DEAL OF PEOPLE A GREAT DEAL OF PLEASURE.) She came of age as the taller, ungainly younger sister of Joan, an almond-eyed, preternaturally composed actress who made her Hollywood debut starring alongside Bette Davis in 1955’s The Virgin Queen. Joan and Jackie had grown up together in a basement apartment in dingy postwar London, the daughters of a dance teacher and a talent agent whose parties, Jackie once said, were where she first became aware of how men talk about women when they think no one’s listening. “I get an awful inferiority complex when I’m with Joan,” the teenage Jackie wrote in her diary. In a photo of the pair together from 1955, Joan stands front and center, insouciant in a fur coat, while Jackie looks at the camera semi-apologetically from behind her. Jackie was, however, entrepreneurial; by the age of 13, inspired by Harold Robbins and Henry Miller, she had a sideline writing sex scenes longhand and charging her classmates to read them. When Joan’s career took her to Hollywood, Jackie followed, moving with her sister to an apartment in the Chateau Marmont hotel, and having a brief fling—at 15—with the 29-year-old Marlon Brando. (He was “only my height, and kind of fat,” she noted in her journal, and also recorded that he called her “sincere, sweet, and luscious.”) But Jackie couldn’t get a work permit and so reluctantly returned to England, where she appeared in a handful of schlocky B movies before marrying the businessman Wallace Austin at 22. Four years later, Austin’s drug addiction had led the couple to divorce, and he died of an overdose shortly after. It was Jackie’s second husband, the producer and nightclub owner Oscar Lerman, who encouraged her to pursue writing, and to draw inspiration from the vivid social scenes the couple mixed in. (At one of her husband’s clubs, she told The Hollywood Reporter, Lerman had to put a guard outside the men’s room because teenage girls kept following movie stars in to offer them sexual favors.) At 31, she published The World Is Full of Married Men, which was an immediate best seller in the United Kingdom and promptly banned in Australia for its inventive array of four-letter words; the next year, the romance novelist Barbara Cartland lambasted her new novel, The Stud, as “awful, terrible, it’s evil really.” Jackie and Lerman relocated to Los Angeles in 1980, and if you walk down the Beverly Hills Hotel’s unabashedly red-carpeted stairs and under a gloriously cinematic green-and-white striped awning, then stroll to the bottom of the hill, and wander for about 10 minutes beneath towering palm trees, you will arrive at the house that Jackie’s “awful, terrible” books built. Only a modest-seeming driveway was visible from the street. The place is now available for rent (for the trivial sum of $175,000 a month), and when I say that I begged the real-estate agent to let me view it, please know that I really and truly groveled. I spent months emailing a man who assured me that he was entreating the owners (real-estate developers who’d bought it after her death, gutted it, remodeled all the interiors) on my behalf—but to no avail. So instead I examined the signs affixed to palm trees warning me that I was on camera, to ensure the security of the neighborhood’s current residents, who—unlike the movie stars and moguls of Jackie’s day—are apparently financiers, minor Middle Eastern royals, and crypto magnates. (The current owner of the Pickfair mansion, I later learned, is the technology corporation Unicom Global, which uses it for conferences and events.) But based on the listing, archival photographs, and the author photo on Jackie’s many hardcovers, I can tell you that it’s a 22,000-square-foot museum of a mansion, a defiant middle finger to the critics who belittled her for writing “bonkbusters,” and a visual testament to her success. The interiors are now predominantly beige, but in Jackie’s day, the pillows were all animal print. She designed the house around a huge rectangular swimming pool after seeing David Hockney’s A Bigger Splash in London. On her book jackets, she stands, radiant and shoulder-padded, next to the cool blue water and her imposing white box of a home. But she also took great pride in being a hands-on mother, cooking at home for her three daughters, doing school drop-offs in her silver Mustang, and keeping her children away from the sleazy Hollywood scenes she chronicled. Right as Jackie’s writing started appearing on the best-seller list, Joan’s acting career was floundering—in 1977, she appeared in the dismal sci-fi horror Empire of the Ants, playing a land developer set on by giant irradiated insects. It was Jackie who revived her sister’s reputation, after Joan was cast as the lead in the movie adaptation of The Stud. (A hit in Britain, the movie paved the way for Joan to get her most indelible American role, as Alexis Colby in Dynasty.) The charged sense of competition between the pair continued apace; in a 1988 Vanity Fair profile of both sisters, Dominick Dunne noted that a publicist had instructed him to dedicate equal copy to each woman, while also citing the rumors that Silver Anderson, the prickly 47-year-old TV star in Hollywood Husbands, was based on Joan. Mindful of the security cameras, I walked quickly past Jackie’s house to a restaurant in downtown Beverly Hills called Bacari, where I took out my notebook and tried my hand at Jackie-style anthropology. At the table next to me, a talent agent was trying to lure another agent away from a major conglomerate, where she was unhappy. “They keep trying to buy us off with ice-cream socials,” she said to him plaintively. “Everyone is on a diet!” The conversation turned to her stable of clients, who all seemed to be social-media stars. She spoke proudly about one woman she represented who, under her mentorship, went from having 700,000 followers to more than 1 million. “That’s the kind of nurturing I bring to my job,” she said. The man asked her if she might be able to double her client list in the first three months; to help her in the effort, he could offer her a “digital assistant—no person.” He paid the bill. “Let’s get those wheels turning,” he said, ushering her out, and I wondered what Jackie would make of this version of Hollywood, with its brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails, where celebrity is its own art form and product is paramount. In Jackie’s Hollywood novels, Rodeo Drive—my next stop—is where the women of Beverly Hills go to arm themselves for the soft warfare of self-presentation. When every outfit, every hairdo, is minutely studied for signs of decline, keeping up appearances is essential. In Hollywood Husbands, Poppy Solomon, the secretary turned fourth wife of a studio head, gets ready for parties in much the same way General Patton commanded the Third Army: with ostentatious and pleasurable aggression. (“She wore a turquoise frilled, strapless dress, and many real diamonds. Her new tits protruded nicely.”) The day I was there, the picture-perfect palms gently fluttering down Rodeo bore signs for an upcoming car show, which seemed unnecessary given that every day brings a parade of tricked-out vehicles: I watched a procession of Porsches, G-Wagons, two separate Maybachs with hydraulic suspension systems that had them bouncing up and down like sugared-up toddlers. No one was actually shopping, despite the lavish window displays. Instead, everyone was posing for pictures, wearing outfits they’d put together for this exact purpose and drafting husbands and friends to play photographer. A slender blond woman clutching a tan Birkin pouted while reclining against a lamppost outside Stefano Ricci. Someone whispered that she was a Russian influencer with a superstar-athlete partner, which seemed perfectly plausible, but outside the subset of her followers, how would the rest of us know? I was accompanied by a photographer, Dina, who approached the influencer to take her picture, but the woman scuttled away like a cartoon mouse. Something odd was happening, we quickly realized: Everyone was out posing in public, but no one wanted to cede control of how they might be perceived. When Dina tried to take photos of the Beverly Hills Hotel from a public sidewalk, a voice instantly came over a loudspeaker warning her to stop. In a weak attempt to consider some of the box-office excess of 1980s Hollywood (Footloose, Top Gun, Beverly Hills Cop), I booked us a Paramount Pictures studio tour, but when I asked a publicist about Dina bringing her camera, I was told approval would be required, a studio representative would accompany us, and anything said on the tour could not be quoted. (All that’s worth saying about what followed is that while being driven around the lot where Citizen Kane, Breakfast at Tiffany’s, and Chinatown were shot, the most enthralling thing we saw was the plasticky interior set from the CBS reboot of Matlock.) Jackie would find Hollywood’s new power dynamics perplexing: Many of her female characters are writers and reporters on the movie-celebrity beat, who see their job as pushing past the sanitized narratives that publicists try to present. But as media jobs have dwindled, influencers have stepped in to fill a void. Why would you trust a possibly unfriendly reporter with access to an actor or a director or a TV set when you can invite a photogenic social-media star to a premiere and be assured that they’ll rave about whatever they see to their hundreds of thousands of followers? In Hollywood Husbands, Silver, the soap star possibly based on Joan, is interviewed by an English journalist, “a middle-aged woman with brittle looks and dyed yellow hair” who sucks up to her subjects as energetically in person as she tears them apart in print. “So what?” Silver thinks. “Someone had once said As long as they spell your name right.” The internet has long since retooled this bargain. And what are celebrities now, anyway? During my four days in Beverly Hills, which Jackie portrays as a superstar playground—Clint Eastwood, Jack Lemmon, Richard Gere, and Tom Selleck all feature in one lunch scene at Ma Maison—I saw not a single recognizably famous person. A dozen or so women looked similar enough to Kim Kardashian to stop me short; they were clearly modeled after her, but the image fell apart on second glance. One night I went to dinner at Funke, a purported newish hot spot for stars (Gwyneth Paltrow is a fan) where the chef used to have his own show on the disastrous short-form streaming platform Quibi. No sightings. My L.A.-based friends advised heading east, to Los Feliz and Silver Lake, or west, to Venice and Santa Monica. Beverly Hills today is a bastion of the über-wealthy—Jeff Bezos owns the estate built by Jack Warner of Warner Bros.—and a drop-by for people who come to pose for Instagram. Like SoHo in New York and Notting Hill in London, the place feels like a simulacrum of a film set, where everyone is perpetually performing for unseen audiences and nothing feels quite real. In her books, Jackie is unsentimental about creative work. Her characters tend to hustle for money and power, not self-indulgent awards or critical acclaim. When good movies get made, it’s largely by accident, because someone took their eye off the ball. But one character in Hollywood Wives seems to genuinely care about the integrity of the work she makes: Montana Gray, the tall, raven-haired, strikingly offbeat writer who—coincidentally—has a biography that seems a lot like Jackie’s own. By 15, Montana is a worldly soul who’s traveled the globe, learned French and Italian, and had two affairs. After spending a few years in bohemian circles, she meets the much older film director Neil Gray in Paris and falls in love with him. She helps him get sober and working again; he encourages her to write. At the start of the novel, her gritty screenplay, Street People, is the talk of Hollywood, with actors and agents fighting for copies. And, because Montana is the wife of a major director, no one can accept that she actually wrote it. “Good-looking women had roles in life and they were supposed to stick to them,” Jackie writes. “They could be movie stars, models, housewives, hookers, but God forbid they should skirt onto what was strictly regarded as Big Boys’ Territory. Writing a major movie for a major director was Big Boys’ Territory. And in their own petty little way everyone wanted to let her know that.” When Neil pushes to cast the craggy movie star George Lancaster in a leading role in the film, Montana acquiesces reluctantly—he can’t act—only for George to assume that she’s a secretary the very first time they meet. “I’m Montana Gray,” she tells him. “I wrote Street People.” “You did?” he replies. “My, my, things sure are changing around here. I could still use that coffee, little lady.” You might wonder whether things are actually different for women in Hollywood today. The statistics are still dismal: 8.1 percent of the 100 highest-grossing movies in 2025 were directed by women, a seven-year low, and the percentage of movies with any major female characters at all fell from 39 percent the previous year to 36 percent. But TV is faring better: More than a third of all streaming shows now have at least one female creator. One of those women is Lisa Joy, formerly a writer and co-creator of HBO’s adaptation of Westworld, a futuristic sci-fi show with a notably feminist question at its core: What might men do to women if those women didn’t seem fully human and the men thought they could get away with it? In 2019, Joy and her husband, the screenwriter and producer Jonathan Nolan, signed a reported $150 million deal to create shows for Amazon, including the acclaimed video-game adaptation Fallout and an upcoming TV version of Rebecca Yarros’s blockbuster romantasy series, Fourth Wing. Jackie would have liked the all-caps plaque on Joy’s desk—I’M CEO, BITCH—that greeted me in the Hollywood offices of her production company, a glass-walled room facing the Capitol Records building. Like Montana, Joy is impossibly glamorous and all too familiar with having people presume that her accomplishments are secretly a man’s. So much of Westworld, she told me, came from her experiences being the lone woman in what felt like male playgrounds. But, like Jackie, she’s convinced that writing a different world gets us one step closer to manifesting it. Post-MeToo, Joy said, she’s noticed some really positive changes, such as a junior writer she knows speaking out against a serial harasser whom no one had ever dared confront before, and who was subsequently fired. But reminders abound of all the ways in which things have stayed the same. “There are so many yacht trips I’ve heard about for male directors and writers,” she said. “I don’t know why they all get yachts, but there doesn’t ever seem to be a woman invited. But fuck the yachts, you know? They make you seasick. They’re no fun. Let’s make the reality we want.” I left Joy’s office feeling energized by her work, by her enthusiasm, by her determination. And then, as I was crossing Hollywood Boulevard, the universe gave me a palpable reality check: a 50-foot billboard advertising Louis C.K.’s upcoming comedy special for Netflix. On my last morning in L.A., I went downstairs to get breakfast in my hotel, and ended up sitting near two men who were discussing potential merchandising deals for one of their clients. “Makeup is really splintered; it’s a challenging category for sure,” one said. “But fragrance is booming. What about hair?” The client has a personal connection to hair, the other said excitedly. (Who among us? I thought.) The first man proceeded to expound on how hair brands are working quickly to address the issues—thinning, shedding—that can come from GLP‑1 use. The other circled back to his client, whom he talked about with such reverence that I leaned closer, convinced she was a huge household name. “Her pull on her community is so strong,” he said. “What feeds her passion is serving her community and improving people’s lives. She’s built for this.” Only by the end of the conversation, and after much furtive Googling on my part, did it become clear whom they were talking about: a Goth-makeup influencer on TikTok who has more than 6 million followers. You could argue that the content-creator model has democratized entertainment and broken down conventional gatekeeping, enabling anyone with a ring light, a front-facing camera, and a compelling personality to find their following. I don’t disagree. But it’s also restored youth and overconfidence as the preeminent characteristics for women on camera. Whereas what I’ve always loved about Jackie’s books is how they enshrine success and power as being hard-won and worth the hustle—and the wait. Midlife is when things get interesting for her characters, because they know the stakes they’re playing for, and they’ve accrued enough wisdom and battle scars to rival and even occasionally best the Big Boys. But the waning public interest in traditional storytelling (because you’re reading this, I’ll diplomatically ignore the even gloomier fate of the written word) has other consequences too. If you’re someone who doesn’t just love movies and TV shows but has felt genuinely changed by some of them, it’s hard not to mourn what we lose when our mass culture has all the bells and whistles of entertainment—hair, makeup, stars, product placement—but none of the curiosity about human predicaments underpinning it. Jackie’s work was berated during her lifetime by critics (“It starts off as nothing and ends as nothing” — Clive James) and high-school English teachers like mine (“trash”), but it graphically exposed a Hollywood full of sexual harassment and gender inequity. Not least, it imagined alternative paths for women to pursue. Now her books are mostly out of fashion; when I stopped by the Barnes & Noble inside the Grove, where Jackie liked to shop before going to the movies, the store had not a single copy of any of her novels. I was feeling despondent when I went for a last outing, to Mariposa: one of Jackie’s favorite restaurants, where she met for lunch each week with her closest friends, an elegant dining room tucked into the basement of the Neiman Marcus Beverly Hills. I had learned in emailing beforehand that Jackie was still a much-loved figure there. I was met by the store’s manager of brand experience, Mary Kate Steinmiller, who looks exactly like the actress Malin Akerman and used to be a fashion editor at Teen Vogue. She took me downstairs to Jackie’s favorite blue booth. For days, I’d been traipsing through Beverly Hills trying to find a little spiritual proximity to Jackie, and here it was, on the lower floor, by the beauty counters. Groups of women wearing Christian Dior tennis whites and Pucci wrap dresses chatted ebulliently over cocktails (it was 12:15 p.m.). Every table featured floral arrangements nicer than the ones at my wedding. Over in a corner, an older couple wearing acid-green designer outfits sat absorbed in each other. A table of women told me that Mariposa was their country club. They had known and liked Jackie, but quickly pushed back against the lingering stereotype of the Hollywood Wife. One was a high-powered divorce attorney. Another was a sports photographer. The restaurant was gorgeous (and don’t sleep on the lobster salad), but it was also clear what it meant to these women: community, affirmation, a clubby dining room of their own. Watching them, I felt as though what Jackie’s novels had promised might actually be true: If you can muster enough ambition and persistence to keep pushing through, the payoff could well be worth the wait. Travel Notes Spago Ma Maison, immortalized in Hollywood Wives, is long gone, but in 1982 its star chef, a telegenic Austrian named Wolfgang Puck, left to open Spago on the Sunset Strip, redefining L.A. dining in the process. The original location closed decades ago, but Spago Beverly Hills lives on, with its twinkly lit courtyard, casual-luxe menu (Jackie loved the smoked-salmon pizza and wrote it into multiple books), and luxe-luxe prices. If you never get to go to the Academy Awards’ Governors Ball, which Puck has catered for more than three decades, this is at least a chance to eat stardust by association. Bob’s Coffee and Doughnuts Doughnuts and Hollywood physiques go together like deep-dish and Ozempic. Don’t let that keep you away from Bob’s, a 56-year-old stand inside the historic Los Angeles Farmers Market, where writers have come to eat and procrastinate since the 1930s. According to legend, Robert Altman used to have breakfast here, scribbling away under the slatted awnings. And the doughnuts really are great—pillowy and sugar-sprinkled. Fun fact: A branded Farmers Market tote bag costs $2, compared with $50 for one at the nearby Erewhon. Hollywood Books Is this tiny spot on Melrose a bookstore in the conventional sense? Not really, at least not if you’re looking for a popular novel or Belle Burden’s monster-hit memoir, Strangers. At Hollywood Books, the shelves are stacked with secondhand art volumes and reissued classics. Despite—because of?—its unfussed approach to business, the store has become extremely chic among the literary girlies of Los Angeles; at one point it hosted an event for the supermodel Kaia Gerber’s book club, Library Science. I left with a copy of Picture, Lillian Ross’s 1952 analysis of the clash between art and corporate interests in moviemaking, just to remember that things were ever thus. Wrapstar I can’t endorse the wraps or salads here, because I had only a sparkling water. But for eavesdropping like Jackie, you can’t beat the location—across the street from William Morris Endeavor’s boxy Beverly Hills headquarters, and next door to Cipriani. Sit, snoop, rubberneck. (Yes, wraps are passé, but power agents sometimes need sad-desk lunches that you can eat with one hand while scrolling through social media, just like the rest of us.) Bar Funke Funke regrettably did not provide any celebrity sightings, but it did furnish a gorgeous twist on a margarita, made with Sicilian-blood-orange bitters and prickly pear. The rooftop, after you enter through a jasmine-strewn trellis, looks out over the palms and offices of Beverly Hills, but from my spot at the bar, all I wanted to stare at were the pink quartzite counters and Chef Evan Funke’s elaborate collection of Amaro aperitifs. Jackie’s literary alter ego, the glamorous and hot-blooded Italian businesswoman Lucky Santangelo, would have appreciated both. Mariposa Here’s to the ladies who lunch, and to playing one in this delightful department-store-basement restaurant, with its velvety blue booths and popovers accompanied by strawberry butter. The waitstaff are lovely, the diners’ outfits are extraordinary, and the food—lobster salad, crab cakes, tuna tartare—is opulent and calorie-conscious, and so good you’ll be wondering why the guests aren’t eating more of it. If I ever die and get to (at least) purgatory, I hope it’s a little like Mariposa. This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Jackie Oh!” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: How ‘Somatics’ Became the Solution to Modern Life
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Score: 3.66
When clients go to Sybil Ottenstein for therapy, they tend to arrive with answers. Many of them have seen shrinks before. They can tell her which events from their past were formative, and point to the ripple effects in their current life. They’re like detectives, she told me, with all the dots connected on their corkboard of evidence. Intellectually, they’ve cracked the case. The problem is that they don’t feel any better. That’s why they’re seeking something different from Ottenstein: somatic psychotherapy. Traditional talk therapy could be seen as a top-down approach. You identify problems in your thinking, your habits, or your life, and hope that by working through them, you can resolve physical manifestations of emotional issues—the chest palpitations of anxiety, the stomachache of stress. Somatic therapy, by contrast, works from the bottom up. Ottenstein typically starts her sessions by asking clients to slow down and pay attention to corporeal sensations: “What does it feel like in your chest? In your throat?” As they talk, she encourages them to stay in their body, to let themselves feel whatever is coming up. People cry. They yawn. They scream. They stretch. They dance. The word somatic, according to Merriam-Webster, merely means “of, relating to, or affecting the body.” But recently, it’s been popping up everywhere, appended to a variety of practices that involve tuning in to physical symptoms in order to ameliorate psychological ones. Somatic therapists like Ottenstein have noticed a significant bump in interest; one of the major somatic-therapy training programs reported that its applicants more than doubled from 2020 to 2023. Other practitioners offer somatic dance, somatic yoga, somatic workouts. (The terms seem a touch redundant.) On Instagram, hundreds of thousands of posts appear with the hashtag #somatic. A “somatic exercise” trainer who goes by the “Workout Witch” (nearly 2 million followers) teaches small, repetitive movements meant to discharge negative feelings—curl your head down for “sorrow/despair,” pull your right ear for “overwhelm”—and promises that “trauma can be released from your hips.” All over my feed, fit young women are humming, hitting their sternum, pinching their nose bridge, and bouncing their knees all the way to inner peace. Much of the time, as with many other wellness ventures, someone stands to make money. At one somatic-workout class I attended, where a staffer told me that the goal was to “move stagnant energy out,” the lobby featured a gift-shop corner with jewelry, T-shirts, and $65 “body gloss” from a brand called Oui the People. But clearly, plenty of Americans are willing to pay for the promise of a psychic cleanse. Practitioners refer to “stuck energy,” to “trapped emotions,” to “resetting” a nervous system caught in fight-or-flight mode. “We have all these ways of just storing that gunk inside,” Ottenstein told me. I pictured, uncomfortably, a thick, black goo running through my veins. Somatics—the whole roomy umbrella of practices—might seem like an odd fit for the information age, when people are more accustomed to finding answers on the internet than within themselves. But that could be precisely the draw for thinkers and analyzers who are tired of ruminating in anxious circles, who spend their days in front of a laptop and nights scrolling an iPhone. For millennia, people have yearned to break out of the confines of their bodies; they’ve searched—through religion, spirituality, drugs—for transcendence. Now, for some, the existential quest is inverted: Instead of seeking to escape their prison of flesh and bones, they want to reinhabit it. The origin of somatics is difficult to pinpoint, though it’s certainly not recent. Some credit Wilhelm Reich, a student of Freud’s, who theorized in the early 1900s that patients held tension in their bodies—“muscular armor”—as a subconscious defense against trauma, leading to aches, pains, and inflammation. But it wasn’t until the 1970s that the field began to formalize, developed in part by the American philosophy professor Thomas Hanna, who defined somatics as the study of “the body as perceived from within.” That same decade, a UC Berkeley biophysics doctoral student, Peter Levine, developed “somatic experiencing”: a therapeutic method based on the idea that people, like other animals, react to trauma with a flight, fight, or freeze response, powered by a burst of adrenaline. After the source of danger is gone, Levine argued, they have pent-up “survival energy” to unleash: They need to physically shake it off. He pointed to videos of impalas, quaking and buckling after surviving a cheetah attack. When humans go through something upsetting, Ottenstein told me, “we go to work the next day.” This idea—that trauma is held in the body, and thus must be physically remedied—was once fairly niche. In recent years, though, it has been jolted into prominence. The psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk’s book The Body Keeps the Score, which argues for somatic treatments of PTSD, was first released in 2014 and was not an immediate hit. In 2021, it reached the No. 1 spot on the New York Times best-seller list for paperback nonfiction. And although it has been accused of resting on shaky science, it has continued to dominate the charts for years. Van der Kolk wrote about violent assaults, wartime atrocities, severe childhood abuse—circumstances that many readers hadn’t directly experienced. Yet The Body Keeps the Score seemed to resonate anyway. When it gained momentum, lots of Americans had spent the previous year safe in their homes, baking bread and taking Zoom calls. (“When people say the pandemic has been a collective trauma,” van der Kolk told The Atlantic that year, “I say, absolutely not.”) Most had also, however, been detached from the rich sensory experience of interacting with the external world. Now here was a book about people who’d felt estranged from their own body—and then, through simple movement, play, and touch, found their way back to their surroundings, and to themselves. In the years since, most people have emerged from pandemic isolation. Yet the share of Americans who say they frequently experience stress, which has been rising for decades, has continued its upward trend. Talk therapy remains popular, but it’s not always affordable or accessible—and much of the time, it doesn’t take physical symptoms into account. Meanwhile, many medical doctors don’t consider psychological causes of physical ailments. Stress in particular is “like this mythical creature,” Aditi Nerurkar, a physician at Harvard Medical School, told me. “And we don’t have a lot of time. We have to focus on your hemoglobin. Did you get a mammogram? Did you get a pap smear? What is your cholesterol?” No wonder, then, that somatics is a flourishing industry. Many Americans already distrust medical institutions; maybe they want to bypass the dismissive doctor, or the therapist who wants to rehash every daddy issue but can’t seem to fix anything. So they turn to this strange constellation of New Age–y courses, TikTok sages, and licensed counselors. Some offerings target people with capital-T Trauma; others claim to be for just about anyone. Many present themselves as alternatives to more traditional paths to mental well-being. The question is whether they can really help the frazzled masses. Somatics does get a lot of things right. Plenty of bodily sensations are, at root, psychological. Some communication does need to happen between the brain and the rest of the body. That’s how you know to respond to danger: The amygdala triggers the nervous system to increase your heart rate, deliver more blood to muscles, and release a flood of adrenaline. When I spoke with Nerurkar, she rattled off an incomplete list of physical symptoms that might result from stress: headaches, dizziness, nausea, vision changes. When she was in residency training, she said, she experienced what felt like a “stampede of wild horses” across her chest and was convinced that she had a heart problem—until her doctors, having conducted a battery of tests, recommended that she seriously consider chilling out. And many components of somatic practice have evidence to back them up. Interoception, or awareness of one’s own physical signals, really can be important for well-being—perhaps because it increases people’s sense of attunement with their body, connection with the present moment, or agency over otherwise vague and inscrutable sensations. Mindfulness meditation, which involves interoception, has been shown to decrease stress and anxiety and even reduce physical pain. Yoga and breathing exercises can decrease amygdala activation and lead to better concentration, memory, and executive function. But the somatics packaging of these techniques is alluring partly because of the emotional liberation it promises. Somaticists tend to describe a clear path: identify a physical signal, connect it to its psychic cause, then let it go. If the nervous system overactivates, surely you can just reset it. If the body holds trauma, surely the body can relinquish it. These were always just metaphors, though, and imperfect ones. The amygdala doesn’t have a reboot button. There is no viscous gunk of emotional pain to flush out. The Body Keeps the Score has been somewhat debunked; critics have argued that van der Kolk incorrectly described certain studies, and that he seems to have made up others entirely. (Responding to the writer Emi Nietfeld’s critique in Mother Jones, van der Kolk said that at times he drew on unpublished data.) Trauma experts have pushed back on his wholesale condemnation of talk therapy, which can be, according to a mountain of evidence, very helpful for treating PTSD. There’s also something ironic in how certain somaticists—ostensibly advocates for the mind-body connection—talk as if the two are separated by a nearly unbridgeable gap: the physical burden of trauma unreachable through thinking or conversation, and perhaps not even accessible to conscious awareness. So somatics isn’t a miracle cure. And it’s probably right to be skeptical of influencers who seek to collect on people’s need to feel at home in their body. But that doesn’t mean somatics can’t be helpful. Much of it, after all, turns out to be pretty straightforward. Movement is good, generally. Breathing is good. Stepping away from your screen—stretching your limbs, remembering you are real and tangible and mortal—is good. When I signed up for that somatic-exercise class, I expected that I might leave rolling my eyes, but I secretly hoped I’d walk out lighter, more alive and connected to myself and the world. What I found was something in between. The actual workout couldn’t have been more basic: It consisted largely of squats, jumping jacks, crunches, some yoga—downward dog, child’s pose. Occasionally the instructor would remind us to check in with our bodies: “What are you being invited into? And I don’t mean the burpee.” Or: “Let the chin enter the conversation.” Otherwise it hardly seemed uniquely somatic, or uniquely anything. Then again, I had the post-workout endorphin glow. I’d left my apartment and shut my phone in a locker. An hour later, I exited the studio somewhat baffled. But walking out onto a busy Manhattan street, I felt a little more conscious of the sun on my cheek, the solidness of the ground pushing against my feet. This was silly, I thought. And also: Maybe I’ll come back. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic

item.title: The Birth of the New Legal Right
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 2.59
America’s highest court didn’t take on a deeply partisan, conservative bent overnight. This transformation began decades ago, with a simple purpose: In the early 1980s, three law students were fed up with what they saw as a liberal monoculture at their elite universities. They wanted a place to freely debate conservative ideas and to refine their arguments. So the students—Lee Liberman, Steve Calabresi, and David McIntosh—decided to build one. In late April 1982, their newly formed group, the Federalist Society, held its first conference, at Yale University. The formal title of the three-day affair was “A Symposium on Federalism: Legal and Political Ramifications,” but the snoozy name belied the energy of the weekend. Young Reaganites packed their sleeping bags and overnighted on the floors of fellow students they’d never met before. During smoke breaks, they chatted up Robert Bork, the famous Yale professor, and Antonin Scalia, then a lesser-known professor from the University of Chicago. But if the attendees were idealistic about the Reagan era and the emergence of a harder-core strain of conservatism known as the New Right, they also understood that they were still a tiny minority in both the academic and legal worlds. Movements opposed to racism, sexism, and injustice remained the animating forces of campus life. Many students across the country were embracing Marxism and socialism. To make headway, young conservatives needed a voice—and a strategy. To this end, Bork proved essential. He had recently been nominated by President Ronald Reagan to serve on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals and spoke with both knowledge and authority. Bork announced to his eager audience that media and academia had become left-wing machines. The Supreme Court was inventing new “rights” with no basis in the Constitution, he said, and the only path forward was to return to the words of the Founding Fathers. Whether Bork truly believed in the conspiracies he outlined or whether he was merely exaggerating is unclear. But in his remarks at that first Federalist Society conference, Bork effectively mapped out what the right-wing legal movement would do over the course of the next four decades. “We have a Court,” Bork declared in his speech, “which is creating individual rights which are not to be found in the Constitution by any standard method of interpretation.” He went on to outline the formation of a nascent conservative approach called originalism. In the originalist view, constitutional rights existed only as the Founding Fathers imagined them, unless officially added via constitutional amendment. By embracing what Bork called a “strict” or “textualist” reading of the Constitution, conservatives could argue that recent social changes never specifically considered by the Founders were not constitutionally protected. The approach could return the country to its true, “conservative” values. In championing this interpretation of the law, Bork proved to be ahead of his time. He saw benches and courtrooms as the final frontier in the right-wing culture war. Effete liberals either had persuaded judges to ignore the Constitution, he said, or had themselves colonized the bench. Bork railed against the media and academia as corrupting influences: “The institutions to which the court responds are the press and the law-school faculties. Those are the people they talk to; those are the people who are responsible for the reputations of individual judges.” And those people were liberals. Bork cited a survey from the magazine Public Opinion, which concluded that the people who worked in American media were “heavily left liberal.” More than 80 percent of the press, he continued, had voted for the Democratic candidate in every presidential election since 1968. The values of the press were “egalitarian and permissive.” And professors were no better: “They want sexual freedoms; they want freedom for abortions; they want the death penalty outlawed.” Bork believed academic elites were bastardizing the First Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment to suit their ends, creating “new constitutional values which are nothing more than the imposition of upper-middle-class values on society.” He blamed the “enormous industry in the law schools” and their faculty for these invented “rights.” If the professors had their way, he warned, they would indoctrinate a new class of law students that would promote liberal ideals on benches across the country. This all added up to, Bork stated with thinly veiled disgust, “the gentrification of the Constitution.” Bork closed his remarks by outlining the constitutional means by which the New Right could overturn federal protection for abortion. Abortion and “acceptable sexual behavior” were matters for the states to decide—not constitutionally protected rights, as Roe v. Wade had recently found. Reproductive freedom, Bork advised, was “a classical case for local control. There is simply no national moral consensus about abortion, and there is not about to be.” Soon, the Reagan administration would call upon the students that Bork had trained to carry out this strategy of curtailing rights, one case at a time. Four decades later, the Roberts Court would echo Bork’s language when it struck down Roe. If the Federalist Society had begun as a campus alt-community, it quickly blossomed into something much more important. As Calabresi, one of its co-founders, later recalled, “Our conference was covered by the National Review and suddenly conservatives at fifteen other law schools began calling us and telling us they wanted to attend the conference and they wanted to form chapters, too. That was a process of almost spontaneous generation.” Less than a year after the 1982 Yale conference, 17 law schools across the country had a Federalist Society chapter. Soon after its inception, the student group was on the White House’s radar. In attendance at that first conference were several members of the Reagan Justice Department, including the future acting solicitor general and the next assistant attorney general at the Office of Legal Counsel. By 1985, all three founding members of the Federalist Society—Liberman, Calabresi, and McIntosh—had positions at DOJ. Half a century later, every sitting Supreme Court justice appointed by a Republican president is a member of the Federalist Society. During the first Trump presidency, 46 of his 54 nominees to the federal appeals courts were members. His White House counsel, two attorneys general, and deputy attorney general were all members as well. From that very first conference, the Federalist Society awoke a power lying dormant among marginalized conservatives. It offered them an identity, a larger community, and hope—clarifying the battle at hand and, most essentially, suggesting that they might win it. This article has been adapted from Alex Wagner’s new book, The Steal: Four Right-Wing Hard-Liners, One Republican Presidency, and the Raid on America's Courts. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: The Property-Tax Revolution
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 2.52
The United States is in the throes of the largest tax revolt in a generation, and the revolutionaries are winning. Since 2020, nationwide home values have climbed roughly 50 percent, leading property-tax bills to increase 19 percent and contributing to a 71 percent increase in the cost of homeowner’s insurance. At the same time, the price of gas, utilities, food, and everything else has risen, stamping out entrepreneurship, dimming the fertility rate, and making even six-figure earners feel financially strained. Homeowners have had enough, and grassroots groups have mobilized to turn private kvetching into public policy. Over the past four years, nearly two dozen states have slashed property taxes: Alabama by capping annual assessment increases, Colorado by lowering marginal rates, Indiana by creating credits, Nebraska by setting a limit on local collections, New York by sending checks to homeowners, Wyoming by carving out loopholes for seniors. My back-of-the-envelope accounting suggests that the measures have reduced property-tax revenue in those states by 7 percent, saving homeowners as much as $45 billion a year. This November, voters will consider a spate of similar proposals, the most radical one coming from legislators in Tallahassee, Florida. Amendment 3, popularly known as “Save Our Homes,” would raise the “homestead” exemption on owner-occupied properties in the state from $50,000 to $250,000, meaning a couple with a condo with an assessed value of $400,000 would pay their county’s property-tax rate on $150,000 of their home’s value, rather than on $350,000. The amendment would eliminate levies on more than half of dwellings. In time, Florida legislators want to phase out property taxes on owner-occupied homes entirely. Amendment 3 would give property owners a giant tax cut: $12 billion a year by one estimate. It would ease the local cost-of-living crisis too, its proponents argue. “Affordability is a problem for all Floridians,” Byron Donalds, a Republican congressman and the front-runner in the governor’s race, said on the stump last month. “It doesn’t matter what your politics are. It doesn’t matter what the color of your skin is. Because when taxes and insurance are more than principal and interest, you got a problem.” Yet what is being framed as a populist fight for affordability is in reality a form of class and generational warfare. Property-tax relief gives to the rich and takes from the poor. It aids seniors and harms children. It puts homeownership even further out of reach for many Americans, and it makes daily life even more expensive for low-income Americans. To be fair to the amendment’s supporters, these arguments are not exactly intuitive. The annual cost of owning a home has climbed precipitously. Millions of working-class and middle-income families own their home. If you cut property taxes, you reduce their costs. This much is true. Yet homeowners’ insurance and property taxes don’t function on a family’s balance sheet in the same way that rent, groceries, gas, cars, child care, and airfare do. Their cost goes up when familial wealth goes up. In Florida, real-estate appraisals have increased 83 percent since 2019, according to the state’s revenue department, suggesting that homeowners’ net worth has increased by trillions of dollars. Does public policy really need to solve the problem of rising taxes due to rising valuations? Is it even a problem at all? If retirees on fixed incomes can’t afford their insurance payments and families can’t figure out how to cover their tax bill, maybe. Yet the number of Florida homes and buildings that are delinquent on their property taxes has fallen slightly since 2020. The number of foreclosures has increased a bit, but remains low. The state’s housing market is fraying and distressed sales are increasing, but that’s because of climate change and mortgage rates, not tax assessments. Floridians may not like paying a higher tax bill, and carrying costs might be spurring some of them to downsize. But in general, property taxes are levied on people who can afford them. The typical homeowner earns twice as much as the typical renter, and has 43 times the net worth. Tenants are “the loser in all this,” Ken Johnson, a professor of finance at the University of Mississippi, told me. Many cities and counties offset lower taxes on owner-occupied properties with higher taxes on commercial residential properties. Landlords pass those costs on to their renters. The policy will also benefit longtime homeowners at the expense of prospective homebuyers. Low property taxes increase home prices, making it harder for people without a lot of money in the bank—such as new parents and just-married couples—to get approved for a mortgage. Then they remain tenants, subject to never-ending rent increases. In addition to distorting the housing market, Amendment 3 will devastate public finances. Property taxes provide 43 percent of revenue to Florida’s municipal general funds, the bank accounts that cities and counties use to finance day-to-day services. Amendment 3 will cut collections by as much as 30 percent, and will hit hardest in areas with a lot of homes and not a lot of commerce. To cover the $12 billion budget hole, cities and towns will likely raise or impose sales taxes and sin taxes; increase fees at the DMV, permit offices, registrars, and courts; charge more for waste removal and water; and put additional taxes on tourists. The state will trade out a solidly progressive, uniformly applied tax for an obscure, regressive mishmash of charges. But municipalities aren’t expected to make up all of the lost revenue. They’re expected to cut. Amendment 3 explicitly protects tax-financing streams for schools, meaning that cities and counties are contemplating draconian budget reductions for public-safety offices, libraries, after-school programs, summer camp, day care, flood prevention, public transit, roads, parks, senior services, homeless shelters, legal-aid clinics, domestic-violence shelters, and many other things. Austerity will be regressive too, harming the poor more than the wealthy. Rich Floridians aren’t relying on the bus to get to work. They’re not picking up free meals, taking adult-literacy classes at the library, or seeing a dentist at a pop-up clinic in a middle-school gymnasium either. In the worst-case scenario, State Senator Tina Polsky told me, cities and counties “wouldn’t have enough money to keep going, even to pay their elected officials.” They would need to merge, or “come begging in Tallahassee, and those with the best lobbyists and the best connections are going to get the money.” Add the possibility of a recession to that worst case. In a downturn, Florida would have no revenue from individual income taxes. (Florida voters banned them in a 1924 constitutional amendment.) It would have less income from property taxes than it did before. Yields from sales, corporate, and tourist taxes would fall. The state’s revenue base would collapse, meaning cuts to public services and layoffs and a secondary decline in consumer spending, leading the revenue base to shrink even more. Despite these risks, Amendment 3 is expected to pass, as are many similar measures on the ballot in November. Voters have approved 78 percent of statewide property-tax measures in recent years. No wonder: Americans hate inflation and love homeownership. They believe in higher taxes, but also think other people should be the ones paying them. They may not perceive the connection between slashing property taxes and cuts to services, rising sales taxes, and increasing fees. They don’t understand that slashing property taxes means gutting the most effective wealth tax the country has, or taking from the poor to give to the rich. “It is an intellectual challenge to figure out ways to talk about these things, if you even have the guts to talk about them at all,” Texas State Senator Nathan Johnson, the solitary holdout on a property-tax relief measure that passed last year, told me. Maybe California could convince them. Back in 1978, state residents revolted against a brutal cost-of-living crisis, a miserable housing market, and ever-increasing tax bills. By a two-to-one margin, they passed Proposition 13, which capped most property-tax rates at 1 percent, reset assessments to their 1976 level, and barred assessments from increasing more than 2 percent a year, unless a property changes hands or a new structure is built. Prop 13 broke California. It nudged homeowners to remain in their properties for as long as possible, freezing neighborhoods in amber and trapping would-be buyers in rentals. (One recent study found that raising California’s average property-tax rate from 0.8 percent to 2 percent would increase the state’s homeownership rate by 4.6 percent.) It starved towns and cities of revenue, prompting them to rely on less progressive, less reliable, less equitable, and more distortionary taxes. It helped Boomers and it hurt younger generations. (I would say, “It helped Boomers and hurt their grandchildren,” but that would not be literally true. In California, Pappy and Gamma can bequeath their home to Junior without triggering a property-tax reassessment, meaning the state directly subsidizes dynastic fortunes.) Perhaps most salient: Prop 13 made California less affordable, radically so. It stymied real-estate development and created a trillion-dollar incentive for property owners to fight against reform. What California did two generations ago might be the best argument against what Florida and other states are doing today. With these property-tax measures, well-off families are helping themselves now and hurting everyone else tomorrow.

item.title: The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Science Score: 2.43
Confronted with a seasoned, boiled, arguably delicious crayfish, some of the people of the Netherlands are not sure exactly what to do. “Do you suck the head out?” I heard from the table next to me earlier this summer, at Two Chefs, a restaurant in Amsterdam that hosts a monthly crayfish boil.
Yes is the answer: The best way to eat a crayfish is to shell the tail, then slurp the flavored juices out of the head, and pick out the remaining meat with your hands. This strategy might not be an immediate transatlantic hit. At the boil, one 29-year-old from Maastricht likened the meal to shrimp but with more work. Two twins told me that the crayfish would need to look a little more chic on the plate to appeal to the Dutch public. But, given the ever-growing population of crayfish in the Netherlands, coming around to eating more of them could benefit the country. Because if Dutch consumers aren’t sure how they feel about crayfish, crayfish inarguably love the Netherlands. They have invaded the country’s waterways so thoroughly that they have become a real problem, and dealing with them will mean persuading more creatures—including Dutch people—to eat more crayfish. The crayfish invasion started decades ago, but in recent years, the red swamp crayfish (also known as the Louisiana crawfish) has become a particular pest, Pim Lemmers, an ecologist at Radboud University who has dedicated his career to researching crayfish, told me. In the 1980s, it was brought to the Netherlands as food, and people naively released the animals into the environment. The waterways in the Netherlands are very interconnected and became a “crayfish highway” of sorts, Ivo Roessink, an aquatic ecotoxicologist at Wageningen University & Research, told me. But crayfish can walk and breathe on land, too, and have been spotted in parks, along bike lanes, and at Schiphol airport, where the birds use the runway to crush them. And they can dig—burrows up to three feet long that can collapse the edges of fields into the water and that some people fear could damage the country’s extensive system of dams, dikes, and canals. Scientists emphasize that the risk to dams and dikes is low; from their point of view, the bigger risk is to other creatures that live in the water. Crayfish are omnivorous: “They totally destroy underwater vegetation,” Roessink said. They also eat detritus, amphibian and insect larvae, snails and other invertebrates, small fish, and one another—a sight I witnessed for myself. But crayfish cannibalism will not end the invasion; in fact, although the Netherlands’ central government is working on a program for crayfish management, getting rid of the species will likely be impossible. “I know of one example where they effectively eradicated crayfish, and that was in the U.S.,” Roessink said. “There was an infected pond, and they turned it into a parking lot.” (Resorting to this solution in the Netherlands would require paving over the entire country.) Research in the Netherlands and elsewhere has shown that even extensive trapping won’t necessarily eliminate crayfish. The most anyone can hope for is fewer of them. Some water boards of the Netherlands are trying to persuade all sorts of creatures to eat more crayfish, including herons, eels, and European catfish, which are themselves something of an invasive threat. And, in theory, one of the crayfish’s most effective predators could be Dutch people. Stefan van Ekris and Maarten van der Sanden, who are both managing directors at CrawFish Farm Holland, are trying their best to make it happen. This July, I joined them as they put on waders and immersed themselves in irrigation ditches to set and check their crayfish nets in the Groene Hart, or “Green Heart,” of the Netherlands, the thinly populated pastures and peatlands among some of the country’s largest cities. They get paid per kilogram caught—the expedition I joined yielded about 150 kilograms, or 330 pounds, of live crayfish—but this is really a passion project for them. CrawFish Farm Holland is approved to sell live and prepared catch directly to restaurants and other wholesalers, and hopes to sell its crayfish in supermarkets in the next two years. “We’re not cultivating them,” Van der Sanden told me. “We’re fighting them and eating them.” In America, Van der Sanden pointed out, Louisiana was able to quickly ramp up crayfish production and demand in the 1980s. But the scientists I spoke with were skeptical of this strategy. “You will never eat yourself out of this crisis,” Roessink said. And if people like crayfish too much, Lemmers said, they might start cultivating crayfish in their backyard or trapping them without oversight, which could promote further spread. Even if more Dutch people come around to the pleasures of a messy boil, the crayfish still could come out ahead. The image originally accompanying this article did not show a red swamp crayfish. That image has been replaced.

item.title: AI’s Code-Red Moment
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Score: 4.68
Four days after a researcher publicly quit his job at Anthropic, warning that top AI firms are not “acting responsibly” and that their products might be on track to “kill us all,” the company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, seemed to basically agree. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a 3,800-word essay that he published today on his personal website and posted to social media. By now, we’ve all become accustomed to AI-industry figures issuing dire prophecies about the power of their products. Yet Amodei’s essay stands out for its urgency and for the moment at which it arrived. Worries about AI agents running amok have gone from hypothetical to real after OpenAI, Anthropic, and others reported alarming incidents in recent weeks. The question now is whether Amodei’s warning will have any more impact than past warnings, which is to say, any at all. There are reasons to believe it could. Amodei spelled out a three-step plan for what he called “pacing the frontier,” or tempering the speed at which top AI models improve in order to prioritize safety precautions. He argued that this would reduce the chances of things going awry—such as when an OpenAI model spawned swarms of AI agents that worked together in secret to hack into another company’s systems and cheat on an internal test. He said the top AI firms, including his own, are locked in a dangerous “race to the bottom” that could lead to more serious cyberattacks, such as a full takeover of the internet. He called instead for a “race to the top”—a phrase that President Obama once used for his education policy—in which firms vie to develop the safest models rather than the most powerful ones. “The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy,” Amodei wrote. “But I believe we owe it to humanity to try.” The first step in his plan entails AI labs committing to bringing in outside monitors to look out for hazards; he said Anthropic will commit to that right now and hopes rivals will join. The second step involves AI firms in democratic countries agreeing—maybe with support from their governments—to certain limits and safety standards. The last and tallest order is “global coordination,” which mostly means getting China to buy in somehow.
